## Page 2475

what he intends is true and accords with what the messengers brought and with the Book and the Sunnah, whether in negation or affirmation, we accept it. But if it is false and contradicts what the Book and the Sunnah teach, whether in negation or affirmation, we prohibit saying it.

They held that the approach presented in the Quran accords with clear reason and authentic revelation, and that it is the approach of the prophets and messengers. The messengers—may Allah’s blessings be upon them—brought general negation and detailed affirmation. Hence He, glorified and exalted, says:

“Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they ascribe to Him. And peace be upon the messengers. And praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds.”

He thus declared Himself far above what those who oppose the messengers ascribe to Him, and pronounced peace upon the messengers because their statements were free of deficiency and fault. The messengers’ approach is the one presented in the Quran: Allah Most High affirms His attributes in detail in the Quran, while denying, in general terms, that anything resembles Him or is His equal.

In the Quran, He states that He knows all things and has power over all things; that He is Almighty, All-Wise, All-Forgiving, Most Merciful; that He is All-Hearing, All-Seeing; that He is All-Forgiving, Most Loving; and that He, exalted in the greatness of His essence, loves the believers and is pleased with them, while He is angry with the disbelievers and displeased with them. He states that He created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne; that He spoke directly to Moses; and that He manifested Himself to the mountain and made it crumble—and other such statements.

By way of negation, He says:

“There is nothing like Him.”

“Do you know of any equal to Him?”

“So do not draw comparisons with Allah.”

“Say: He is Allah, One.”

“Allah, the Self-Sufficient, upon whom all depend.”

“He neither begets nor is born.”

“And there is none comparable to Him.”

Thus He affirms His attributes and denies any likeness to created beings.

---

## Page 2476

The approach of the early generations was to describe Allah as He described Himself and, at times, as His Messenger described Him, without distortion or denial, and without specifying how His attributes are or likening Him to created beings.

Those who oppose the messengers describe Him through negations: “He is not this; He is not that.” When they are told, “Then affirm what He is,” they say, “He is absolute existence,” or, “An essence without attributes.” Yet clear reason establishes that what is absolute on condition of absoluteness exists only in the mind, not in concrete reality. What is absolute without any condition does not exist externally as an absolute, but only as a determinate particular. In their account, the Lord has no reality distinct from created beings. Rather, they either deny Him altogether or make Him the existence of created beings, a part of them, or an attribute of them.

As for ambiguous expressions, they withhold judgment on their meaning. Thus, when some people say, “Allah is in a direction or a spatial location,” and others say, “Allah is neither in a direction nor in a spatial location,” they ask each speaker what he intends, since the terms “direction” and “spatial location” are ambiguous and have multiple meanings.

They say: Nothing exists except the Creator and creation. Allah Most High is transcendent and separate from His creatures. He, glorified be He, created them separate and distinct from Himself, outside His essence. Nothing of His essence is within His creatures, and nothing of His creatures is within His essence. Were He not separate from them, He would either be intermingled with them, indwelling in them, or a locus in which they dwell. Allah Most High is far above that. Alternatively, if He were neither separate from them nor intermingled with them, He would be nonexistent. Allah Most High is far above that.

The Jahmiyyah, who deny the attributes, sometimes make statements that entail indwelling and union, or explicitly affirm

---

## Page 2477

this; at other times, they make statements that entail denial and the negation of His attributes. Thus, those among them who deny worship nothing, while those who affirm worship everything. It is also said: Since nothing exists except the Creator and creation, the Creator is separate from creation.

If someone says, “He is in a direction,” or, “He is not in a direction,” he is asked: “Does ‘direction’ refer to something existent or nonexistent?” If it is something existent, then—since nothing exists except the Creator and creation, and the Creator is separate from creation—the Lord is not within an existent, created direction. If direction is something nonexistent, in that what lies beyond the world is called a direction, then if the Creator is separate from the world, and what lies beyond the world is called a direction without being something existent, Allah would be in a nonexistent direction in this sense.

Yet there is no difference between saying, “He is within something nonexistent,” and saying, “He is not within anything other than Himself,” for all rational people agree that what is nonexistent is not a thing.

There is no doubt that by the word “direction” they sometimes mean something existent and sometimes something nonexistent. Indeed, a single speaker may combine both meanings in his discourse. Once the ambiguity is removed, the truth of the matter becomes clear. If someone says, “If He were in a direction, that direction would be coeternal with Him,” he is told: “That would follow if ‘direction’ meant something existent other than Him. Allah is not in a direction in this sense.”

If he says, “If He could be seen, He would be in a direction, and that is impossible,” he is told: “If you mean that He would be in an existent direction, then that is impossible. For something existent can be seen even if it is not within another existent thing. The world, for example, has a surface that can be seen, yet it is not within another world.”

If he says: “I mean that He must be in what is called a direction, even if it is nonexistent; for if He were

---

## Page 2478

separate from the world, what lies beyond the world would be called a direction.”

He is asked: “Why, then, do you say that His being in a direction in this sense would be impossible?”

If he replies, “Because whatever is separate from the world and can be seen must be a body or spatially located,” the discussion returns to the terms “body” and “spatially located,” just as it returned to the term “direction.”

He is then told: “The term ‘spatially located’ may refer to something encompassed by something else, or to something distinct from something else—and thus spatially separate from it. If you intend the former meaning, He—glory be to Him—is not spatially located, for He is separate from created things and nothing else encompasses Him. If you intend the latter, He—glory be to Him—is distinct and separate from created things; He neither inheres in them nor is united with them.”

These distinctions remove confusion and misrepresentation. Otherwise, anyone who denies any of the names or attributes calls whoever affirms them a corporealist who maintains that Allah is spatially located and in a direction. Thus, the Mu'tazilah and others like them call those who affirm the attributes—who say that Allah Most High is living by virtue of life, knowing by virtue of knowledge, powerful by virtue of power, hearing by virtue of hearing, seeing by virtue of sight, and speaking by virtue of speech—corporealists, anthropomorphists, and Hashwiyyah. Those who affirm the attributes include the early generations, the imams, and all the groups that affirm the attributes, such as the Kullābiyyah, Karrāmiyyah, Ash'ariyyah, Sālimiyyah, and other groups within the Muslim community.

Those who deny the attributes among the Jahmiyyah, the Mu'tazilah, and a group of philosophers said to these affirmers: “If you affirm life, power, and speech for Him, these are accidents, and accidents can subsist only in a body. If you say that He can be seen, vision can only be of something directly beheld in a direction, and this entails corporealism.”

If the Ash'arīs and their followers say, “We affirm these attributes but do not call them accidents, because an accident is something that occurs in its subject, whereas these attributes endure and do not cease,” the deniers reply: “This is a verbal dispute. In your own usage, accidents are divided into those inseparable from their subject, never leaving it—so long as

---

## Page 2479

its subject exists—and those that may depart from their subject. The former include a body’s spatial location, or indeed a human being’s animality and rationality: as long as he remains human, these attributes never leave him.

As for your claim that an accident cannot persist for two successive instants, this is a position in which you stand alone among all rational people. You have obstinately denied sensory evidence, resorting to sophistry to escape these decisive objections. Moreover, you maintain that its like is continually renewed; yet this is precisely what it means for an accident to persist. This resembles your assertion that He is seen without the beholder either facing Him or having his back to Him, and without turning toward Him in any direction. Here too, you stand alone among rational people and obstinately deny both sensory evidence and reason.”

The deniers said to them: “You have either affirmed what entails corporealism, anthropomorphism, and the views of the Hashwiyyah, or denied that entailment, thereby contradicting clear reason and self-evident necessity. This is why the most discerning among you have concluded that you actually agree with us in denying that Allah Most High can be seen, but outwardly affirm it because it is the well-known position of the ‘Hashwiyyah,’ who are known as the people of the Sunnah and the community, so that you may be counted among them. Alternatively, you have affirmed it in contradiction to your own principles. Thus, you waver between self-contradiction and dissimulation.”

If a person agrees with those who deny the attributes but affirms Allah’s most beautiful names—as the Mu‘tazilah do, who are leading authorities in speculative theology—those who deny Allah’s most beautiful names call him an anthropomorphist, a Hashwī, and a corporealist. This is what the Hākimī Bātinī Qarmatians and others have done. They said: “If you say that He is existent, knowing, living, and powerful, this amounts to advocating anthropomorphism, corporealism, and the views of the Hashwiyyah, since it makes Him resemble other, created beings. Moreover, no existent, living, knowing, powerful being can be conceived of except as a body, and these names necessarily entail attributes, while attributes necessarily entail corporealism.”

---

## Page 2480

If a man is among those who deny the names and attributes—as do the extreme Jahmiyyah, the Qarmatians, and the philosophers—he must nevertheless affirm that He exists. The deniers then say to him: “You are a corporealist, an anthropomorphist, and a Hashwī! For if He exists, other beings share with Him in the meaning of existence, and that constitutes resemblance; moreover, nothing existent can be conceived of except as a body or something subsisting in a body.”

He would then have to say: “He is neither existent nor non-existent, neither living nor dead,” or: “He is neither existent nor not existent, neither living nor not living.” This entails denying both sides of a contradiction, as well as opposites equivalent to contradictories. This is among the most manifest absurdities according to self-evident reason. Moreover, the logic of their position entails likening Him to impossibilities, for that which is neither existent nor non-existent can have no reality whatsoever—neither existent nor non-existent. Rather, it is merely something conceived in the mind, with no realization in external reality. All this is in addition to the outright disbelief to which he has committed himself.

Even if he were to deny necessary, beginningless existence altogether, then, besides committing the disbelief that is the root of all disbelief, he would be obstinately rejecting self-evident truths. For we observe existing things and know that every existent is either beginningless or originated, and either necessarily existent in itself or contingent in itself and existent through another. Everything originated and contingent in itself exists through another, and thus necessarily requires something beginningless and necessarily existent in itself. Existence therefore necessarily entails affirming a beginningless existent.

Some existence is contingent and originated, as we observe in originated things such as animals and plants. Thus, once it is known by rational necessity that among existing things there is that which is beginningless and necessarily existent in itself, and that which is originated and contingent in itself, these two existents share in what is denoted by the term

---

## Page 2481

existence, while each is distinguished from the other by its particular existence. Whoever fails to affirm both what these two existents have in common and what distinguishes them must hold either that all existing things are beginningless and necessarily existent in themselves, or that they are all originated, contingent, and dependent on something else. Both conclusions are self-evidently false. It is therefore necessary to affirm commonality in one respect and distinction in another.

We know that what distinguishes the existent Creator from all other existing things is far greater than what distinguishes those other things from one another. Thus, if the “king” and the “mosquito” share in the meanings of existence and being alive despite the disparity between them, then the Creator—glory be to Him—is all the more distinct from created beings, even though there is commonality in some names and attributes.

---

## Page 2482

Section

With this premise established, it becomes clear that the statement, “Anything that rational proof establishes as implying corporeality is ambiguous,” is an answer that neither settles the dispute nor yields any benefit, nor distinguishes the sound from the unsound or the deviant from the upright.

For everyone who denies any of the names and attributes claims to possess rational proof that what he denies implies corporeality and is therefore ambiguous. This would require treating all the names and attributes as ambiguous. In turn, this would entail complete negation: no meaning could be understood from Allah’s names and attributes, nor could any distinction be drawn between the meanings of the Ever-Living, the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, the Most Merciful, the Compeller, and the Source of Peace; nor between creation and rising over, on the one hand, and causing death and giving life, on the other; nor between coming and arrival, on the one hand, and pardon and forgiveness, on the other.

To explain: those who deny the attributes among the Jahmiyyah, the Mu‘tazilah, the esoteric Qarmatians, and the philosophers who agree with them say:

“If you say that the Quran is uncreated and that Allah Most High possesses knowledge, power, and will, then you have ascribed corporeality to Him. For rational proof has established that this implies corporeality, since these are properties that do not subsist independently, but only in something else—whether they are called attributes, accidents, or anything else.”

---

## Page 2483

They say:
“We can conceive of a property subsisting only in a body. Thus, affirming a property that subsists in something other than a body is inconceivable.”

If someone who affirms these attributes says:
“Rather, these properties can subsist in something other than a body, just as both we and you can affirm a knowing, powerful being who is not a body,”

then those who affirm pleasure, anger, the Face, the Hand, rising over, coming, and other such attributes say:
“Affirm these attributes as well, and say that they subsist in something other than a body.”

If they say:
“We can conceive of pleasure and anger only as subsisting in a heart, which is a body; and we can conceive of a face and a hand only as parts of a body,”

they are told:
“Nor can we conceive of knowledge or power except as subsisting in a body; nor can we conceive of hearing, sight, or speech except as subsisting in a body. Why, then, have you distinguished between like things? You say, ‘These can subsist in something other than a body, whereas those can subsist only in a body,’ although both are alike from the standpoint of reason.”

If they say:
“Anger is the boiling of the heart’s blood in pursuit of vengeance, and the face is that which has a nose, two lips, a tongue, and a cheek,” or something similar,

they are told:
“If you mean the servant’s anger and face, the corresponding argument against you would be: sight is conceivable only through an eyeball, hearing only through an ear canal, speech only through two lips and a tongue, and will only for securing a benefit or warding off harm. Yet you affirm hearing, sight, speech, and will for the Lord in a manner unlike the servant’s attributes. If what you affirm resembles the servant’s attributes, you are committed to likening Him to creation in all these attributes. But if you affirm them in a manner befitting the majesty of Allah Most High, without any resemblance to the attributes of created beings, then affirm them all in this specified manner. There is no distinction between one attribute and another, for what you have denied

---

## Page 2484

of the attributes carries the same implications for you as what you have affirmed. Either you deny all the attributes—which is impossible—or you liken Him to created beings—which is impossible—or you affirm them all in a manner unique to Him, in which none resembles Him. In that case, there is no distinction between one attribute and another. Distinguishing between them by affirming one and denying another to avoid likening Him to creation and attributing corporeality to Him is a false position: it distinguishes between like things and renders the two claims contradictory.”

If someone says:
“Rational evidence establishes one but not the other—as when it is said that it establishes life, knowledge, and will, but not pleasure, anger, and similar attributes.”

The answer has several aspects:

(First: The absence of evidence does not entail the absence of what it would establish. Suppose that reason does not establish one of these attributes; neither reason nor revelation establishes its negation either. It therefore cannot be denied. Rather, it must be affirmed if evidence establishes it; otherwise, judgment must be suspended.

(Second: It may be said that rational evidence can be adduced for His love, hatred, wisdom, mercy, and other attributes, just as it can for His will, as has been explained elsewhere.

(Third: It may be said that revelation establishes these attributes, while reason does not negate them. Evidence free of any countervailing proof must therefore be accepted.

If he then says:
“Rather, reason does negate them, because these attributes necessarily entail attributing corporeality to Him, and reason rules that out.”

He is told:
“What is said about these attributes that you deny is like what is said about the attributes that I affirm. For if this necessarily entails

---

## Page 2485

attributing corporeality to Him, so does the other; and if it does not entail attributing corporeality to Him, neither does the other. To claim a distinction between them on the grounds that one entails likening Him to creation or attributing corporeality to Him while the other does not is to distinguish between like things and combine contradictions. For what he denies in one, he affirms in the other, and what he affirms in one, he denies in the other. Thus he combines contradictions.”

For this reason, scholars of thorough understanding have said:

“Whoever denies any of the names and attributes established by the Quran and Sunnah inevitably contradicts himself. The very argument he uses to deny what he denies applies equally to what he affirms. If the rational argument for denial is valid, all must be denied; if it is not, none of them need be denied. Affirming something while denying its like is an invalid contradiction.”

If the Mu‘tazilī says:

“The attributes imply corporeality, because attributes are accidents that can subsist only in a body. This is why I interpret the texts concerning the attributes figuratively, but not those concerning the names.”

He is told:

“The same consequence follows for you regarding the names. The very argument by which you infer that one possessing life, knowledge, and power can only be a body is used by your opponent to infer that the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, the Ever-Living can only be a body.”

You are therefore told:

“Affirming One who is living, knowing, and powerful must either entail attributing corporeality to Him or not. If it does, you must affirm that He is a body; thus He would not be bounded with respect to being seen, on either supposition. If it does not, it may equally be said that affirming knowledge, power, and will does not entail attributing corporeality to Him. If the one does not entail it, neither does the other; and if the one entails it, so does the other. There is therefore no distinction between them. To distinguish between them is a manifest contradiction.”

If the Jahmī, the Qarmatī, and the philosopher who agrees with them say:

“I deny the names

---

## Page 2486

and attributes alike.” He is told:

“You cannot deny all names, for your mind must refer to what you affirm, and your tongue must express it. If you say, ‘real, existent, actual, known, eternal, necessarily existent’—whatever you say, you have named Him. Suppose you do not speak at all: either you affirm in your mind an eternal, necessarily existent being, or you do not. If you do not, existence would be devoid of an eternal, necessarily existent Originator. All existing things would then have come into being and would be contingent. Yet it is known of necessity that whatever comes into being and is contingent can exist only through an eternal, necessarily existent being. Your denial of Him thus entails affirming Him. Moreover, this is outright disbelief and negation, which no rational person would profess.”

If you say:

“I do not entertain this question in my mind, nor do I speak of it.”

You are told:

“Your mind’s refusal to know and your tongue’s refusal to speak do not overturn realities or cause existing things to cease to exist. For whatever is true, existent, and established within yourself remains so, whether you know it or are ignorant of it, remember it or forget it. This amounts only to ignorance of Allah Most High, heedlessness of His remembrance, turning away from Him, and disbelief in Him. It does not mean that He is not, in Himself, real and existent, possessing the most beautiful names and the most exalted attributes.”

There is no doubt that this is the ultimate outcome for the Qarmatian esotericists and the eternalist deniers: they remain in the darkness of ignorance and the error of disbelief, neither knowing Allah nor remembering Him. They have no evidence for denying Him or His names and attributes, for that would be a categorical denial, whereas they make no such categorical assertion and have no evidence for denial. They have turned away from His names and signs and have become ignorant of Him, disbelieving in Him and heedless of His remembrance—their hearts dead to knowing Him, loving Him, and worshipping Him.

---

## Page 2487

Then, if they do this, claiming that it is to avoid “likening Allah to creation and attributing a body to Him,” they are told:

“What you have fled to is worse than what you have fled from. Acknowledging the Creator, in whatever manner, is better than denying Him.

“Moreover, if this observable world, including the heavens and the earth, is eternal and necessarily existent in itself, then you have made observable bodies eternal and necessarily existent in themselves. This is worse than what you sought to escape. If, however, it is not eternal and necessarily existent in itself, it must have a Creator who is eternal and necessarily existent in Himself. It then becomes clear that knowing Him and speaking of Him—affirming the Lord in heart and speech—is undoubtedly true, according to both revelation and reason. If this necessarily entails what you call likening Him to creation and attributing a body to Him, then whatever necessarily follows from truth is itself true. If it does not entail this, you can affirm Him without such language.”

Thus, the inconsistency of those who negate the attributes becomes evident, however the proofs are brought to bear against them. So too does the inconsistency of those who affirm some attributes but not others.

If the “negators” say, “We denied the attributes only because our proof that the world came into being and that the Creator exists also demonstrated that these attributes must be denied. We established the Creator’s existence through the world’s having come into being; we established that the world came into being only by establishing that bodies came into being; and we established that bodies came into being only through the coming into being of attributes, which are accidents.”

Or they say:

“We established that bodies came into being only through the coming into being of actions, which are motions, and through the fact that whatever admits them is never without them, while whatever is never without things that come into being must itself have come into being. Alternatively, whatever admits coming, arrival, and descent would be characterized by motion; whatever is characterized by motion is never without either motion or its opposite, rest; and whatever is never without things that come into being must itself have come into being. Once it was established that bodies came into being, we said that whatever is brought into being must have one who brings it into being. Through this, we established the Creator’s existence;

---

## Page 2488

so if we were to ascribe to Him attributes or actions subsisting in Him, it would be possible for actions and attributes to subsist in the Eternal One. In that case, this would no longer constitute evidence that bodies came into being, and the proof for affirming the attributes would be invalidated.”

They are answered as follows:

The reply has several aspects:

(First: The invalidity of this particular proof does not entail the invalidity of all proofs. There are many ways to establish the Creator’s existence, whose details cannot all be encompassed, even though their general categories can be.

Second: None of the Companions, the Successors, or the leading scholars of the Muslims used this proof. If knowing the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and believing in Him depended upon it, this would entail that they neither knew Allah nor believed in Him. By the consensus of the Muslims, this is among the gravest forms of disbelief.

Third: The Prophets and Messengers did not command anyone to follow this path. If knowledge of Allah depended upon it—and such knowledge is obligatory—then following this path would be obligatory. If such knowledge were recommended, following this path would be recommended. Had it been obligatory or recommended, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have prescribed it. Had it been prescribed, the Companions would have transmitted it.

---

## Page 2489

Chapter: An Overview of the Doctrines of the Various Groups and Their Sources

Regarding the divine attributes and Allah’s oneness, denial of the attributes is, broadly speaking, the position of “the philosophers, the Muʿtazila, and other Jahmīs,” although there are certain differences between the philosophers and the Muʿtazila. Likewise, the Baghdad and Basra schools differ concerning hearing and sight—whether they constitute knowledge or a perception distinct from knowledge—and concerning will.

This is the doctrine that the early generations call “the position of Jahm,” because he was the first to propagate it within Islam. Elsewhere, I have explained the chain through which he received it: it derives from the Sabian philosophers, the polytheist Brahmins, and the Jewish sorcerers.

Affirmation of the attributes, broadly speaking, is the doctrine of “those who affirm the attributes”: the Kullābīs, Ashʿarīs, Karrāmīs, scholars of hadith, the majority of Sufis and Hanbalis, most Mālikīs and Shāfiʿīs apart from rare exceptions among them, and many—or most—Hanafīs. It is also the position of [the Salafiyya] (*). However, taking affirmation to the point of likening Allah to His creation is the position of extremists among the Rāfida, ignorant adherents of hadith, and certain others who have deviated. Between the denial of the Jahmīs and the affirmation of those who liken Allah to His creation, there are varying degrees.

> **Footnotes:**
> (*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd (p. 257) said: Perhaps the correct reading is “the view of the Sālimiyya.”

---

## Page 2490

“As for the Ash'arīs,” some of them agreed with them concerning the attributes known through transmitted reports, and the majority agreed with them concerning the attributes reported in hadith. Regarding the attributes mentioned in the Quran, however, they hold two positions: al-Ash'arī, al-Bāqillānī, and their early adherents affirm them, while some acknowledge only some of them.

Yet they also exhibit Jahmī tendencies in another respect. Al-Ash'arī absorbed the speculative theology of al-Jubbā'ī, the leading Mu'tazilī scholar, and both his followers and others acknowledge his theological affiliation with him. Ibn al-Bāqillānī is the foremost in affirming the attributes after al-Ash'arī in his “al-Ibāna” (The Elucidation). After Ibn al-Bāqillānī comes Ibn Fūrak, who affirmed some of the attributes mentioned in the Quran.

“As for al-Juwaynī” and those who followed his approach, they inclined toward the Mu'tazilī doctrine. Abū al-Ma'ālī read Abū Hāshim’s books extensively but had little knowledge of transmitted reports; these two factors combined to influence him. Al-Qushayrī was a student of Ibn Fūrak. Thus, from that time onward, al-Ash'arī’s school grew harsher, and estrangement arose between it and the Hanbalis after they had previously been on friendly terms, or at least at peace with one another.

And “as for the Hanbalis, Abū 'Abd Allāh ibn Hāmid was firm and earnest in affirming the attributes, with a particular inclination toward questions concerning the attributes known through transmitted reports. His companion, Judge Abū Ya'lā, followed his approach, but was milder than he and less inclined to go beyond bounds in affirmation. As for Abū 'Abd Allāh ibn Batta, his approach was purely that of the hadith scholars, such as Abū Bakr

---

## Page 2491

al-Ājurrī in “al-Sharī'a” (The Sacred Law), and al-Lālakā'ī in al-Sunan (The Traditions). Al-Khallāl likewise followed an approach close to his, and Shaykh Abū Muhammad and the later hadith scholars incline toward his approach.

[“As for the Tamīmīs,” such as Abū al-Hasan, Ibn Abī al-Fadl, and Ibn Rizq Allāh] (*), they are less inclined toward affirmation, more disposed to agree with others, and more accommodating toward them. Hence the Sufis follow them, and distinguished Ash'arīs, such as al-Bāqillānī and al-Bayhaqī, incline toward them. Indeed, the account of Ahmad’s creed written by Abū al-Fadl is the one upon which al-Bayhaqī relied. Nevertheless, these men follow the Sunnah.

As for Ibn 'Aqīl, if he deviates, a strong Mu'tazilī strain enters his discussions of the divine attributes, divine decree, and the miraculous gifts granted to Allah’s righteous servants—to the point that al-Ash'arī’s statements are sounder than his and closer to the Sunnah.

Al-Ash'arī professed allegiance solely to the school of the hadith scholars, whose imam, in his view, was Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Abū Bakr 'Abd al-'Azīz and others made statements in their debates indicating that they regarded him as one of the speculative theologians among the hadith scholars, rather than as someone separate from them. In earlier times they were close to one another, although some of them criticized him for things they might likewise criticize in one of their own who ventured into speculative theology, because of the religious innovation involved. Nevertheless, the foundations of his doctrine do not conform to the pure Sunnah; rather, they fall short of it in well-known ways.

In what they affirm of the Sunnah, the “Ash'arīs” are dependent upon the Hanbalis, just as the speculative theologians among the Hanbalis are dependent upon them for the rational analogies they use as arguments. The division arose only because of the turmoil surrounding al-Qushayrī.
