## Page 2543

Section

As for the assertion:

“If acts subsisted in Him, He would be a locus of temporally originated events. If a temporally originated event entailed a perfection for Him, He would have lacked that perfection before it occurred, which is a deficiency. If it did not entail a perfection for Him, it would not be permissible to attribute it to Him.”

The first response is that this argument is countered by its counterpart concerning the temporally originated events He brings about. Both come into being through His power and will; they differ only in their locus. This same dilemma applies in both cases.

If the distinction proposed is, “The effect produced is not an attribute of Him, unlike an act subsisting in Him,” the answer is: Rather, they do ascribe attributes of action to Him, dividing attributes into intrinsic attributes and attributes of action. Thus, they describe Him as Creator and Provider after He had not been so. This dilemma therefore applies to them. Indeed, the philosophers raised it against them concerning “the temporal origination of the world,” whereupon they claimed that attributes of action are attributes of neither perfection nor deficiency.

They may therefore be given the same answer that they gave these others: the “acts” that subsist in Him are neither a perfection nor a deficiency.

If it is said, “He must be characterized by either deficiency or perfection,” the reply is: “He must be characterized, in respect of

---

## Page 2544

attributes of action, by either deficiency or perfection. If one may claim that either of the two falls into neither category, the same claim may be made for the other. Otherwise, the answer applies equally to both.”

As for the “philosophers,” they may be told: According to you, the eternal is not indwelt by temporally originated events, yet it has always been a locus of such events. Thus, in your view, eternity does not preclude this. Indeed, you regard this as the “possible perfection” beyond which no other is possible. They deny it of the Necessary Existent only because they think He is not characterized by it. The invalidity of their position on this has already been indicated, particularly since whatever is the locus of successive temporally originated events cannot derive its existence from an eternal, complete cause that necessarily produces its effect. For the effect of a complete, necessitating cause—or any part of that effect—cannot come after the cause. Whenever any part of its effect comes after it, it is a cause of that effect potentially, not actually; and its becoming an actual cause requires another cause.

If it is He Himself who brings it from potentiality into actuality, then there is something potential in Him, and He is the one who actualizes it. This entails that He is receptive or active, which they disallow because they hold attributes—which they call composition—to be impossible. If someone other than Him brings Him into actuality, that is necessarily impossible, as all agree, because it contradicts necessary existence and entails “simultaneous circular dependence” and an “infinite regress of efficient causes.”

If He became the agent producing a particular thing after not having been its agent, He could not be an eternal, complete cause. Thus, the eternity of anything in the world would entail His being a complete cause from eternity. That, in turn, would entail that nothing temporally originated could proceed from Him, whether through an intermediary or without one. This contradicts what is observed.

---

## Page 2545

Secondly, in refuting the claim that the occurrence of temporally originated events is impossible, it may be said:

This rests on the renewal of these matters through the renewal of relations, states, and privations, for people agree that these matters undergo renewal. Al-Āmidī distinguished between the two verbally, saying: “These are temporally originated events, while those are renewals.” Verbal distinctions, however, do not affect substantive truths.

It may therefore be said: If the renewal of these things confers perfection on Him, then He previously lacked that perfection, which is a deficiency. If it confers deficiency on Him, He cannot be characterized by it.

Thirdly, it may be said:

The perfection with which He must be characterized is that whose existence is possible. As for what is impossible, it is not a perfection with which any existing being can be characterized. It is impossible for the temporally originated events connected with His power and will to exist all together from eternity. Their absence from eternity is therefore not a deficiency, because the absence of what is impossible is no deficiency.

Fourthly, it may be said:

If we posit a being that performs one act after another and is itself capable of acting, and another being that cannot itself do anything, but is like an inanimate object incapable of movement, the former is more perfect than the latter. The absence of these acts is therefore necessarily a deficiency, whereas their existence, insofar as it is possible, is perfection.

Fifthly, it may be said:

We do not concede that their absence is, without qualification, either a deficiency or a perfection, nor that their existence is, without qualification, either a deficiency or a perfection. Rather, their existence at the time determined by His will and power

---

## Page 2546

and wisdom is perfection, whereas their existence otherwise is a deficiency. Their absence when wisdom requires their absence is perfection, and their existence when wisdom requires their existence is perfection. Since the existence of one and the same thing may sometimes be a perfection and sometimes a deficiency, and likewise its absence, this unqualified dichotomy is invalid.

Similarly, something may be a mercy to creation when they need it, as with rain, yet a punishment when it harms them. Sending it down to meet their need is therefore mercy and beneficence, and the One who is beneficent and merciful is characterized by perfection. Not sending it down when it would harm them is no deficiency; rather, this too is mercy and beneficence. Thus, He is beneficent by granting it when its presence is a mercy, and by withholding it when its absence is a mercy.

## Page 2547

Section

As for the denial of particular “attributes known through revelation” on the grounds that they entail composition, which in turn entails need and dependence, an argument of this kind has already been answered.

If “composition” means what is understood by it in the language, in common usage, or in the usage of certain people—something assembled by another, something previously separate that then came together, something combining indivisible atoms or matter and form, or something whose parts can be separated from one another—then we do not concede the first premise. We do not concede that affirming the Face and Hand entails composition in this sense.

If, however, it means inseparability, while one thing is intrinsically distinct from another, so that this is not that, then the same consequence is binding upon them regarding the qualitative attributes known through reason, such as knowledge, power, hearing, and sight. None of these attributes is identical to another; rather, each is intrinsically distinct from the other, even though the two are inseparable and characterize one and the same being. We understand this in the attributes of created things, as with the sun’s parts and accidental properties.

Furthermore, if by need and dependence it is meant that He cannot exist without something distinct from Him, this is not conceded. But if it means that whatever is included in what His name designates must exist, and that the Necessary Existent cannot exist without those things included in what His name designates,

---

## Page 2548

then it is clear that He cannot exist without His own self; all the more, then, He cannot exist without what is included in it.

If it is said, “He depends upon His own self,” this does not mean that His self brings itself into being. The same applies to what is included in it. The expression, however, is misleading and ambiguous; once its meaning is explained, the difficulty disappears.

It may also be said: We do not apply the term “other” to this, so it does not follow that He needs something other than Himself. This concerns the use of language. As for demonstrative proof, the evidence establishes the existence of a self-existent being, with no agent or efficient cause bringing Him into being, and that He is, in Himself, independent of everything distinct from Him.

As for an existence that has no attribute, and whose name includes no positive meaning within its designation—if someone claims that this is what is meant by necessary existence and self-sufficiency, he is told: But this meaning is not what the evidence establishes. Rather, you have assumed that this is what the name designates. Making the term evidence for this meaning will not help you unless that meaning is established as true in itself. You have no evidence for that; indeed, the evidence establishes its opposite.

These people took the terms “the Self-Sufficient,” “the Eternal,” and “the Necessary Existent in Himself” and began interpreting them in senses that entail further meanings incompatible with affirming the attributes. They stretched the language, then imagined that what they had done was what rational and other evidence necessarily required. This is an error on their part.

---

## Page 2549

What rational evidence entails cannot be derived from mere wording, while what revealed evidence entails must be understood according to the speaker’s customary usage, not newly devised definitions.

No one, therefore, may claim that the words found in the Quran have been assigned certain meanings and then seek to explain Allah’s intent through those meanings. This is the practice of those who deviate from the truth and fabricate lies. They adopted meanings they supposed to be established and made them the meanings of “the One,” “the Necessary Existent,” “the Self-Sufficient,” “the Eternal,” and the denial of any likeness to Him. They then turned to the Quran and Sunnah, where Allah Most High is described as Unique, One, Most High, and in similar terms denying that He has any likeness or equal. They said: “This indicates the meanings to which we have assigned these names.” This is among the gravest fabrications against Allah.

Likewise, the “philosophizers” took such terms as “Creator,” “Agent,” “Maker,” and “Originator” and assigned them a meaning they had invented. They divided origination into two kinds: essential and temporal. By essential origination, they meant that what is subject to the Lord exists alongside the Lord from eternity and forever. Yet the term is not known to bear this meaning in the language of any people. Had they merely adopted this as their own terminology, you would not dispute it with them. But their purpose was to mislead people and to be able to say: “We affirm that the world originated and that Allah is its Creator, the One who brings it about, and its Maker,” and other expressions whose meanings necessarily and self-evidently entail that what is produced comes after its producer. Such expressions do not apply to something that is beginningless as the Lord is beginningless, existing alongside Him from eternity and forever.

The same applies to those who have treated the term “Speaker” and other designations in this way. And if the same were done

---

## Page 2550

to the words of Sībawayh and Hippocrates, their teachings on grammar and medicine would be corrupted. If this were done to the words of individual scholars such as Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and Abū Hanīfah, knowledge would thereby be corrupted and obscured for them. What, then, if this is done to the words of the Lord of all worlds? This is the way of the heretics who deviate concerning Allah’s names and signs, and of those who share in some of their practices.

For example, someone may say that “the One” is that which is indivisible. By “indivisible,” he means that nothing in it can be distinguished from anything else; he also says that no attribute inheres in it. They then claim that this is what “the Unique” and “the One” mean in the Quran.

Yet it is well known that every occurrence in the Quran of the terms for “one” and “anyone” contradicts what they have asserted. Examples include His words, Most High:

“If there is only one, she shall have half”; 

“One of the two women said, ‘O my father, hire him’”; 

“And there is none comparable to Him”; 

“If any of the polytheists seeks your protection”; 

and “Leave Me to deal with the one whom I created alone.”

These terms and others like them are applied to something that exists in its own right, can be pointed to, and has distinguishable parts. This is what they call a “body” in their terminology.

Likewise, suppose they say that entities possessing attributes are alike, bodies are alike, and substances are alike, and then seek to use His words, Most High—“There is nothing like Him”—to deny the realities to which they have assigned these names in their newly devised terminology. This would be a fabrication against the Quran, for this is not what likeness means in the Arabic language, in the language of the Quran, or in any other language.

Allah Most High says:

“If you turn away, He will replace you with another people, who will not be like you.”

---

## Page 2551

Thus He denied that these people were alike, although they shared a common humanity. How, then, can it be said that the Arabic language requires everything that can be pointed to to be like everything else that can be pointed to?

Allah Most High says:

Iram, of the pillars—
the like of which was never created in the lands?”

He thus states that its like was never created in the lands, although both are cities. How, then, can it be said that, in the Arabic language, every body is like every other body, so that His words,

“There is nothing like Him,”

should be understood on that basis?

The poet said:

“None is like the young man Zuhayr.”

And another said:

“No human being among mankind is like them.”

The poet did not intend thereby to deny the existence of any body whatsoever.

Likewise, the term “resemblance” does not mean “being alike” in the language. Allah Most High says:

“And they will be given it in similar form.”

And He Most High says:

“Similar and dissimilar.”

He did not mean thereby that these things are alike in the linguistic sense. The issue here is not whether substances are alike according to reason or not; that is discussed at length elsewhere. Rather, the point is that speakers of the language in which the Quran was revealed do not regard this alone as sufficient grounds for calling things alike, nor do they regard the denial of likeness as a denial of this. To interpret the Quran on that basis is therefore to attribute a falsehood to it.

## Page 2552

Section

The term “affinity” has several possible meanings. It may refer to descent and kinship: one says, “This man is so-and-so’s relative,” or “He is related to him,” when they share a kinship based on birth and human descent. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is far above that.

It may also mean likeness: one says, “This corresponds to that,” meaning that it is like it. Yet Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is One, the Self-Sufficient. He neither begets nor is born, and there is none comparable to Him.

It may also mean agreement in some respect, the opposite of which is disagreement. “Affinity” in this sense is indeed established. For the allies of Allah Most High agree with Him concerning what He commands, so they do it; concerning what He loves, so they love it; concerning what He forbids, so they refrain from it; and concerning what He gives, so they receive it.

Allah is One and loves what is odd-numbered; He is Beautiful and loves beauty; All-Knowing and loves knowledge; Pure and loves cleanliness; Good to His creation and loves those who do good; Just and loves those who act justly—and likewise with other such qualities.

Indeed, glorified is He, He rejoices at the repentance of the repentant person more than a man rejoices upon finding his lost mount, carrying his food and drink, in a deadly wilderness after he has despaired of finding it. Allah rejoices more at His servant’s repentance than this man rejoices at recovering his mount, as is established in the authentic hadith collections from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

## Page 2553

Thus, if “affinity” means this and similar things, then such affinity is real and is an attribute of perfection, as indicated earlier. Suppose there are two beings: one loves knowledge, truthfulness, justice, benevolence, and similar things; the other makes no distinction between these things and ignorance, falsehood, injustice, and the like, neither loving the former nor hating the latter. The one who loves those things is more perfect than the other. This shows that if someone strips Him of “attributes of perfection and existence,” denying Him knowledge so that He is like an inanimate object, then a being who knows would be more perfect than Him. The foundation of “this issue” is the distinction between Allah’s love, pleasure, anger, and displeasure, on the one hand, and His will, on the other. This is the position of the early generations, the jurists, and most of those who affirm divine decree, whether among Ahl al-Sunnah or others. Some of the Qadariyyah and some of those who affirm divine decree, however, have held that there is no distinction between them.

The “Qadariyyah” then said: He does not love disbelief, wickedness, or disobedience, nor does He will them. Thus, what He does not will occurs, and He wills what does not occur.

The “affirmers of divine decree” said: Whatever He wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur. ## Page 2556

Furthermore, even if mercy necessarily entailed such weakness in created beings, it would not follow that it necessarily entailed the same in Allah Most High. Likewise, our knowledge, power, hearing, sight and speech entail imperfections and needs from which Allah must be declared free. Similarly, our “existence” and “subsistence in ourselves” entail our need for a Creator who brings us into existence, whereas Allah’s existence is free of the needs inherent in ours. We, our attributes and our acts are bound up with dependence on another. Need is intrinsic to us, and we can never be free of it. He, glorified be He, is the Self-Sufficient; His freedom from need is intrinsic to Him and can never cease. In Himself, He is Ever-Living, All-Sustaining and necessarily existent, whereas in ourselves we are needy and dependent.

Thus, although our essence, attributes and acts, and the perfections we possess—such as knowledge, power and the like—are bound up with need, having come into existence and contingency, this does not require denying Allah an essence, attributes or acts, or denying Him power and knowledge, merely because these things are inseparable from need in us. The same applies to “mercy” and other attributes: even supposing that they are inseparable from need and weakness in us, it does not follow that they must be inseparable from these in Allah.

Furthermore, we know self-evidently that if we suppose two beings, one of whom shows mercy to another, bringing him benefit and warding off harm from him, while the other is indifferent to both and has nothing within him that calls for bringing benefit or warding off harm, then the former is more perfect.

## Page 2557

As for the statement, “Anger is the boiling of the heart’s blood in pursuit of revenge,” this is not correct even with regard to us. Anger may arise to ward off something harmful before it occurs, in which case there is no revenge at all.

Furthermore, anger accompanies the boiling of the heart’s blood; anger itself is not simply that boiling. Likewise, modesty accompanies a reddening of the face, and fear accompanies a paling of the face, but neither is identical to the accompanying change. This is because, when the soul is moved to repel something harmful, if it senses that it has the power to do so, the blood surges outward, giving rise to anger. If it senses its own inability, the blood retreats inward, causing the face to grow pale, as happens to someone who is sorrowful.

Moreover, even supposing that this were the true nature of our anger, it would not follow that Allah Most High’s anger must be like ours, just as the reality of Allah’s essence is not like ours. He resembles neither our essence nor our souls, and His attributes are like His essence in this respect.

We know self-evidently that if we suppose two beings, one possessing a strength by which he wards off corruption, while the other is indifferent to righteousness and corruption, the one possessing that strength is more perfect.

Indeed, everything that takes place in existence occurs by His will and power. Nothing occurs except what He wills, and nothing He wills fails to occur. To Him belongs dominion, and to Him belongs all praise.

If laughter in us necessarily involves some imperfection, Allah is far exalted above that. Such imperfection is, for the most part, particular rather than universal: laughter as such is not inherently associated with imperfection. Likewise, our essences and attributes are associated with imperfection, as is our existence. Nor does it follow that the Lord is an originator and that He has no essence.

This is where the extremist Qarmatians went astray, including the author of al-Iqlīd (The Key) and others like him. They sought to deny of Him everything the heart knows and the tongue expresses, whether by negation or affirmation. They said, “We do not say ‘existent’ or ‘not existent,’ nor ‘possessing attributes’ or ‘not possessing attributes,’” because, they claimed, this would involve likening Him to creation. Yet this entails that His existence is impossible—the consequence of likening Him to what cannot exist.

The resemblance that is impossible for Allah is that He should share any property exclusive to created beings—such as coming into being, death, passing away, and contingency—or resemble them in any of His attributes, such as life, knowledge, and power. For although He is described by these attributes, the Creator’s attribute does not resemble the creature’s attribute.

“If He decreed and punished, that would be injustice, and injustice is an imperfection,”

the reply is as follows:

The first statement is clear. If it were supposed that there existed within His dominion something He did not will, over which He had no power, and which He neither created nor brought into being, that would constitute an imperfection in several respects.

First, for anything to bring things into being independently of Him would constitute an imperfection even if it were supposed to be outside His dominion. How much more so within His dominion? For we know that, if we posit two beings—one upon whom everything depends, while he depends on nothing, and another upon whom some things depend, while others have no need of him—the first would be more perfect. Thus, the mere fact that anything should fall outside His power and creative activity would constitute an imperfection.

These are proofs of divine oneness, for sharing entails an imperfection in each of the two partners, and absolute perfection lies only in oneness. We know that one who has power in his own right is more perfect than one who needs a helper; one who accomplishes everything by himself is more perfect than one who has a partner and helper in accomplishing some of it; and one upon whom everything depends is more perfect than one of whom some things have no need.

---

## Page 2564

Another consideration is this: being the Creator of everything and having power over everything is more perfect than being the Creator of only some things and having power over only some things. The “Qadariyyah” do not acknowledge Him as the Creator of everything or as having power over everything. Those who espouse philosophy and hold that He is a final cause are worse than them. They do not acknowledge Him as the Creator of any events arising in the world—neither the motions of the celestial spheres nor any other moving things—nor as the Creator of what comes about through them. Nor do they acknowledge that He has power over any of this or knows its details. Yet Allah, glorified and exalted is He, says:

“It is Allah who created seven heavens, and of the earth their like. His command descends among them so that you may know that Allah has power over all things and that Allah encompasses all things in knowledge.”

These people examine the world, yet do not know that Allah has power over all things or that Allah encompasses all things in knowledge.

Another consideration is that, if we suppose two sovereigns—one who wills something that does not come to pass, while what he does not will does come to pass; and another whose every will comes to pass, and nothing comes to pass except what he wills—we know necessarily that the latter is more perfect.

In short, the position of “those who affirm divine power” entails that He is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of everything, that He has power over all things, and that whatever He wills comes to pass. It thus entails the perfection of His creative activity, power, and will. The “deniers of divine decree” deny Him these perfections.

As for his statement, “For Him to punish for what has been decreed is injustice on His part,” this is a bare assertion for which they have no support beyond drawing an analogy between the Lord and themselves. No rational person would say that everything that constitutes an imperfection

---

## Page 2565

in any being whatsoever must necessarily constitute an imperfection in Allah. Indeed, such conduct is not invariably reprehensible even in a human being. Rather, if a person has a beneficial purpose in causing some animal to suffer or doing something to it that causes suffering, then doing so is right. Consider someone who produces silk: he takes steps to have silkworms spin it, then to have it placed in the sun so that he may obtain the intended benefit from the silk. Here, he has contributed to the activity of the worms that became the cause of their suffering. Likewise, someone who takes steps to have livestock breed and hens lay eggs, then slaughters the resulting animals to benefit from them, has contributed to bringing those animals into existence in a way that ultimately leads to their suffering, for a benefit he gains thereby. In “short,” it is right for a person to cause an animal pain for an outweighing benefit. Thus, this kind of action is not inherently blameworthy, reprehensible, or unjust, although some instances of it are unjust.

Accordingly, regarding injustice on Allah’s part, one may say that it is intrinsically impossible, because injustice means exercising control over what one does not own, whereas everything belongs to Allah; or that injustice means disobeying a command that one is obliged to obey. It is impossible for Allah Most High to exercise control over another’s property or to disobey the command of anyone whom He is obliged to obey. If injustice consists solely of either of these, then injustice on His part is impossible.

Alternatively, one may say that it is possible, but that He, glorified is He, does not commit it because of His self-sufficiency and His knowledge of its reprehensibility, and because He has declared that He does not commit it. The perfection of His being precludes injustice on His part, since justice and mercy are inseparable from His essence. Thus, He cannot be characterized by the opposites of the attributes of perfection that are inseparable from Him, according to this

---

## Page 2566

view. Thus, whatever He does is done for a wisdom that calls for it, just as whatever He refrains from doing is avoided for a wisdom that requires Him to be exalted above it. Accordingly, we know that there is wisdom in everything He does. This general knowledge suffices us, even if we do not know the details. Our lack of knowledge of the details of His wisdom is comparable to our lack of knowledge of the nature of His essence. Just as we know that He possesses the attributes of perfection, although the true nature of His essence is unknown to us, we do not reject what we know because of what we do not know.

Likewise, we know that He is “Wise” in what He does and commands. Our lack of knowledge of the wisdom behind certain particular matters does not undermine our knowledge of His wisdom in principle. We therefore do not reject what we know of His wisdom because we do not know its details.

We know that someone who recognizes the expertise of specialists in arithmetic, medicine, and grammar, but does not possess the qualifications that make them specialists in these fields, cannot impugn their statements merely because he does not understand their reasoning. His servants are further from understanding Allah and His wisdom in His creation than the laypeople among them are from understanding arithmetic, medicine, and grammar. Their objections to His wisdom therefore display greater ignorance and a greater presumption in speaking without knowledge than those of a complete layperson who criticizes arithmetic, medicine, and grammar without knowing anything about them.

This becomes clear through the principle concerning perfection that we mentioned, namely our statement that perfection

---

## Page 2567

that entails no deficiency in a contingent being must be attributed to Him, and He must be declared free of whatever contradicts it. Thus, we ask:

Is creating certain living beings and their actions that cause their punishment necessarily a deficiency, or does this vary? Moreover, if creating them serves a great wisdom that cannot be realized otherwise, which is more perfect: bringing this about together with that great wisdom, or forfeiting that wisdom? Furthermore, can the intended wisdom be realized without this occurring? Whoever reflects on these matters will realize that he cannot say that creating a living being’s action that causes its punishment is necessarily a deficiency.

“Those who affirm divine decree” may offer another answer, though the majority dispute it. They say:

“That He does whatever He wills and perfects whatever He intends is an attribute of perfection, unlike one who is subject to commands and prohibitions, being commanded to do one thing and forbidden to do another.” They also say: “For anyone other than Him, doing whatever he wills is reprehensible only because of the harm that befalls him; but He, glorified be He, cannot suffer any harm.”

The majority say:

“If we suppose someone who does whatever he wills without any beloved wise purpose relating to himself, or any mercy and beneficence extending to others, then one who acts with wisdom and mercy is more perfect than one who acts without wisdom or mercy.”

They also say:

“If we suppose a willing agent who does not distinguish between what he wills and what another wills, and another willing agent who distinguishes between them, willing what is fitting and proper to will rather than its opposite, then the second is more perfect.”

They also say:

“One who is subject to commands and prohibitions from a superior who commands and forbids is deficient in comparison with one who has no

---

## Page 2568

superior commanding or forbidding him. Yet if he commands himself to do what he ought to do and forbids himself what he ought not to do, while another does whatever he wills without commanding or forbidding himself, then the one who abides by his own commands and prohibitions—which accord with wisdom—is more perfect than the other. Allah, Most High, has said:

‘Your Lord has prescribed mercy for Himself.’

And He has said:

‘O My servants, I have forbidden oppression for Myself and have made it forbidden among you, so do not oppress one another.’”

They also say:

“If saying that He does whatever He wills and decrees whatever He intends serves to explain His power—that nothing can hinder Him, and that no other can prevent what He wills or cause Him to will—then this is more perfect than the condition of one who has an obstacle preventing what he wills and a helper without whom he can neither will nor carry out what he wills.

“But if ‘doing whatever one wills’ means acting without regard to what knowledge and wisdom require, indeed acting foolishly, whereas another does whatever he wills but his will is joined with knowledge and wisdom, then the second is more perfect.”

The crux of the matter is that perfect power is an attribute of perfection, and a will that takes effect without needing a helper or encountering any obstacle is likewise an attribute of perfection. But a “will” that does not distinguish between one object of willing and another, treating all kinds alike, is not an attribute of perfection. Rather, the will that distinguishes between one object and another—as knowledge and wisdom require—is the will characterized by perfection.

Whoever diminishes His power, His creating, or His will has not esteemed Him as He deserves. And whoever diminishes His wisdom or His mercy has not esteemed Him as He truly deserves. The perfection that is His due requires affirming both.

As for “those who deny prophethood” and their assertion that people are unworthy of Allah sending them a messenger, just as people of lowly standing are unworthy of a ruler sending them a messenger—this betrays clear ignorance concerning both the creature and the Creator. Among the things for which kings are most highly praised is personally addressing the weakest of their subjects, let alone sending them a messenger.

As for the Creator, glorified is He, He is more merciful to His servants than a mother is to her child, and His power accompanies His perfect mercy. Since His power and mercy are perfect, what could prevent Him from sending them a messenger as a mercy from Him? As He, Most High, says:

“We have sent you only as a mercy to the worlds.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah has certainly bestowed a great favor upon the believers by sending among them a Messenger from among themselves, reciting His verses to them, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom.”

Thus He, Most High, has made clear that this is among His favors to His believing servants.

---

## Page 2570

If the denier denies His power to do this, he impugns the perfection of His power; if he denies His kindness in doing so, he impugns the perfection of His mercy and kindness. It is thus clear that sending a messenger is among the greatest proofs of the perfection of His power and kindness. Power and kindness are attributes of perfection, not deficiency.

As for punishing those who reject the message, this falls within the divine decree, owing to the wisdom He has in doing so.

## Page 2571

Section:

As for “the polytheists’ claim” that His greatness and majesty require that He be approached only through an intermediary and a barrier, and that approaching Him without these detracts from His exalted dignity, this is false on several grounds.

One is that someone who can be approached only through intermediaries and a barrier is either able to hear his soldiers’ words and meet their needs without those intermediaries and that barrier, or he is not. If he is not able, this is a deficiency. Allah Most High, however, is characterized by perfection. He must therefore hear His servants’ words without intermediaries, answer their supplications, and show them kindness without any need for a barrier. If a king can conduct his affairs without a barrier and dispenses with it out of kindness and mercy, that is an attribute of perfection.

Furthermore, the claim that this detracts from His dignity applies only to someone whom others can harm and who depends on them for his own benefit. Given His perfect power, His complete independence of them, and His immunity to any harm they might cause Him, their drawing near to Him does not detract from His dignity. Indeed, if there are two people, one of whom brings the weak close to him out of kindness toward them and has no fear of them, while the other does not do so, whether out of fear, arrogance, or some other reason, the first is more perfect than the second.

---

## Page 2572

Moreover, this objection does not apply when the one in authority has commanded it. If he permits people to approach him and enter his home, doing so is neither disrespectful to him nor demeaning to his dignity. Such censure therefore applies to those who worship Him in ways He has not prescribed. For this reason, Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of good news, and a warner”

“and as one who calls to Allah by His permission.”

And He Most High says:

“Or do they have partners who have prescribed for them in religion what Allah has not authorized?”

## Page 2573

Section

As for the statement:

“If they were asked, ‘Which is more perfect: a being characterized by every kind of perception, including taste, smell, and touch, or a being not characterized by them?’ they would answer, ‘The former is more perfect,’ yet they do not ascribe these to Him.”

Those who affirm the divine attributes reply:

There are three well-known positions concerning these kinds of perception.

The first is to affirm these kinds of perception for Allah Most High, just as hearing and sight are ascribed to Him. This is the position of the judge Abū Bakr and Abū al-Maʿālī, and I believe it is also the position of al-Ashʿarī himself. Indeed, it is also the position of the Basran Muʿtazilites who ascribe these kinds of perception to Him.

These scholars and others also hold that He can be perceived through all five senses, just as He can be seen. The judge Abū Yaʿlā agreed with them on this in al-Muʿtamad and elsewhere.

The second position is to deny these three kinds of perception, as do many who affirm the divine attributes, both among the Sifātiyya and others. This is the position of groups of jurists among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, and of many followers of al-Ashʿarī and others.

The third position is to affirm perception by touch but not by taste, because taste pertains only to what is eaten: only one who eats can possess the sense of taste, and only something eaten can be its object.

---

## Page 2574

and Allah, glorified is He, is far above eating. Touch, by contrast, is comparable to sight. Most scholars of hadith ascribe touch to Him, as do many followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others, but they do not ascribe taste to Him.

The reason for this is that the Muʿtazilites who deny the divine attributes said to those who affirm them:

“If you say that He can be seen, then say that He can be perceived through all the other senses. And if you say that He is All-Hearing and All-Seeing, then ascribe all five kinds of perception to Him.”

All those who affirm the divine attributes replied:

“We describe Him as One who can be seen and whose speech can be heard, as the scriptural texts state. We likewise describe Him as One who hears and sees.”

The majority of the scholars of hadith and the Sunnah said:

“We also ascribe perception by touch to Him, because it is a perfection involving no deficiency, and the scriptural texts indicate it. Perception by taste, however, necessarily entails eating, which in turn entails deficiency, as explained earlier.”

A group of speculative theologians who affirm the divine attributes ascribed all five kinds of perception to Him in both respects: as perceiver and as the object of perception.

Some of them said that He could be the object of these kinds of perception, just as He can be seen, because they believed that existence is what makes something capable of being seen. They did not, however, say that He possesses these kinds of perception.

Most of those who affirm that He can be seen did not hold that mere existence is what makes something capable of being seen. Rather, they said that the basis for this consists of positive, existent realities—not that everything that exists can be seen. There is a difference between the two claims: the latter entails that every existent thing can be seen, whereas the former does not. If what makes something capable of being seen consists of positive, existent realities, without requiring any conditions involving nonexistence, then the more fully something possesses existence and the further it is from nonexistence, the stronger the grounds for its being capable of being seen.

Others among them denied everything apart from hearing and sight in both respects: perceiving and being perceived.

## Page 2575

Section

As for the statement, “Perfection and deficiency are relative matters,” we have explained that the perfection befitting the Lord is that which involves no deficiency whatsoever, and that it is the perfection possible for an existent being. Such perfection can never be absent from Allah. Relative perfection, however, entails deficiency: it is perfection in one respect but not another. Eating, for example, is a perfection for someone who is hungry, but a deficiency for someone who is full, because it is not pure perfection; rather, it is accompanied by deficiency.

Self-exaltation, self-magnification, self-praise, commanding people to worship Him, call upon Him, and turn to Him with longing, and other such things exclusive to lordship are praiseworthy perfections in the Lord, blessed and exalted is He, but blameworthy deficiencies in a created being. The same applies to statements concerning what is exclusive to lordship, such as His saying:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me.”

And His saying, exalted is He:

“Call upon Me; I will respond to you.”

And His saying:

“Whether you reveal what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it.”

And His saying:

“Or do those who commit evil deeds think they can escape Us?”

And His saying:

“Indeed, you have no authority over My servants.”

And His saying:

“Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers and those who believe, both in the life of this world and on the Day when the witnesses stand forth.”

And His saying:

“Whoever fears Allah, He will make a way out for him”

“and provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever puts his trust

---

## Page 2576

in Allah, He will suffice him.”

These and similar statements, in which the Lord speaks of certain attributes exclusive to Him and truthfully describes Himself with attributes of perfection, are themselves part of His perfection. His explaining these matters to His servants and making them known to them is also part of His perfection. Anyone else who made such claims about himself would be a liar and a fabricator, and lying is among the greatest faults and deficiencies.

When a created being speaks truthfully about himself, however, this is not unconditionally blameworthy. Indeed, it may be praiseworthy if it serves a beneficial purpose, as in the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“I am the foremost of Adam’s descendants, and I say this without boasting.”

If, however, this causes harm that outweighs or equals its benefit, he is blamed for doing something harmful, not for lying. The Lord, exalted is He, does nothing for which He is blameworthy. Rather, all praise belongs to Him in every circumstance, and every act of His is good, beautiful, and praiseworthy.

This is evident according to those who hold that injustice on His part is intrinsically impossible. According to the majority among Ahl al-Sunnah and the Qadariyyah, He acts only in accordance with wisdom and justice. Thus, all His reports, statements, and actions are good and praiseworthy, proceeding with the perfection for which He deserves praise. He possesses qualities exclusive to Him, blessed and exalted is He, by virtue of which He deserves supreme greatness and majesty. His supreme greatness and majesty are thus like His being living, self-subsisting, beginningless, and necessarily existent in His own right; His knowing all things and having power over all things; His being the Almighty, who cannot be assailed; and His being the Subduer of everything besides Him.

---

## Page 2577

All these, then, are attributes of perfection that belong to Him alone. How could something that belongs to Him alone constitute perfection in anyone else, when no one else possesses it? Whoever claims it is a fabricator who contests the exclusive prerogatives of Lordship. As established in an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘Majesty is My lower garment, and supreme greatness is My cloak. Whoever contests either of them with Me, I shall punish him.’”

In short, no one else has any share in the perfection exclusive to Lordship. This affirms that He possesses a perfection in which no one else has any share. Such perfection cannot belong to anyone else; claiming it therefore amounts to contesting His Lordship and fabricating a lie against Allah. It is well known that prophethood is a perfection in a prophet. Yet when impostors—such as Musaylimah and his like—claim it, this constitutes a deficiency in them, not because prophethood is a deficiency, but because claiming it without possessing it is itself the deficiency. Likewise, anyone who claims knowledge, power, or righteousness without possessing them is blameworthy and detestable.

This entails that the Lord Most High possesses perfection that cannot belong to a created being. This does not contradict the principle that whatever constitutes perfection for an existent being simply insofar as it exists is something of which the Creator is all the more deserving. Rather, it means that when a created being is described with a perfection in the manner proper to it, and the Creator is described with that perfection in the manner proper to Him, what belongs to the created being neither equals nor even approaches what belongs to the Creator.

This is true: the Lord Most High deserves perfection and possesses it uniquely, in a manner in which nothing resembles Him. He has neither peer nor equal, whether the perfection is one of which nothing belongs to created beings—such as Lordship over His servants, absolute self-sufficiency, and the like—or one of which a kind is found in created beings;

---

## Page 2578

for the kind of perfection that belongs to the Creator surpasses what belongs to the created being by more than the highest of created beings surpasses the lowest. “The upshot of this” is that a created being is blameworthy for arrogance, domineering pride, and, at times, self-praise, and similar things.

As for the questioner’s statement:

“If you say, ‘We set aside the subject to which the attribute pertains and consider whether the attribute is a perfection or a deficiency,’ we likewise deem it impossible to judge it to be either, since it may be a perfection for one being and a deficiency for another, as mentioned.”

The reply is:

Rather, we say that a perfection involving no deficiency for a contingently existing being is an absolute perfection for everything that possesses it. Moreover, a perfection that constitutes perfection for an existent being—simply insofar as it exists—cannot constitute a deficiency in some instances. For whatever constitutes a deficiency in some instances and a perfection in others is a perfection for one kind of existent being but not another. It therefore cannot be a perfection for an existent being simply insofar as it exists.

One way to establish this is to suppose two existent beings, one possessing this attribute and the other its opposite. It then becomes apparent which of them is more perfect. If it is said, “This is more perfect in one respect but less perfect in another,” then it is not an absolute perfection.

Allah knows best. All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds. May Allah bless our master Muhammad and his family, and grant them peace.

He also said:

Allah Most High says:

He Most High also says:

“He is Allah, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner. To Him belong the most beautiful names.”

Al-husnā (“most beautiful”) denotes what surpasses al-hasanah (“beautiful”); its singular form is al-ahāsin (“most beautiful”). There are three positions here:

One may say that His names are exclusively the most beautiful, and that He may be invoked only by such names.

Alternatively, one may say that He may be invoked only by the most beautiful names, although He may be named by other permissible names, even if they are not among the most beautiful. These are two well-known positions.

Or one may say that such names may be used both in invoking Him and in speaking about Him.

For in His words:

“To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them,”

and His words:

“Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names,”

He affirms that the most beautiful names belong to Him and commands that He be invoked by them. The apparent meaning of this is that all the most beautiful names belong to Him.

---

## Page 2580

It may also be said that the reference is to “the most beautiful names” as a category: these must not be denied of Him, as the disbelievers did. He commanded that He be invoked by them and addressed using them, contrary to the polytheists’ practice of forbidding people to invoke Him by His name “the Most Merciful.”

Thus, it may be said that His words, “Call upon Him by them,” command that He be invoked by the most beautiful names and not by others. Similarly, His words, “Call them by their fathers’ names,” prohibit calling them by names attributing them to anyone other than their fathers.

A distinction is drawn between invoking Him and speaking about Him. He is to be invoked only by the most beautiful names. When speaking about Him, however, no bad designation may be used, but a good designation may be used, or one that is not bad even if it is not judged to be good. Examples include “thing,” “essence,” and “existent,” when the last means that which has real existence. If, however, it means “the One who is present in times of hardship,” then it is among the most beautiful names. Likewise, “the One who wills” and “the One who speaks” are not among the most beautiful names, since willing and speaking may be either praiseworthy or blameworthy. This is unlike “the All-Wise,” “the Most Merciful,” “the Truthful,” and similar names, which can only be praiseworthy.

The same distinction applies to the Messenger, concerning whom He said:

“Do not address the Messenger among yourselves as you address one another.”

He thus commanded them to say, “O Messenger of Allah” and “O Prophet of Allah,” just as Allah addressed him by saying, “O Prophet” and “O Messenger.” One should not say, “O Muhammad,” “O Ahmad,” or “O Abū al-Qāsim,” even though, when speaking about him—as in the call to prayer and the like—they would say, “I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.” Likewise, Allah Most High said:

“Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.”

He also said:

“And bringing good tidings of a messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad.”

And He said:

“Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah.”

## Page 2581

Thus He, glorified be He, addressed Muhammad only by titles of honour, such as “the Messenger,” “the Prophet,” “the Enwrapped One,” and “the Cloaked One,” whereas He addressed the other prophets by their names, even though He sometimes mentions Muhammad’s name when speaking about him. He, glorified be He, thus distinguished between these two forms of discourse concerning the Messenger and commanded us to observe that distinction in his case. This also accords with people’s customary understanding: when addressing eminent rulers, scholars, shaykhs, and leaders, they address and call them only by honourable names. Yet when speaking about one of them, they may say that he is a human being, a rational animal, a body, a being brought into existence, a creature, one subject to a Lord, a fashioned being, someone born of a woman, and someone who eats food and drinks.

But every name and attribute mentioned when speaking about him is used when addressing him privately and speaking to him directly. Although some designations of created beings indicate their imperfection and their having come into existence, Allah’s names indicate neither imperfection nor His having come into existence. Rather, they include the most beautiful names, which indicate perfection, and these are the names by which He is invoked. When speaking about Him, however, one may use a good designation, or one that does not negate goodness without necessarily being good in itself (1).

As for the names handed down in revelation, every one of them conveys a good meaning. This should therefore be carefully considered with regard to supplication and statements about Him, whether transmitted or not transmitted. Such untransmitted statements have been formulated out of necessity because opponents arose—to distinguish between supplication and statements about Him, and to distinguish the transmitted wording that is used—or to acquaint them with what they did not know. Accordingly, not every designation mentioned in one context is to be mentioned in another; rather, the contexts must be distinguished.

## Page 2585

the Hanbalīs and those jurists, Sufis, and others who follow them—is that this category must be assigned to one of the two preceding categories. It must therefore be either pre-eternal and subsisting in Him, according to those who allow this, namely the Kullābiyyah, or created and separate from Him. It is impossible, they maintain, for any attribute, state, act, or anything that is not pre-eternal to subsist in Him.

They call this question “the question of temporal events indwelling in His essence.” They say that temporal events cannot indwell in His essence. Others call this “the essence acting by itself or within itself.” They held that allowing this would entail His having a beginning, because the proof by which they established that bodies have a beginning was the subsistence of temporal events in them. Thus, if such events subsisted in Him, one of two consequences would follow: either He would have a beginning, or knowledge that the world has a beginning would be invalidated.

Those who disagree with them on this say: The proof that the world has a beginning is that it cannot be free of temporal events and does not precede them. If, however, it could precede them, their subsistence in it would not indicate that it has a beginning.

Others say: This is not the proof that the world has a beginning; rather, it is a weak argument. They have other lines of reasoning.

They in turn fall into two groups. The first consists of those who also hold that attributes cannot subsist in Him, because they believe that attributes are accidents and that an accident subsisting in Him would likewise entail His having a beginning. These are the deniers of the attributes among

the Muʿtazilah, who consequently maintained that the Quran is created and that Allah has no will subsisting in Him, nor love, hatred, or the like. This is the view held by the adherents of this position who belong to Ahl al-Sunnah among the Hanbalīs, and by the Ashʿarīs and others who agree with them on all or part of it.

Alternatively, they say that these are “mere acts” occurring in created things, without any relational ascription or relation. Their disagreement, then, concerns whether these relations and relational ascriptions are affirmed for Allah, despite the general agreement that “relations” and “relational ascriptions” involving Allah Most High must arise in time, such as His being with His creation and the like.

Ibn ʿAqīl calls these relations “states” of Allah. These are not the “states” disputed by the theologians, such as being knowing and being powerful; rather, it is these relations and relational ascriptions that he calls states. He says that the arising of these states is not the arising of attributes, for these states are relations between Allah and creation, and this does not entail the existence of a reality subsisting

in the one to whom the relation is ascribed. For example, a person climbs towards a roof, which is above him, and then sits on it, so that it is beneath him. Likewise, when a child is born to a man, his brother becomes a paternal uncle, his father a grandfather, his son a brother, and his wife’s brother a maternal uncle. These relations and relational ascriptions apply to them without any change occurring in them.

The second view—held by the Karrāmiyyah, many Hanbalīs, most scholars of hadith, and their followers among the jurists, Sufis, and the general body of Muslims—is that these attributes of action and similar attributes ascribed to Allah constitute a “third category.” Most statements of the early generations and of those who have described their position, even al-Ashʿarī, indicate this view. These attributes are neither created things separate from Him, nor are they on a par with His essence and the pre-eternal, necessary attributes that are not subject to His will, whether in their kinds or their individual instances.

Those holding this view may say that He speaks when He wills and is silent when He wills, and that He has always been One who speaks—meaning that He has always spoken when He wills and been silent when He wills. His speech is from Him; it is not created.

They likewise say that, although He has a pre-eternal will, He wills when He wishes, becomes angry, and abhors.

These scholars, or most of them, affirm the apparent meaning of the scriptural texts, such as His saying:

“Then He rose over the Throne,”

meaning that He rose over it after not having been established over it

## Page 2589

and that He draws near to His servants, comes close to them, descends to the lowest heaven, and comes on the Day of Resurrection after not having been coming.

Some of these scholars may say that “temporally originated events” subsist in His essence. Others refrain from using this expression, either because it has not been transmitted in the religious reports, or because it may suggest a false meaning: that this resembles the inherence of “accidents” in created beings. Similarly, most theologians refrain from calling His attributes accidents, even though they are attributes subsisting in the one described by them, as accidents do.

Ibn al-Khatīb maintained that most schools and rational thinkers acknowledge this position in reality, even if they deny it verbally—including the philosophers, the Muʿtazilah, and the Ashʿarīs.

As for the “philosophers,” they hold that relations exist in external reality, and Allah exists with every temporally originated thing. This “being with” is a temporally originated attribute in His essence. Abū al-Barakāt al-Baghdādī, author of al-Muʿtabar, explicitly affirmed that particular instances of knowledge and will originate in His particular essence. He said that acknowledging Him as the God of this world is inconceivable without affirming this. He then said: “He must be exalted above such exaltation, and declared transcendent above such declarations of transcendence.”

As for the “Muʿtazilah,” the Basrans, such as Abū ʿAlī and Abū Hāshim, maintain that things seen and heard come into existence, and that thereby the qualities of being one who hears and sees arise for Allah. Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī maintains that new instances of knowledge arise in His essence as new objects of knowledge arise.

The Ashʿarīs likewise maintain that nonexistent things were neither heard nor seen, but became heard and seen after coming into existence. Yet hearing and sight, in their view, are not merely relations; rather, they are attributes subsisting in the essence of the All-Hearing,

---

## Page 2590

the All-Seeing. They may also be held to this consequence on the basis of their statement that abrogation is the lifting or termination of a ruling, their affirmation of His knowledge of particulars, and likewise the cessation of the relation of His power and will.

The truth of the matter is that explicit disagreement over this principle exists among most schools; it is not confined to the people of hadith. As for “the deniers,” it may be said that this position follows necessarily from their views if they affirm attributes of Allah that are not eternal; this principle would then become a matter of agreement. They may, however, offer answers to these implications: sometimes valid answers, in which case the conclusion does not follow from their position, and sometimes invalid ones, in which case it does. There is no doubt about this.

As for the texts of the Quran and Sunnah, there is no doubt that their apparent meaning accords with this position. Those holding the former view may, however, reinterpret them or leave the matter to Allah. Those holding this position say that some of these texts admit of no reinterpretation, while those that do are accompanied by contextual indications and corroborating evidence (1) (*) establishing with certainty that Allah and His Messenger intended that meaning, or that this is what is understood from them.

They say that the deniers have no reliable proof: all they have is uncritical adherence to their predecessors, coupled with vilification and intimidation directed at listeners unfamiliar with the subtleties of theological argument. They also say that this is the position of most adherents of religious traditions and of Allah’s elect servants, and that only the innovators within those traditions have opposed it. Those holding the former view may say: “This contradicts consensus; this is disbelief; this entails change and temporal origination.” I have seen astonishing things from people concerning this principle.

“Chapter: The Jahmiyyah’s Denial That Allah Spoke to Moses

## Page 2594

A related question concerns the attributes involving movement, such as coming, arrival, and descent: are they to be interpreted as meaning the coming of His power and His command? Two positions are reported:

The first is that they mean the coming of His power. This is Hanbal’s report concerning the ordeal.

The second is that they are to be accepted as they have come, like the other attributes. This is the apparent position of the school, well known among our scholars. Some held that Hanbal had erred; others said that Ahmad had said this to argue against his opponents on their own premises. Still others, such as Ibn al-Zāghūnī, treated it as a report confined to this particular case, whereas Ibn ‘Aqīl extended it to all the other attributes.

This principle has ramifications for most questions concerning the divine attributes, especially speech, will, and the attributes connected with His will, such as descent and rising over the Throne. It was the cause of the dispute between the imam of imams, Muhammad ibn Ishāq ibn Khuzaymah, and a group of his distinguished companions.

## Page 2596

Abū Bakr ‘Abd al-‘Azīz, in the first volume of the “Book of the Sunnah” within al-Muqni‘, was presented with the objection: “If you say that He has always been speaking, that would be purposeless.” He replied:

“Our scholars hold two views. The first is that He has always been speaking, just as He has always been knowing, because the opposite of speech is muteness, just as the opposite of knowledge is ignorance.”

He said: “Some of our scholars say: ‘He has affirmed that He is the Creator, yet He cannot be creating at all times. Rather, we say that He creates when He wills to create. His not creating at all times does not invalidate His being the Creator. Likewise, His not speaking at all times does not invalidate His being one who speaks. Rather, He speaks and creates, even though He is not creating at all times or speaking at all times.’”

When this question was put to Judge Abū Ya‘lā in his book Īdāh al-Bayān fī Mas’alat al-Qur’ān (Clarifying the Explanation Concerning the Quran), he said: “We say that He has always been speaking, without being spoken to or addressed, and without commanding or forbidding. Ahmad explicitly stated this in Hanbal’s report.” He continued his discussion until he cited from Abū Bakr what the latter had related in al-Muqni‘. He then said: “Perhaps the scholar among our companions who holds this view follows Ahmad ibn Hanbal’s statement in ‘Abd Allāh’s report: ‘He has always spoken whenever He wills.’”

He said: “Whoever holds this view holds that the Quran came into being. We have already interpreted Ahmad’s words, ‘He speaks whenever He wills,’ at the beginning of this discussion. This is not analogous to His being described as creating and providing, because those attributes

## Page 2598

and he did not say, “He has always been addressing others whenever He wills.” According to those who hold that speech is eternal and necessary, what depends on His will is only His addressing others—a contingent act—not His speaking.

This is clarified by Ahmad’s statement elsewhere—may Allah be pleased with him:

“Allah has always been speaking, knowing and forgiving.”

He thus mentioned three attributes: the attribute that is eternal and necessary, namely knowledge; and the attribute that is contingent and dependent on His will, namely forgiveness. There is agreement concerning these two. He also mentioned speaking, the third category, concerning which there is disagreement. It resembles knowledge insofar as it is an attribute subsisting in Him that does not relate to created beings, and it resembles forgiveness insofar as it depends on His will, as he explained elsewhere.

It is therefore clear that, for Ahmad, its eternity means that Allah has always been such that, if He wills, He speaks, and if He wills, He remains silent. He did not newly acquire the ability to speak, which is an attribute of perfection, just as He did not newly acquire the ability to forgive—although perfection consists in speaking when He wills and remaining silent when He wills.

As for the judge’s statement that this amounts to saying that His speech comes into being, they offer two replies.

The first is that it should not be called muhdath (newly originated), but should be called hadīth (discourse), since muhdath denotes something created and separate from Allah, whereas Allah Himself has called His speech hadīth. This is the position of the Karrāmiyya and most hadith scholars and Hanbalīs.

The second is that it may be called muhdath, as in His words:

“a new reminder from their Lord”

without being created. This is the position of many jurists, hadith scholars and speculative theologians

## Page 2599

such as Dāwūd ibn Alī al-Asbahānī—the founder of the school. However, Ahmad is reported to have denounced this, and his denunciation may be cited in support of one of the two views held by our companions.

Al-Marwadhī reported that Abū Abd Allāh said:

“Who is Dāwūd ibn Alī al-Asbahānī? May Allah grant him no relief! I received a letter from Muhammad ibn Yahyā al-Naysābūrī stating that Dāwūd al-Asbahānī had falsely declared that the Quran is newly originated.”

Abū Bakr al-Khallāl recorded this report in his Book of the Sunnah.

Abd Allāh ibn Ahmad said: “Dāwūd sought permission to visit my father, who said, ‘Who is this? Dāwūd? May Allah’s love never mend his heart, and may Allah fill his grave with worms!’ He subsequently died infested with worms.”

Unqualified expressions may suggest something other than the intended meaning. One should therefore say:

“If, by ‘newly originated,’ you mean that it is something created and separate from Allah, as the Jahmiyya, Mu'tazila and Najjāriyya maintain, then this is false, and we do not affirm it. But if you mean that it is speech which Allah uttered by His will after not having uttered that particular speech—although He had uttered other speech before it, and has always spoken whenever He wills—then we do affirm this.”

This is what the Quran and Sunnah indicate, and it is the position of the early generations and the hadith scholars. The opposing position was an innovation introduced by the Kullābiyya and Ash'ariyya. Those who affirm the former position, however, hold two views.

The first is that He began speaking after not having spoken, although He had been capable of speech—just as He created the heavens and the earth after not having created them, although He had been capable of creating them. This is the position of the Karrāmiyya and others who say that newly occurring events come to subsist in Him after not having subsisted in Him. The statement that His speech is ‘newly originated’ can bear this meaning, and Ahmad’s denunciation can be understood as directed at it.

---

## Page 2600

The second is that He has always been One who speaks, speaking whenever He wills. This is the position held by those hadith scholars who affirm this view.

Those who hold this position may say that His speech is eternal, neither newly occurring nor newly originated. By this they mean speech as a kind, since He has always spoken whenever He wills, although He utters particular speech whenever He wills. Someone who says, “Newly occurring events do not subsist in His essence,” may intend this meaning, on the basis that speech as a kind did not newly arise in how His essence is characterized.

Abū Abd Allāh ibn Hāmid said in his Usūl:

“Among the things that must be believed and affirmed is that Allah speaks; that His speech is eternal; and that He has always been One who speaks, being characterized by this at all times. His speech is eternal, not newly originated, like His knowledge and power. The school’s position may also allow that speech is an attribute of One who has always been characterized by it and who speaks whenever He wills and when He wills. We do not say that He is silent at one time and speaking at another, beginning with the origination of speech.

“The evidence establishing that He speaks in the manner we have described is the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Prophet, and the consensus of the people of truth, apart from the misguided faction—the Muʿtazila—and other speculative theologians, who refused to affirm that Allah speaks.”

He then mentioned some evidence from the Book and the Sunnah. After that, he said:

Yūsuf ibn Mūsā said: “I asked Abū Abd Allāh: ‘Does Allah descend to the lowest heaven however He wills, without description?’ He replied: ‘Yes.’”

In al-Marwadhī’s report, he was asked concerning Ibn al-Mubārak: “Is Allah known to be upon the Throne with a limit?” He replied: “That has reached me,” and he approved of it.

Ibn Hāmid said: “The school’s position, as we have explained, admits of no disagreement: His Essence descends. I have seen some of our companions report that Abū Abd Allāh said concerning His coming: ‘He comes in His Essence.’”

He said: “This amounts to supposition on the part of the person saying it, and attributing it to him is an error, as is clear from the explicit statement we have established from him.”

As for ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Yahyā al-Kinānī, the author of al-Hayda (The Evasion) and al-Radd ʿalā al-Jahmiyya wa-l-Qadariyya (Refutation of the Jahmiyya and the Qadariyya), his statements in al-Hayda and his refutation of the Jahmiyya admit of that interpretation. For the substance of al-Hayda is that he refuted Bishr al-Marīsī’s appeal to His words:

“Allah is the Creator of all things,”

and His words:

“Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Quran.”

He then advanced three arguments against al-Marīsī:

(The first was that he said: “If it is created, then you must say either that He created it within Himself, that He created it within something other than Himself, or that He created it as something subsisting independently in and of itself.”

He said: “If he says, ‘He created His speech within Himself,’ this is impossible, and there is no way to maintain it on the basis of analogy, reflection, or reason, for Allah cannot be a locus for temporally originated things

## Page 2605

and nothing created can exist within Him, nor can He be deficient such that something is added to Him when He creates it—exalted, majestic and supremely great is Allah, far above that.

If he says, ‘He created it within something other than Himself,’ then reflection and analogy necessarily commit him to saying that every utterance Allah creates within another is Allah’s speech; no distinction can be drawn between the two. Is poetry, then, to be considered Allah’s speech? Is filthy speech to be considered Allah’s speech? Are obscenity and disbelief to be considered Allah’s speech? Is every utterance that Allah has condemned, along with the one who uttered it, to be considered Allah’s speech? This is impossible. There is no way for him to establish or maintain it, given the manifest enormity, disgrace and disbelief it entails for anyone who says it.

If he says, ‘He created it as something subsisting independently in and of itself,’ this is an impossible falsehood that cannot be maintained on the basis of analogy, reflection or reason. Speech can only proceed from a speaker, just as will can only proceed from one who wills, knowledge from one who knows, and power from one who possesses power. No one has ever seen, nor will anyone ever see, speech subsisting independently and speaking by itself. Since its being created is impossible in all three of these ways, it is established that it is an attribute of Allah, and all of Allah’s attributes are uncreated.”

He and Bishr agreed that Allah existed when nothing else existed, and that He existed before He had acted or created anything.

Whoever claims that Allah does not address His servants or repeatedly recount His narratives and reiterate His commands and prohibitions to them is astray and an innovator. Rather, Allah, with all the attributes of His essence, is One, and has always been and will always remain so. I say:

In the hadith narrated by Salmān from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:
