## Page 2718

The twelfth response is as follows:

The principal argument of those who deny this is that, if He were receptive to these events from eternity, this would entail their existence, or the possibility of their existence, from eternity. They established this in the “well-known method” by arguing that whatever is receptive to a thing cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite. The majority disputed this “premise,” as did al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī, and others.

They say that every body necessarily possesses one member of each genus of accidents, because whatever is receptive to a thing cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite. For this reason, some turned instead to the following argument: if He were receptive to these events, His receptivity to them would be inseparable from His Essence. This requires the following explanation: if He were receptive to temporally originated events, He would never be devoid of an originated event or its opposite.

As for their statement, “Whatever is receptive to a thing is not devoid of its opposite,” it may be argued, on this approach, that this applies exclusively to Him and not to anything else. Alternatively, it may be said that it applies universally as well.

Their own associates then say to them: What you have stated concerning Him is refuted by the receptivity of all other subjects to the attributes they receive. If their receptivity to what they receive is inseparable from their essence, they must always be receptive to it. If it is an accidental property of their essence, then they are receptive to that receptivity. This necessarily entails either an infinite regress or an ultimate receptivity that is inseparable from the essence. It would therefore follow that, for everything receptive to anything, its receptivity to it is inseparable from its essence. Yet this is not the case, for human beings and other existing things are receptive to attributes in one state but not in another.

The answer to this is that a created being which is receptive to certain attributes in certain circumstances

---

## Page 2719

must have undergone a change that made it receptive to what it had not previously been receptive to. For example, as a person grows older, he acquires a receptivity to knowledge and understanding that he did not previously possess. This differs from a being whose essence has always remained in the same state and which then becomes receptive to something to which it was not previously receptive: that is impossible.

As for those who say that whatever is receptive to something must have its receptivity to it inseparable from its essence: if they claim that every body is receptive to every kind of accident, they say that this receptivity is inseparable from its essence. They also say that a body cannot be without one member of each kind of accident. Their assertion—that receptivity is inseparable from the essence of whatever is receptive—would thus serve as evidence for them on both questions. If, however, they do not make that claim, they say that bodies change, becoming receptive in one state to what they were not receptive to in another. They need not say that whatever is receptive to something cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite.

Those who say that whatever is receptive to something cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite may be answered as follows: at most, this entails that temporally originated events have always subsisted in Him, and we accept this implication. This is established in the thirteenth response, as follows:

Precisely the same holds for one who possesses power: whoever is capable of something cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite. This is why commanding something constitutes prohibiting its opposite, while prohibiting something constitutes commanding one of its opposites.

The majority said that what a prohibition requires is an act contrary to what is prohibited. It has also been said that refraining has positive existence and is what the one issuing the prohibition seeks. If someone capable of contrary acts could be devoid of

---

## Page 2720

all contrary acts, then being forbidden to perform some of them would not necessarily mean that he was commanded to perform any of the others, since he could refrain from that act without performing any of its contraries. Since, however, they regard him as commanded to perform some of them, it follows that whoever is capable of either of two contrary acts cannot be devoid of both. Accordingly, if the Lord has always possessed power, He must always have been performing some act or its opposite. This entails that He has always been acting. If it is possible that He has always been bringing about temporally originated events, it is also possible that He has always been receptive to them. This response can also be presented in a form that leaves no room for dispute.

(The fourteenth response:

It may be said: If whatever is receptive to something cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite, then whoever is capable of something cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite, since whoever possesses power is receptive to performing the act within his power. If receptivity to temporally originated events entails the possibility of their existence from eternity, then eternal power to bring about temporally originated events likewise entails the possibility of their existence from eternity. If it is possible to possess power while its object is impossible, it is also possible to be receptive while the object of that receptivity is impossible.

If it is said, “His receptivity to them is inseparable from His essence,” the reply is: “His power over them is inseparable from His essence.” Accordingly, if the perpetual occurrence of temporally originated events is possible, it is possible that He has always possessed power over them and been receptive to them. If their perpetual occurrence is not possible, then His receptivity to them and His power over them have become possible after not having been so. If this is admissible in one case, it is admissible in the other; if it is impossible in one, it is impossible in the other. Thus, “this question” comes back to the very possibility of exercising power to bring about temporally originated events perpetually, which is “

---

## Page 2721

the well-known principle.” Those imams of the Sunnah and hadith who affirm this principle—that He has always been able to speak by His will and power and to act by His will—allow this and affirm the possibility of temporally originated events having no beginning.

Thus, the arguments advanced by the leading “philosophers” for the eternity of the world do not establish the eternity of anything in the world. Rather, they establish only the principles upheld by the imams of the Sunnah and hadith who devote themselves to what the Messenger brought. The ultimate result of rigorously examining the rational arguments of speculative theologians and philosophical thinkers is thus to agree with, support, and serve what the messengers brought.

Those speculative theologians who do not affirm this, but instead maintain that the perpetual occurrence of temporally originated events is impossible, have no basis for distinguishing between His receptivity to them and His power over them. Among these theologians, those who say that He speaks by His will and power, with speech subsisting in His essence, hold a position closer to reason and revelation than those who say that His speech is created, or that eternal speech subsists in Him without His being able to speak by His power or His will.

Any position closer to reason and revelation deserves preference over positions further removed from them. And Allah Most High knows best.

## Page 2722

Section

Al-Rāzī said:

“The third argument”

The account of Allah’s close friend:

“I do not love those that set.”

Setting means change. This indicates that whatever undergoes change cannot be a god at all.

The response has several aspects:

First: We do not concede that setting means change. He has offered no proof for this, but merely asserted it.

Second: This contradicts the consensus of scholars of language and Quranic exegesis. Indeed, it contradicts what is necessarily known in religion, as well as the mass-transmitted record of linguistic usage and Quranic exegesis. For “setting” means disappearing from view. One says, afalat al-shamsu (the sun set), with the present-tense forms ta’fulu and ta’filu and the verbal noun ufūl, when it disappears from view.

No one has ever said that it means change, or that the sun is said to have set when its colour changes, or when it is moving through the sky. Nor is the wind said to have set when it blows, water when it flows, trees when they move, or human beings when they speak, walk, and perform their activities. Indeed, no one has ever said that a person who falls ill, or whose face turns yellow or red, is said to have set. This claim is thus among the gravest fabrications against Allah, against Allah’s close friend, and against

---

## Page 2723

the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, against His Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), who conveys His message, against the entire community of Muhammad, against all those versed in the language, and against everyone who understands the meanings of the Quran.

Third: The account of Allah’s close friend, peace be upon him, is evidence against you. When he saw a star and it moved towards the horizon, it had indeed moved, yet he did not regard it as having set. When he saw the moon rising, he saw it in motion, yet he did not regard it as having set. When he saw the sun rising, he knew that it was moving, yet he did not regard it as having set. As it moved until it disappeared—and likewise the moon until it disappeared—he did not regard it as having set.

Fourth: Regarding his statement that setting means change: if by change he means transformation, then the sun, moon, and stars did not undergo transformation by disappearing from view. If he means motion, the celestial body is continually moving.

The words,

“But when it set,”

indicate that it sometimes sets and at other times does not. For lammā (“when”) is a temporal adverb that links the time of one action to that of the other. The meaning is that, when it set,

“he said, ‘I do not love those that set.’”

He said this only when it set.

The words,

“But when it set,”

indicate that setting occurs anew, whereas motion is inseparable from it. Setting, therefore, is not motion. The terms “change” and “motion” are ambiguous. If what is meant is motion or the occurrence of temporal events within a thing, that is not the linguistic meaning of change. Setting is not motion, nor is motion change. Rather, setting is narrower in scope than motion, and change is narrower in scope than motion. As for change and setting, each is broader in one respect and narrower in another. Thus, a thing may undergo change without

---

## Page 2724

setting; it may set without undergoing change, move without undergoing change, or move without setting.

This holds even if change is narrower in scope than motion according to one of the two terminological usages. For “motion” may mean spatial motion, which does not necessarily entail change. It may also have a broader meaning, encompassing motion in quality and quantity, such as a plant’s motion through growth, or the motions of the human soul through love, contentment, anger, and remembrance. Such motion may be described as change, while in some contexts “change” may mean transformation.

In short, if an argument employing the term “change” is based on revelation, setting is not change. If it is a rational argument, and “change”—which is held to be impossible for the Lord—means the very matter under dispute, it cannot serve as evidence. If it means matters on which there is consensus, there is no dispute concerning them.

Still more unsound is the claim that setting means contingency, as Ibn Sīnā said: “Descending into the realm of contingency is, in a certain respect, a setting.” This would entail that everything other than Allah is setting and perpetually remains so, since everything other than Him is contingent and perpetually remains contingent. Setting would thus be an inseparable attribute of everything other than Allah, just as being contingent and dependent upon Allah is an inseparable attribute of it.

On this account, the sun, moon, and stars would always have been, and would forever remain, setting

---

## Page 2725

and everything in the heavens and the earth would perpetually be setting.

How, then, can His words make sense on that basis:

“But when it set, he said, ‘I do not love those that set’”?

According to these people who distort the words of Allah Most High and those of His intimate friend Abraham—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—away from their intended meanings, it was setting before it rose, from the moment it rose, and until it disappeared. Likewise, everything in the world, seen and unseen, is setting. Yet the Quran makes clear that when he saw it rising, he said:

“This is my Lord.”

Then, when it subsequently set, he said:

“I do not love those that set.”

And Allah knows best.

## Page 2726

And he said—may Allah Most High have mercy on him:

Section: A Noble Principle

“All the scriptural and rational proofs invoked by one who upholds falsehood point only to the truth; they do not support his position.”

This is obvious and known to everyone, for sound proof points only to truth, not falsehood. What remains is to examine individual proofs and explain how they do not support falsehood but instead support the truth. This provides a detailed exposition of that general principle.

The point here, however, is something else: the very proof invoked by someone who upholds falsehood, when given its due consideration, when the truth and falsehood within it are distinguished, and when its implications are clarified, turns out to demonstrate the falsity of his position on the very issue for which he invoked it. This is remarkable. I have reflected upon as many scriptural proofs as Allah willed, and have found this to be the case.

The aim here is to show that the same holds for the “rational proofs” upon which they rely concerning foundational matters, the universal sciences, and theology. As for “scriptural proofs,” I have already mentioned in this connection

---

## Page 2727

several examples of arguments advanced by the Jahmiyyah, the Rāfidah, and others. These include the Jahmiyyah’s appeal, in denying Allah’s attributes, to His words:

“Say: He is Allah, One;
Allah, the Eternal Refuge.”

It has been established in several places that these verses indicate the opposite of what they seek to prove and support affirming the attributes. This is discussed at length elsewhere in the refutation of the Jahmiyyah, which includes an examination of the foundations of their principles as compiled by Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Rāzī in his work entitled Ta’sīs al-Taqdīs (Establishing Divine Transcendence). He gathered most of their arguments in it, and I have seen no comparable work of theirs.

The same applies to their appeal, in denying that Allah will be seen, to His words:

“Vision cannot encompass Him, but He encompasses all vision.”

This verse affirms that He will be seen while denying that vision can encompass Him.

Likewise, they appeal to His words:

“There is nothing like Him,”

and similar passages. The same applies to the Shī‘ah’s appeal to His words:

“Your ally is none but Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe,”

and to the Prophet’s words:

“Are you not content to be to me as Aaron was to Moses?”

These and similar texts are evidence for the opposite of their doctrine, as explained at length in Minhāj Ahl al-Sunnah al-Nabawiyyah (The Path of the People of the Prophetic Sunnah), in refutation of the Rāfidah. There are numerous comparable examples.

Our concern here, however, is with “rational proofs,” for everyone with knowledge knows that scriptural evidence points only to the affirmation of the attributes. As for the Rāfidah, their mainstay is scriptural evidence, but they fabricated a great many hadiths, many of which gained acceptance among the people of the Sunnah. Many people transmitted some of these hadiths, until distinguishing truth from falsehood became difficult for most people, except the leading hadith scholars versed in the hidden defects of both their texts and their chains of transmission.

---

## Page 2728

Similarly, the Jahmiyyah advanced rational arguments that confused most people and gained acceptance among them, except for a few with expertise in these matters. Discussion of the Rāfidah’s hadiths and an explanation of how to distinguish truthful reports from fabricated ones can be found elsewhere, such as in the refutation of the Rāfidah.

Our concern here is to discuss the “rational proofs” invoked by proponents of falsehood among the Jahmiyyah, who deny Allah’s attributes, and among those who liken Him to His creation, as well as the proofs invoked by the Qadariyyah who deny divine decree and the Jahmī Qadariyyah who affirm compulsion. These two fundamental matters—“the attributes” and “divine decree,” also called divine oneness and justice—are the greatest and most momentous subjects discussed in the foundations of religion. The need to understand them is more universal, and knowing the truth concerning them is more beneficial than knowing it concerning other matters. Indeed, the same applies to all other rational and scriptural arguments advanced concerning the foundations of religion. At the foundation of all this is discussion of the Lord’s actions and words in relation to “the question of the world’s coming into existence” and “the question of the Quran and Allah’s speech.”

We therefore say: when someone with expertise carefully considers the arguments advanced by those who say that the Quran is eternal—such as al-Ash‘arī and his followers, and those who agreed with them, including al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā and his followers, Abū al-Ma‘ālī, Abū al-Walīd al-Bājī, Abū Mansūr al-Māturīdī, and others among the Hanbalīs, Shāfi‘īs, Mālikīs, and Hanafīs—these arguments, upon close examination, are found to support only the position of the early generations and the leading scholars, which is indicated by the Quran and Sunnah.

---

## Page 2729

Likewise, careful consideration of the arguments advanced by those who say that the Quran is created shows that they support only the position of the early generations and the leading scholars.

As for the first point: those who maintain that speech is eternal rely principally on two rational arguments. These are the arguments relied upon by al-Ash‘arī and his followers, and by those who agreed with them, such as al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā, Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī, and others like them. They are, in fact, the principal rational arguments of leading speculative theologians such as Ibn Kullāb, al-Ash‘arī, al-Qalānisī, and their like. They are also the mainstay of those who, in foundational matters such as this question and others like it, rely exclusively on rational arguments, such as Abū al-Ma‘ālī and his followers.

The first argument is that, if speech were not eternal, He would necessarily have been characterized from eternity by one of its opposites: either silence or muteness. If either of these were eternal, it could never cease, and He could never speak throughout the eternity to come. Since it is established that He speaks in beginningless eternity, it follows that He has always been speaking. Furthermore, muteness is a defect from which Allah is free.

The second argument is that, if speech were created, He would have created it either within Himself, within something other than Himself, or as something subsisting independently. The first is impossible, because it would entail His being a locus for temporally originated events. The second is invalid, because it would entail that the speech belonged to the locus in which it was created. The third is invalid, because speech is an attribute, and an attribute cannot subsist independently. Since all three possibilities are invalid, it necessarily follows that speech is eternal.

The response is: as for the first argument, it supports the position of the early generations—that He has always been speaking

---

## Page 2730

whenever He wills and however He wills. It therefore shows that speech is eternal in kind, not that He has not spoken by His will and power, or that speech is a single, eternal entity.

Likewise, the argument for the eternity of agency advanced by the “philosophers” who maintain that the world is eternal supports only the position of the early generations. Both those who argue for the eternity of a particular product of His action—the celestial sphere—and those who argue for the eternity of His particular speech offer sound proofs that do not establish their intended conclusions. Rather, those proofs support only the position of the early generations who followed the Messenger.

It thus becomes clear that sound “rational proofs,” from whichever group they come, establish the truthfulness of the Messenger and confirm what he conveyed, rather than contradicting his words. They are among Allah’s signs that establish the truthfulness of the prophets, concerning which Allah said:

“We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.”

They also form part of the balance that Allah Most High sent down. The same applies to the arguments of the “Muʿtazilah and Karrāmiyyah” and others, as we shall explain, Allah willing. For “the purpose here” is to discuss the arguments relied upon by the leading speculative thinkers among the Ashʿarīs and those like them, and among the philosophers and those like them. These two groups oppose one another in both East and West. Many people sometimes side with one group and sometimes with the other, such as al-Ghazālī, al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī, and others like them.

The purpose here is to explain how “rational proofs” support the position of the early generations, which is what the Quran and Sunnah teach.

We therefore say:

As for (the first argument, namely their assertion that if He were not speaking in beginningless eternity, He would have been characterized by its opposite—either silence or muteness—because He is living, and a living being, if not speaking, would be

---

## Page 2731

silent or mute, just as it would be deaf if it could not hear, and blind if it could not see; and because His essence is capable of speech, and whatever is capable of something cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite). This is how they argue for it.

This has been disputed, and rational thinkers have disagreed with them, including their own later followers, such as al-Rāzī and al-Āmidī. Those earlier thinkers claimed that, since a body is capable of bearing accidents, it must possess at least one accident of each kind. They said that air has taste, colour, and smell, but the majority disagreed with them.

The “argument,” however, can be formulated as follows: if the Lord Most High is capable of possessing an attribute, He cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite. Alternatively, one may say: if He is capable of possessing an attribute of perfection, He must possess it. For whatever the Lord is capable of possessing does not depend on anything other than Him for its existence in Him. Nothing other than Him makes Him either possess attributes or act. Rather, His essence alone necessitates whatever He is capable of possessing. Since His essence necessitates whatever He is capable of possessing, and His essence necessarily exists, whatever He can possess must necessarily exist in Him.

If it is supposed that He is capable of possessing either of two opposites, He cannot be without one of them. For if He were without either, the existence of one of them in Him would depend upon a cause other than His essence. The supposition is that He is capable of possessing it and that its existence in Him is possible. It is already known that this does not depend on anything other than Him; and if He did not bring it into existence and His essence did not necessitate it, its existence would otherwise be impossible. For nothing other than Him can cause it to exist in Him. If it comes into existence neither through Himself nor through anything else, it is impossible, whereas the supposition is that it is possible. Thus, whatever is possible for Him is necessary for Him.

---

## Page 2732

Thus, if you formulate the “argument” in this way, there is no need to say that everything capable of possessing something cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite. This universal claim is false. Rather, the claim is made specifically concerning Allah, on the basis of the evidence already mentioned and the distinction between Him and everything else. For when anything other than Him is capable of possessing something, its capacity comes from another—namely, Allah Most High. Allah need not bring that capacity into existence at the same time as the thing capable of possessing it. Rather, it may depend upon conditions that Allah brings about and impediments that He removes. Here, therefore, the capacity comes not from the thing itself but from another, so its essence alone is not sufficient for it.

As for the Lord Most High, none of His attributes or acts depends upon anything other than Him. Rather, He is the One, the Self-Sufficient, who has no need of anything besides Him. Everything besides Him needs Him and is made by Him. It is therefore impossible for the Lord to depend upon it, for that would constitute “circular dependence in causal priority,” which is impossible according to clear reason and the agreement of rational thinkers.

This, then, is the formulation of this argument establishing the “beginninglessness of speech” and that He has always spoken. It also establishes the beginninglessness of all His attributes and that His beginningless essence necessarily entails every attribute of perfection that He can possess. Thus, the Lord possesses every attribute of perfection in which there is no deficiency, and His possession of it is inseparable from His essence. He has always possessed the attributes of perfection, and His essence itself necessarily entails His perfect attributes. He cannot depend upon anything other than Himself for His possession of the attributes of perfection.

Speech is an attribute of perfection, for one who speaks is more perfect than one who does not, just as one who knows and has power is more perfect than one who neither knows nor has power. One who speaks by His will and power is more perfect than one who does not speak by His will and power, and more perfect than one who speaks without His will and power—if such a thing is conceivable.

The argument can also be formulated according to the principles of the early generations by saying: Either He is capable of

---

## Page 2733

speech or incapable of it. If He is incapable, He is mute; if He is capable but does not speak, He is silent. As for the Kullābiyyah, speech, in their view, does not fall within the scope of His power, so they cannot appeal to this argument.

It may therefore be asked: This argument establishes the beginninglessness of speech, but does it establish the beginninglessness of a particular speech that is not by His power and will? Or does it establish that He has always spoken by His will and power? The former is the position of the Kullābiyyah; the latter is the position of the early generations, the leading scholars, and the people of hadith and Sunnah.

The answer is that it establishes the latter, not the former. For speech subsisting in the speaker’s essence without his will and power is neither intelligible nor known, and judging something presupposes conceiving of it. Thus, whoever invokes this argument should be told: Neither you nor any rational person can conceive of speech subsisting in the speaker’s essence without his will and power. How, then, can you establish by rational evidence something that cannot be rationally conceived?

Furthermore, your statement, “If He did not possess the attribute of speech, He would possess the attributes of muteness and silence,” is intelligible only with respect to speech consisting of letters and sounds. For a living being who lacks these is not speaking: either he is capable of speech but does not speak, in which case he is silent, or he is incapable of it, in which case he is mute.

As for what they claim to be “inner speech,” it is not intelligible that someone who lacks it would thereby be silent or mute. Thus, even supposing that it exists, it does not follow that whoever lacks it must be silent or mute.

---

## Page 2734

Furthermore, you have not established what the beginningless “inner” speech you affirm actually is. Indeed, you have not even conceived of it. Affirming something presupposes conceiving of it, so how can someone legitimately affirm something he has not conceived of?

For this reason, Abū Saʿīd ibn Kullāb—the leader of this group and its foremost authority on this question—offers nothing intelligible in explaining it. Rather, he says, “It is a meaning incompatible with silence and muteness.” Yet silence and muteness can only be conceived once speech is conceived: a silent person is someone who refrains from speaking, while a mute person is someone incapable of speech, or whose organs of speech have suffered an impairment that prevents him from speaking. Thus, one cannot understand silence and muteness until one understands speech, yet one cannot understand speech until one understands silence and muteness.

It is therefore clear that they have neither conceived of what they assert nor established it. Rather, in their account of speech, they resemble the Christians in their account of the Word and their assertions concerning the “hypostases,” the Trinity, and “union”: they assert things they neither conceive of nor explain.

When the “messengers,” peace be upon them, inform us of something we cannot conceive of, we must believe them. But whatever is established through reason must be conceived of by the person asserting it; otherwise, he is speaking without knowledge. The Christians speak without knowledge, and so their discourse is contradictory and yields no intelligible account. Likewise, whoever speaks about Allah’s speech without knowledge falls into contradiction and produces no intelligible account.

For this reason, one criticism levelled against these people was that, concerning a foundation of their religion and the true nature of speech—Allah’s speech and the speech of all creation—they relied as proof upon the words of a Christian poet called al-Akhtal:

“Speech lies indeed within the heart;
The tongue was made only to reveal the heart.”

---

## Page 2735

Some have said that this is not his poetry. Even supposing that it is, neither rational truths nor the meaning of the word “speech,” as used by all the children of Adam, can be determined by appealing to the words of a thousand accomplished poets, let alone a Christian poet named al-Akhtal. The Christians are known to make false claims concerning Allah’s Word. In Arabic, khatal means error in speech. As one poet recited concerning them:

“Shame on him who casts the Quran behind his back,
Then, when offering proof, says: ‘Al-Akhtal said.’”

When the Kullābiyyah advanced this argument, the Muʿtazilah countered:

“In our view, speech is like action as both you and we understand it. We all hold that in pre-eternity He was not acting, then began to act. Yet neither we nor you say that in pre-eternity He was incapable or silent. Just as He was not acting, yet is not described by the opposite of action—incapacity or silence—so He was not speaking, yet is not described by the opposite of speech—silence or muteness.”

When these people say to the Muʿtazilah and Jahmiyyah, “In both our view and yours, action does not subsist in Him, whereas speech subsists in Him and is therefore like the attributes,” the Muʿtazilah reject this and say: “In our view, speech is like action: neither the one nor the other subsists in Him.”

If they then say, “If speech did not subsist in Him, it would subsist in another, and speech would be an attribute of that other,” they have moved on to “the second argument.” The first could not be established except through the second; thus, reasoning from the first and making it “a second argument” was invalid. For this reason, many of their later scholars abandoned it and relied only on “the second,” as did Abū al-Maʿālī and his followers.

---

## Page 2736

This objection does not apply to the early generations. For if their opponents say, “Speech is like action, and neither we nor you hold that He was acting in pre-eternity,” the early generations and the Muslim majority reject this premise, saying: “Rather, He has always been creating and acting.” This is the position of the early generations and the majority of Muslim groups. It is also what Ibn Khuzaymah’s associates stated in what they wrote to him, although they were Kullābīs. Thus, this must have been either Ibn Kullāb’s position or that of a group of his followers. On this basis, their argument holds. Otherwise, if someone concedes that He began to act after not acting, this argument is undermined by his own premise, and his opponents can say: “What is said about His speech applies equally to His action.”

The view that the act of creating is distinct from the created thing, and that it is an act subsisting in the Lord, is the position of most Muslims. It is the position of the Hanafīs and most Hanbalīs, and the position to which al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā ultimately returned. It is what al-Baghawī reported from Ahl al-Sunnah, and what Abū Bakr al-Kalābādhī reported from the Sufis in his book al-Ta‘arruf li-madhhab al-tasawwuf (An Introduction to the Sufi Way). It is also what al-Bukhārī reported as the scholars’ consensus in his book Af‘āl al-‘ibād (The Actions of Allah’s Servants), and what Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr and others reported from Ahl al-Sunnah.

But is action a single pre-eternal reality, like will? Or does it originate within His Essence? Or is it a kind of activity with which He has always been characterized? Muslims hold three positions on this. They all agree that everything other than Allah has been brought into existence and is created, as has been transmitted from the prophets through innumerable reports and established by rational proofs. The claim that alongside Allah there is something eternal among His effects, which He preceded—as some philosophers maintain—is invalid according to both reason and revelation, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

---

## Page 2737

If it is said:

“If you maintain that He has always spoken by His will, this entails the existence of speech without a beginning. And if He has always spoken, He must continue to do so forever; thus, He speaks with speech that has no end. This entails the existence of an infinite number of temporal events, for every word preceded by another comes into existence in time. Yet the existence of an infinite number is impossible.”

The reply is:

“This implication is correct.” Indeed, they affirm that Allah’s words have no end, as He, the Most High, says:

“Say, ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as a supplement.’”

As for their assertion that the existence of an infinite number of temporal events is impossible, this rests on their proof that the world and bodies came into existence: bodies are never free of temporal events, and whatever is never free of temporal events must itself have come into existence. This proof is invalid according to both reason and revelation. It is the foundation of the speculative theology condemned by the early generations and the imams, and the foundation of the position of the Jahmiyyah, who deny the divine attributes. Its invalidity has been demonstrated elsewhere. Nevertheless, we shall explain, if Allah wills, that once the truth in this proof is distinguished from its falsehood, it demonstrates that everything other than Allah came into existence and supports the position of the early generations.

Their error lay in their assertion: “Everything that is never free of temporal events—that is, contingent things dependent on another—must itself have come into existence.” They adopted this as a “universal proposition” and used it to draw a false analogy between the Creator and created beings. Likewise, those others asserted, “Whatever is receptive to something cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite,” adopting this as a “universal proposition.”

Error in “analogical reasoning” arises from likening something to what differs from it, and from formulating a universal proposition on the basis of a shared feature without distinguishing between its two categories. This, then, is “false analogical reasoning”

---

## Page 2738

such as the analogy of those who said, “Trade is only like usury,” the analogy of Iblīs, and other such false analogies concerning which some of the early generations said:

“The first to reason by analogy was Iblīs, and the sun and moon were worshipped only through analogies.”

They meant the analogical reasoning of those who oppose revealed texts and those who draw false analogies. Any analogy that contradicts a revealed text can only be false. Sound analogical reasoning, however, belongs to the balance that Allah has sent down. It never contradicts a revealed text; rather, it agrees with it.

This also makes clear that whatever sound rational proofs the philosophers possess support the position of the early generations as well. Their principal argument for “the beginninglessness of the world” rests on the claims that the Lord has always acted; that He cannot begin acting after not having acted; that action cannot become possible for Him after having been impossible; and that He cannot become capable after having been incapable. This argument, and everything else they have adduced, establishes only the beginninglessness of action as a kind. It does not establish that anything in the world has no beginning, whether a celestial sphere or anything else.

Thus, if it is said that He has always acted by His will and power, and that action necessarily accompanies life—as some of the imams of the Sunnah have stated—this affirms what all their sound rational proofs entail. It also agrees with the statement of the early generations:

“He has always spoken whenever He wills.”

He has therefore always spoken whenever He wills and acted as He wills. Everything that the Kullābiyyah, the Ashʿariyyah, the Sālimiyyah and others have adduced to establish the beginninglessness of speech proves only that He has always spoken whenever He wills. It does not establish the beginninglessness of speech independent of His will, nor that any particular speech has no beginning. Rather, it establishes the beginninglessness of speech as a kind.

---

## Page 2739

And all the arguments the philosophers adduce for the beginninglessness of activity establish only that He has always done whatever He wills. They do not establish the beginninglessness of any particular act or any particular effect—neither the celestial sphere nor anything else.

The error shared by both groups arose from confusing a perpetually existing kind with a particular individual instance. One group then said:

“Motion and action as kinds cannot be beginningless, because a series of events without a beginning is impossible.”

They thus denied that the Lord has always spoken by His will and has always acted by His will. Indeed, their position entails that He was incapable of acting and then became capable, and that He was also incapable of speaking by His will.

Some of them, such as the Karrāmiyyah, say that He became capable of speaking by His will after having been incapable of doing so. Others say that He did not become capable of speech and can never speak by His will. These are the Kullābiyyah and those who agree with them among the Ashʿariyyah and the Sālimiyyah.

As for the “philosophers,” they adopted the position of their leading figure, Aristotle: anyone who says that “motion as a kind” came into existence after not having existed is defying his own reason. They maintained that events as a kind cannot come into existence after not having existed without a newly occurring cause, and that this is known necessarily.

They may be answered as follows:

This establishes that this kind has always existed; it does not establish the beginninglessness of the particular motion of the celestial sphere. The same applies to time and body. Their proofs entail that motion has always existed, together with its measure, which is time, and its agent, which they call body. But they do not entail the beginninglessness of any particular thing.

Thus, if it is said that the Lord of all worlds has always spoken by His will and done whatever He wills, then action as a kind has always existed, as has its measure, which is time. Aristotle and his followers, however, erred in supposing that there is no time except the measure of the celestial sphere’s motion, and that there is no motion above the celestial sphere or prior to it. Thus, on their account, its motion had to be beginningless.

---

## Page 2740

But in this they are astray, according to both reason and revelation.

There is no evidence that motion above the celestial sphere or prior to it is impossible. Their argument concerning the splitting of the celestial sphere is utterly unsound, as has been explained at length elsewhere. Likewise, his claim that every motion must have an unmoved mover is utterly unsound, as has been explained at length in its proper place.

The purpose here is to point out that the substance of what these leading theologians and philosophers—said to be the foremost authorities in rational inquiry—have to offer supports only the position of the early generations and the adherents of the Sunnah who follow the Quran and Sunnah. Whatever sound arguments they possess support only this position. But truth became confused with falsehood in their minds, just as the People of the Book mingled truth with falsehood. Whatever truth the latter possess agrees with what was brought by the unlettered Messenger, whom they find described in their Torah and Gospel; it does not contradict it.

The scriptural proofs brought by the prophets do not contradict one another. Nor do sound rational proofs contradict one another, and neither do scriptural and rational proofs contradict each other. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 2741

Section

A group of leading speculative thinkers—versed in theology and philosophy—sought to combine the proofs of both groups. They regarded this as the highest attainment in knowledge and called the “response” with which they answered the philosophers’ arguments “the brilliant response.” They agreed with each of the two groups, thereby falling into error and contradiction because they combined the errors of both. Their arguments thus undermined one another, since the errors of the two groups were utterly contradictory.

Had they instead combined what each group got right, this would have accorded with the scriptural proofs conveyed by the messengers and with rational proofs, such as those to which the messengers directed people. Yet these thinkers departed from what scriptural and rational proofs entail, while imagining that they had attained the pinnacle of rigorous inquiry. In this they followed the example of both groups, for each likewise contravenes what scriptural and rational proofs entail.

The truth is precisely that upon which scriptural and rational proofs concur. This is the position held by the early generations of this community and its leading scholars, who received it from the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—both through what he conveyed and through his teaching and explanation of rational proofs. Yet these thinkers claim that the messengers did not explain this issue, as stated by

---

## Page 2742

al-Rāzī at the beginning of al-Matālib al-‘Āliya (The Lofty Pursuits). They thus claimed that the messengers conveyed no report concerning this issue, let alone explained the rational proofs confirming what they conveyed.

We have discussed elsewhere the unsoundness of what he said on this matter. Our purpose here is to draw attention to the approach of those who sought to combine the proofs of both groups and claimed to possess “the brilliant response.” Al-Rāzī presented this approach in his books and favored it. Al-Armawī adopted it from him and mentioned it in the Book of Forty, and al-Qushayrī al-Misrī adopted it from him. This position resembles the doctrine of the Harnānians, who maintained the existence of five eternal entities—a doctrine that Muhammad ibn Zakariyyā al-Rāzī defended and wrote about. Al-Rāzī lends support to this doctrine in his compendium and elsewhere, although it is internally contradictory, as Muhammad ibn Zakariyyā al-Balkhī, Abū Hātim—the author of Kitāb al-Zīna (The Book of Adornment)—and others demonstrated by exposing its unsoundness. Nevertheless, there is a difference between the doctrine of the Harnānians and that of these thinkers, as we shall explain, if Allah wills.

These thinkers said: “The speculative theologians established proofs only that bodies came into being. For it was bodies that they showed could not be devoid of events that come into being; and whatever cannot be devoid of such events must itself have come into being, since an unceasing succession of events without a beginning is impossible.”

They said: “The speculative theologians offered no proof ruling out the existence of anything other than bodies and the Maker. The philosophers, however, affirmed other existents: intellects and souls.”

They said: “The speculative theologians established no proof that these do not exist, and their proof that things came into being did not encompass them.”

---

## Page 2743

They said: “Nor did the philosophers establish any proof that bodies are eternal. Rather, they established proofs that the Lord has never ceased to act, and that motion and time have always existed. Their principal argument is that the First possesses all the conditions of agency from eternity, so His action must necessarily accompany Him.”

They said: “It is impossible for events to come into being without a newly arising cause. It is impossible that the Lord should have remained inactive from eternity and that action should then have occurred without a newly arising cause. It is impossible for Him to become capable after not having been capable. And it is impossible for action to become possible after having been impossible, without a newly arising cause, thus passing from intrinsic impossibility to intrinsic possibility.”

They said: “If everything indispensable for an agent to act exists from eternity, the action must necessarily exist; for if it does not exist, it remains dependent upon some further condition. We have stated that everything indispensable for the agent to act has existed from eternity. If it is said that everything indispensable for the agent to act has existed, yet the action did not exist and only subsequently came into being without a cause, this would entail the existence of a contingent thing being favored over its nonexistence without a sufficient determining factor. For when a determining factor is sufficient, the alternative it favors must prevail. If that alternative does not prevail, then, if the action can either exist or not exist—and a contingent thing requires a determining factor—it must have such a factor for as long as its existence and nonexistence remain possible. Once the sufficient determining factor is present, the action’s existence becomes necessary; its existence and nonexistence are then no longer both possible.”

---

## Page 2744

These scholars said:

This is the principal argument of these philosophers. Its underlying principle is that anything that comes into being must have a newly arising cause. That something should come into being without a newly arising cause is self-evidently impossible to reason.

For this reason, the various answers offered by the speculative theologians were all unsound. Some said that the determining factor is knowledge; others said it is will; others said it is simply the fact that He possesses power; and others said that the determining factor is action becoming possible after having been impossible—not its impossibility from eternity—and so forth.

They said that these answers are invalid for two reasons:

First, if everything mentioned existed from eternity, it falls under the first alternative; if it did not exist from eternity, it falls under the second. We have already said that if everything required for causal efficacy is eternal, the effect must necessarily be eternal. If, however, some of those requirements are not eternal and subsequently come into being, this entails the existence of a contingent thing being favored over its nonexistence without a determining factor, and events coming into being without anything bringing them about. For if that which completes the cause were brought into being, while the cause had not been complete from eternity, this would have arisen without a cause.

“The second reason”: power, will, knowledge, and eternity itself bear the same relation to the time when the world came into being as they do to what precedes and follows it. It is therefore impossible for these to necessitate its existence at that particular time rather than before or after it.

Al-Rāzī said in his “Great Book”:

“The brilliant answer is to say: the soul was eternal and perpetually in motion. Then, from those successive motions, a particular attribute arose that caused bodies to come into being. This establishes a newly arising cause that necessitated bodies coming into being at that particular time. Accordingly, bodies came into being, as is entailed by the arguments of the speculative theologians; and the Agent has never ceased to act, since the soul, which is His effect, is eternal, as is entailed by the arguments of

---

## Page 2745

the philosophers.”

They may also say:

“The measure of its motion is time. Thus, we affirm the implications of motion and time having existed from eternity as a kind, while maintaining that bodies came into being.”

This, then, is the position of those who follow both groups.

We have already said that they followed each group precisely where it erred. Their contradiction arises because the speculative theologians based their argument that bodies came into being solely on the impossibility of events having no beginning. This is their mainstay. Otherwise, once the existence of beginningless events is admitted, every event could have been preceded by another event. It would then no longer follow that the subject in which successive events occur must itself have come into being.

If this principle upon which the speculative theologians built their argument is sound and established, then an infinite succession of motions is impossible, whether in the soul or anything else. Anyone who accepts the implications of this principle while also affirming beginningless events in the soul or elsewhere therefore contradicts himself.

“The real implication of his position” is that beginningless events are impossible, yet beginningless events must exist. If, however, this principle is false, their arguments that bodies came into being are invalid, and the possibility of beginningless events necessarily follows. In that case, their kind may have existed from eternity. To maintain that they must all have come into being—and that the cause of their coming into being is a state of the soul—is therefore contradictory.

“Furthermore,” according to the philosophers, the soul cannot exist without a body, nor can motion occur in it except in conjunction with a body. It is a soul only when conjoined with a body, as the human soul is with its body. Thus, if the soul of the celestial sphere separates from “matter”—that is, hyle

---

## Page 2746

which is body—just as the human soul separates from its body at death, then, in their view, it becomes an intellect incapable of motion. His supposition of a soul separate from body and perpetually in motion is therefore not something they affirm, nor is there any evidence for it. His supposition thus remains one neither maintained by his opponent nor supported by evidence. This resembles the doctrine of the Harnānians, but is not identical to it.

They say that there are five eternal entities: the Lord, the soul, matter, time, and space. However, they do not say that the soul has always been in motion. Rather, they say that it came to turn its attention toward hyle, which is matter, and grew to love it passionately. The best way to free it from matter was to let it taste the bitter consequences of this attachment. So He fashioned the world and placed the soul together with bodies, so that it might taste the burning heat and bitter consequences of this union and long to escape it.

For this reason, Muhammad ibn Zakariyyā al-Rāzī says: “There is no pleasure whatsoever in this world. Rather, the soul remains tormented until it escapes, and its repose lies in deliverance.”

He was once attending the gathering of a dignitary and illustrated this by the sound that escapes involuntarily from a person’s anus, representing it as coming from that dignitary. Al-Kaʿbī said to him: “You have become entangled in grave difficulties and have not extricated yourself. You were merely trying to avoid an event occurring without a cause. Yet you may be asked: What necessitated the soul’s turning toward hyle at that particular time, rather than before or after it? This, too, is an event without a cause.”

---

## Page 2747

This doctrine contains several kinds of error. Among them is the affirmation, without proof, of an eternal entity other than the First. Another is the affirmation of a soul separate from body that can move without a body. This contradicts the doctrine of Aristotle and his followers. These people, however, say: “We maintain that the soul has motion despite being separate from body.” This is correct, but they may be told:

“You have asserted that it is eternal, that it had always been motionless, and that it then moved without a cause. This is untenable. You have offered no proof of its eternity, nor even of its existence and its not being a body.”

Likewise, those philosophers who affirm intellects and souls that cannot be pointed to may be told: “All your arguments for this are weak—indeed, invalid.” Hence al-Tūsī, the foremost of their later thinkers, came to hold that there is no proof establishing their existence.

As for the dialectical theologians, they say: “We know self-evidently that a contingent being must be such that one can point to it as being here or there. Thus, affirming something that cannot be pointed to is self-evidently untenable.” They have stated this in their books.

Al-Rāzī’s claim that they have offered no proof that contingent beings are confined to bodies and accidents is therefore incorrect. Rather, they said: “We know self-evidently that a contingent being must be such that one can point to it, with one side distinguishable from another.” Moreover, many of them—of this group—stated this without qualification concerning the eternal and the originated, and eternal, beginningless sounds.

Some of these people then said: “Despite this, they constitute a single attribute.” Others said: “Rather, they are multiple.” Some of them said that those beginningless sounds are

---

## Page 2748

the sounds heard from the reciters—or that two sounds are heard from the reciters: a beginningless sound and an originated sound. Regarding the beginningless sound, some said that it indwells the originated sound. Others said that it becomes manifest in it without indwelling it. Still others said: “It is in it, but we do not say that it becomes manifest or indwells.” Those holding this view are a group of scholars of hadith and jurisprudence and practitioners of Sufism among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others. They uphold indwelling with respect to the divine attributes, but not the divine essence.

Another group, from among the Sālimiyyah and the Sufis, agreed with them. These latter also maintain that the divine essence indwells everything and that He manifests Himself to everything in its form. Their position is of the same kind as that of those who say that He is, in His essence, in every place, and those who uphold “the unity of existence.” Yet they also say that He is upon the Throne, that He indwells the hearts of those who know Him in His essence, and that He is in everything, as stated by Abū Tālib al-Makkī and others like him.

The Ashʿarīs, by contrast, take the opposite position. Their doctrine entails negation of the divine reality: that He is neither within the world nor outside it, that His speech is a single meaning, and that the meaning of the Verse of the Throne, the verse concerning debt, the Torah, and the Gospel is one and the same. The invalidity of this is self-evident. Likewise, words, according to them, are one single thing. Their position thus amounts to saying that there is no Lord, no Quran, and no faith. Their doctrine therefore entails negation of the divine reality.

The Sālimiyyah uphold indwelling with respect to both the divine essence and the attributes, whereas those who say that beginningless letters and sounds indwell human beings uphold indwelling with respect to the attributes, but not the essence.

---

## Page 2749

And some of them also say that the servant’s attribute—namely, his faith—is beginningless. Some extend this to his words, but not his deeds. Others say that even his commanded deeds are beginningless, though not his prohibited deeds. Some suspend judgment regarding prohibited deeds, while others say that all human deeds, good and evil alike, are beginningless, because they fall under divine legislation and decree, and divine legislation and decree are beginningless. This fails to distinguish between the Lord’s act of legislating and what He prescribes, or between His decree and what He decrees.

These people say that human deeds are beginningless, meaning not the movements themselves, but what those movements produce, such as what comes on the Day of Resurrection as the reward for their deeds. The imams—Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others—have explicitly stated that all of this is created. These people thus went to excess in asserting that deeds are beginningless in order to carry their position on faith through consistently.

“Another group” said: If these letters, which are sounds heard from the servant, are beginningless, then all audible letters are beginningless. They therefore said that all human speech is beginningless except for its arrangement. Some of them said that all sounds are beginningless, even the sounds of animals and whatever sounds come from human beings. They also said that the movements of the tongue when reciting the Quran are beginningless, as are the movements of the fingers when writing the Quran.

Some of them said that the “ink” is created, but the shapes of the letters are beginningless. Others suspended judgment regarding the ink, saying: We remain silent about it; even though it is created, it should not be called created. Still others said that the ink itself is beginningless.

Some among these people and others maintained that “the souls of human beings are beginningless.” Thus they came to say:

---

## Page 2750

The servant’s soul is created, while his speech is beginningless, and the attributes inhering in him, such as his faith, are beginningless. Their fellows explicitly state that his acts are beginningless. This goes beyond what is affirmed of the Lord Himself, for He, glorified be He, is beginningless and eternal, whereas His acts occur anew, one after another. Likewise, He has always spoken by His will, one utterance after another.

These people maintain that the servant’s soul is beginningless, as is light—the light of the sun and moon, lamplight, and every other light. In claiming that human souls and lights are beginningless, they have echoed the position of the Magians and “the Sabian philosophers” who resemble the Magians. Some Sabians do indeed resemble the Magians, as al-Hasan al-Basrī and others stated when they said of the Sabians: They are like the Magians. These are a class of polytheistic Sabians, not among the Sabians praised in the Quran.

The point is that their claim that the spirits and “souls” of human beings, which depart from their bodies, are beginningless is of the same kind as the claim that the soul is beginningless, discussed earlier. However, these people regard them as being from Allah, since, according to them, nothing is beginningless except Allah and His attributes. Their claim that light is beginningless is of the same kind as the Magians’ position, except that they also regard light as one of Allah’s attributes.

All these claims—that the servant’s soul, words, acts, or sounds are beginningless, or that the light of the sun and moon and similar things is beginningless—are ramifications of that underlying premise. For the “early generations” said: The Quran is the speech of Allah, uncreated. A group supposed that they meant it was beginningless and had always existed. Since the Quran consists of letters and sounds, they concluded that it must be beginningless; and what is heard is the Quran

---

## Page 2751

and it is nothing but the servants’ voices reciting the Quran, so these must be beginningless. Then, upon examining the matter, they found themselves obliged to apply their claims consistently.

The same applies to “faith.” None of the early generations—neither Ahmad ibn Hanbal nor anyone else—ever said that any of the servants’ attributes was uncreated or beginningless. Nor did they describe the Quran as beginningless. Rather, they objected to unqualified assertions that the utterance of the Quran or faith was created. These people then understood “uncreated” to mean “beginningless.” They supposed that an objection to the unqualified assertion that something was created permitted one to say that it was uncreated and beginningless. Thus they said: The servant’s utterance and voice are beginningless, and his faith is beginningless. They then extended their claims consistently to the conclusions we have mentioned.

These matters have been discussed at length elsewhere, in detailed answers to several questions submitted by questioners. This is not the place for those discussions; the purpose here is to draw attention to what follows from this innovated premise.

Underlying all of this is the Jahmiyyah’s argument that bodies have a beginning: whatever is never free of newly occurring events must itself have a beginning. Thus, any being in whom speech subsists by his own choice or will, and who has always been thus, must have a beginning. This committed them to denying the Lord’s speech and action—indeed, to negating His very essence. Matters then culminated in treating created things as beginningless while negating the Lord’s beginningless attributes—indeed, His very essence. And Allah knows best.

Those who uphold this premise and affirm the “indivisible atom” say that the very entities present in the human body and elsewhere existed beforehand, and that their coming into existence cannot be known

---

## Page 2752

except through a proof—namely, the argument that bodies have a beginning because they have never been free of accidents. They say: What observation establishes is only that their composition has a beginning, just as those others say concerning the servant’s speech that only the arrangement of the letters is newly produced.

Those who uphold “the unity of existence” say that the servant’s very existence is identical to the Lord’s existence. I have personally dealt with proponents of all these views—prominent people—and what passed between us concerning these matters would take too long to describe. Allah guided whomever He willed among His creation. Consider, then, how confused people have become about their own selves, concerning which they were told:

“And in yourselves—will you not then see?”

The philosophers say: The matter of the human body, and all other matter, has existed from eternity, without beginning. These views resemble Pharaoh’s claim in certain respects. The proponents of “unity” openly exalt Pharaoh and maintain that he spoke the truth when he said:

“I am your highest lord.”

There is therefore a lesson in Allah’s repetition of Pharaoh’s story in the Quran, for people need to take heed of it. As He said:

“So We made them a precedent and an example for those who came after.”
