## Page 2753

Section:

As for their “second argument,” which is the mainstay of most of them, it may be set out as follows: If it were created, He would have to create it either within Himself, within something else, or without a locus.

The first would entail His being a locus for temporally originated events, which is invalid. The second would entail its being an attribute of the locus in which it inheres. For when an attribute inheres in a locus, it is that locus—not something else—that is characterized by it. Thus, when knowledge, life, power, speech, or any other attribute inheres in a locus, that locus is what is described as living, knowing, powerful, and speaking, just as it is described as moving when motion inheres in it, or as black or white when blackness or whiteness inheres in it, and so forth. As for its subsisting without a locus, that is impossible, since it is an attribute.

The meaning of “this argument” is also sound. Yet it supports only the position of the early Muslim generations. It demonstrates the falsity of the Ash‘arīs’ position just as it demonstrates the falsity of the Mu‘tazilīs’ position and that of the Jahmīs generally. For, among “these alternatives,” the majority of the Mu‘tazilīs and Jahmīs chose the view that He creates it in a locus. They said: When Allah spoke to Moses, He created a sound in the tree, and that created sound coming from the tree was His speech.

---

## Page 2754

This is one of the views for which the imams of the Sunnah declared its adherents to be disbelievers. They said that it entails that the tree itself said:

“I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me.”

For speech belongs to the one in whom it subsists. This is what all people understand, especially since the evidence establishes that Allah gives speech to everyone who speaks. Thus Allah will give speech to people’s skins on the Day of Resurrection, and they will say:

“Allah, who has given speech to all things, has given us speech.”

Thus every utterance in existence would be something He creates in a locus. If what He creates in another were His speech, it would necessarily follow that all speech in existence—even expressions of disbelief, wickedness, and falsehood—was His speech. Exalted is He above that! This is a necessary implication of the position of the determinist Jahmīs. They say that Allah creates His servants’ deeds and words, while, according to them, the servant does nothing and has no power that has any effect in bringing about the act. Hence one of their shaykhs—an adherent of the oneness of existence—said:

All speech in existence is His speech;
Prose or verse—it is all the same to us.

As for the Muʿtazilīs, they do not say that Allah creates His servants’ deeds, but the argument commits them to that conclusion. Their accomplished thinkers, such as Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī, have acknowledged that an act occurs only when there is a motive prompting the agent, and that when the motive and the power are both present, the act must occur. He also said that the motive within the servant is created by Allah. This explicitly affirms the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah, even though he did not use the expression “the creation of the servants’ deeds.” If, then, he says that Allah created the motive and the power—and creating them necessarily entails creating the act—he has conceded the point.

Since this was firmly established in the minds of people generally, it was said by Sulaymān ibn

---

## Page 2755

Dāwūd al-Hāshimī, the imam—a peer of Ahmad ibn Hanbal—concerning whom al-Shāfi'ī said, “I left no one in Baghdad more discerning than these two men: Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd al-Hāshimī”:

“Whoever says that the Quran is created must accept that Pharaoh’s utterance is Allah’s speech, for Allah created in Pharaoh his saying:

‘I am your lord most high.’

According to them, Allah created in the tree the words:

‘Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me.’

If this is His speech because He created it, then the other utterance is also His speech.”

The Ash'arīs and others among Ahl al-Sunnah refuted the claim of the Mu'tazilīs and Jahmīs that He created His speech in another by saying: Any accident Allah creates in another is an attribute of that other, and it is that locus which is characterized accordingly; it is not an attribute of Allah, as explained above. This is “a sound and cogent argument.”

However, the Ash'arīs did not apply it consistently. The Mu'tazilīs therefore gained an argumentative advantage over them: they describe Him as Creator, Provider, Giver of life, Bringer of death, just, and beneficent, without any of these meanings subsisting in Him; rather, they subsist in another. For according to them, creation is the created thing itself, and giving life is the existence of life in a living being, without any act subsisting in the Lord. Thus, they have described Him as the Giver of life on account of life existing in another, and likewise described Him as the Bringer of death. This is one of the objections the Mu'tazilīs raised against them, to which they gave no sound answer.

But “the Salaf and the majority” hold that the act also subsists in Him. This “principle” provides them with an argument against both groups. Both groups divide attributes into attributes of essence and attributes of action, or into attributes of essence, qualitative attributes, and attributes of action. This is a fallacy, for according to them no act subsists in Him, nor is there

---

## Page 2756

any attribute of action belonging to Him, according to them. If they attribute qualities to Him on the basis of what He creates in another, they must say: He is in motion, black, white, tall, short, sweet, bitter, sour, and so forth, among the qualities He creates in another.

Moreover, they contradict themselves: one group describes Him by the speech He creates in another, while the other describes Him by everything created in another. It is thus clear that He is characterized only by what subsists in Him, not by what He creates in another. This is the very nature of an attribute: anything described is described only by what subsists in it, not by something separate from it that is an attribute of something else. If they also deny that attributes subsist in Him, they must conclude that He has no attributes, whether of essence or of action.

If they say, “We have called the act an attribute only because He is described in terms of action, and is thus called Creator and Provider,” the reply is: No one who affirms the attributes can consistently say this, for according to them an attribute subsists in the one described; it is not merely the statement of the one describing.

If this is said by someone who holds that an attribute is simply a description—merely the statement of the one describing—then, unless that statement accords with reality, the speaker is lying. This is why description occurs in the Quran only in connection with falsehood: it is a description that subsists in the one describing, without anything corresponding to it subsisting in the one described. Thus, Allah, glorified is He, says:

“He will repay them for their descriptions.”

“Do not falsely declare with your tongues, ‘This is lawful and this is unlawful,’ fabricating lies against Allah.”

“They attribute to Allah what they dislike, while their tongues falsely claim that the best will be theirs.”

“Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, far above what they describe.”

It has, however, also been used in connection with truth, in the report recorded in the two Sahīhs from ‘Ā’ishah:

“That

---

## Page 2757

a man used to recite frequently, ‘Say: He is Allah, the One.’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Ask him why he does that.’ He replied, ‘Because it describes the Most Merciful, and I love it.’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Tell him that Allah loves him.’”

Anyone who describes something by a quality it does not possess is lying. Thus, whoever describes Allah as Creator, Provider, knowing and powerful, yet also says that He Himself does not possess knowledge and power, or does not perform the acts of creation and giving life, has described Him by something while saying that He does not possess it. He has thereby contradicted his own description of his Lord and combined two contradictories, saying, “He possesses this quality; He does not possess this quality.”

This is the reality of the statements made by those who deny the attributes: they affirm things that are true, yet say what entails their negation. They thus combine two contradictories, and the contradiction becomes apparent in their statements. In effect, they say that He exists but does not exist, knows but does not know, and is alive but is not alive. For this reason, the extremists among them refrain from both affirmation and negation: they describe Him neither affirmatively nor negatively, as has been explained at length elsewhere. Yet it is known that excluding both negation and affirmation is also false, for two contradictories can neither both hold nor both fail to hold.

The point here is that this sound “premise”—that if He created it in a subject, it would be an attribute of that subject—is indeed sound. The early generations, their followers—the people of the Sunnah—and the majority affirm it. The Muʿtazilah and the Ashʿarīs, however, contradict themselves concerning it, as explained above.

---

## Page 2758

As for the third possibility, if He created it as something self-subsisting, that would be impossible, because it is an attribute, and an attribute cannot subsist by itself. This is self-evident.

It has been reported that some of the Muʿtazilah hold that He creates ropes in a subject. The Basrans—who are more eminent and superior to the Baghdadis—say that He creates a will without a subject. They may thus contradict this argument.

As for the first possibility—that if He created it within Himself, He would be a subject in which temporal occurrences inhere—the precise formulation is this: if He created it within Himself, He would be a subject in which something created inheres, whereas He cannot be such a subject.

If they say, “We call everything that comes into being created,” this is precisely a point of dispute. The early generations, the leading scholars of hadith, and many schools of speculative theology—such as the Hishāmiyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, Abū Muʿādh al-Tūmanī and others—do not say that everything that comes into being is created. Rather, they say that temporal occurrences fall into two categories: those that inhere in His Essence through His power and will, including His creation of created things; and those that exist distinct from Him. It is the latter that are created, because anything created necessarily requires an act of creation. The act of creation that inheres in His Essence, however, does not require another act of creation; rather, it occurs solely through His power and will.

In the Quran, power relates to this act, not to the thing produced considered apart from the act, as in His words:

“Is He not able to give life to the dead?”

And His words:

“Say: He is able to send punishment upon you from above you or from beneath your feet.”

And His words:

“Yes indeed, We are able to fashion his very fingertips.”

And His words:

“Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?”

---

## Page 2759

On this basis, this “argument” need only be stated as follows: if He created it, He would either create it in a subject, so that it would be an attribute of that subject, or create it as something self-subsisting. Both are impossible.

The possibility that He creates it within Himself need not be mentioned here. For its being created entails that there is an act by which it is created. If the act of creation inhering in Him were itself created, it too would require an act of creation. This would entail that every act of creation is created, and thus that an act of creation is created without an act of creation—which is impossible.

This reasoning is sound on the principle upheld by the early generations, Ahl al-Sunnah, and the majority, who say that nothing created can be created except through an act of creation.

As for someone who says that a thing can be created without an act of creation, and that the act of creation is nothing other than the created thing itself, it may be said on his premises: one possibility is that He creates it within Himself, with the created thing being the very act of creation—which is what its coming into being means. The matter then comes down to this: if He brings it into being, He does so either within Himself or outside Himself. It has thus become clear how this argument is to be formulated according to the principles of each group.

When this argument is framed according to the position of “the early generations and the majority,” it has two formulations. If you wish, you may say: He either creates it as something self-subsisting or as something subsisting in another. Do not say “within Himself,” because nothing created can exist within Him.

Alternatively, you may include this in the division and say: or He creates it within Himself. Then say: this is impossible, because anything created must have an act by which it is created. If He created it within Himself, it would require an act of creation, and what came into being within Him would be something created that required an act of creation. His act of creating it would therefore also require an act of creation, and so on indefinitely.

If every act of creation is created, no act of creation remains except one that is created. And if no act of creation remains except one that is created, this entails the existence of something created without an act of creation, since there is no uncreated act of creation in this account.

---

## Page 2760

If it is said:

“He may create it within Himself through an act of creation, while that act of creation occurs without another act of creation, through power and will alone. This is like the position of those who say that He speaks by His will and power, and that His speaking is an act that occurs through His power and will. We say that this act is the act of creation.”

They may be answered as follows:

On this account, the division now includes a “temporal occurrence” that subsists in Him without being created. On this supposition, it is possible to say of the Quran that it comes into being, or is brought into being, without being created. If the “first alternative” is correct, then its being uncreated does not entail its being eternal. Rather, it may come into being without being created. Thus, denying that it is created does not entail that it is eternal, and the argument therefore does not establish the position of the Kullābiyyah.

To summarize: either it is said that coming into being is broader than being created, so that something may come into being within Him without being created; or it is said that everything that comes into being is created, on the premise that no temporal occurrence subsists in His essence, or on the premise that whatever subsists in Him, if it comes into being, is created.

If the “first alternative” is correct, then its being uncreated does not entail its being eternal. Rather, it may come into being without being created. If, however, an alternative other than the “first” is correct, then the statement that He does not create it within Himself can only be established by disproving the possibility of temporal occurrences subsisting in Him.

But if the aim is to demonstrate that it is not created within Him—even if it comes into being within Him—this is established by arguing that, if it were created, there would have to be an act by which it was created. The act of creation itself, however, is not created; rather, it comes into being. For if it were created, every act of creation would be created, and there would consequently be something created without an act of creation. This combines two contradictories. It must therefore be the case that the act of creation comes into being without being created.

---

## Page 2761

On this supposition, then, its being uncreated does not entail its being eternal. The aim is only to demonstrate that He did not create it within Himself, whether one holds that temporal occurrences subsist in Him or that they do not. This is a better approach, for it establishes the argument without committing to this view.

Thus it may be said:

Either temporal occurrences subsist in Him or they do not. If they do not, He cannot create it within Himself, because it would then come into being, and temporal occurrences would therefore subsist in Him. If temporal occurrences do subsist in Him, then they occur through His power and will, and they cannot all be created, because whatever is created must have an act of creation, and the act of creation is itself among these temporal occurrences. If the act of creation were itself created through an act of creation, it would follow that every act of creation was created. Something created would then come into being without an act of creation, even though it has already been stated that whatever is created must have an act of creation.

Since whatever subsists in His essence need not be created, if He were to bring it into being within His essence, it would not necessarily be created. Indeed, it could not be created, because a created thing is one whose act of creation subsists in the Lord’s essence and is distinct from the created thing. When He speaks it by His will and power, the term “speech” encompasses both His act of speaking it and the letters themselves. That act of speaking occurs through His power and will, not through an act of creation. For the act of creation likewise occurs through His power and will, and He creates things through His speech. It is therefore impossible for His speech to have an act of creation closer to Him than His speech itself.

It has also been said that His creation of things is His very utterance of “Be.” This, then, would be the act of creation. An act of creation does not occur through another act of creation; rather, the created thing comes into being through the act of creation. Some things He creates through an act that He also performs while speaking.

It has thus become clear, on every supposition, that if He brings His speech into being within His essence, it is not created, without this entailing that temporal occurrences do not subsist in Him.

---

## Page 2762

And if we proceed on that basis, the expression “temporal occurrences” is ambiguous. It may mean that no genus subsists in Him containing a kind of which no instance had previously existed. Or it may mean that neither any kind nor any individual instance of temporal occurrences subsists in Him. If the latter is intended, the early generations, the leading authorities of the Sunnah and hadith, and many groups of speculative theologians hold the contrary view.

If the “former” is intended, the dispute is with the “Karrāmiyyah” and those like them—those who say that attributes arose in His essence which had not existed before: He began speaking by His will after not having done so, and began willing action after not having done so. The speech and will which the Muʿtazilah say come into being apart from Him, these people say come into being within His essence. The “Kullābiyyah” say that these are eternal and exist without His will and power, whereas these others say that they have a temporal beginning as a kind and arise through His power and His eternal will. According to them, His eternal will, together with His power, necessitated what subsists in His essence.

These people therefore say that He brought speech as a kind into being within His essence, having had no speech before that. This is not the position of the early generations. Rather, their position is that He has always been speaking.

It is thus clear that His creating speech within His essence is absolutely impossible: first, because nothing created can subsist in His essence; and second, because it would entail that He began speaking after not having done so. This is distinct from their assertion that temporal occurrences do not subsist in Him.

There are therefore “three approaches” here to refuting this view: the approach of the Kullābiyyah, the approach of the Karrāmiyyah, and the approach of the early generations. This is why this possibility was among those mentioned by Abd al-Azīz ibn Yahyā

---

## Page 2763

al-Kinānī in “al-Haydah.” He refuted it without adopting a position contrary to that of the early generations. I have quoted his words and explained them elsewhere.

“The point here” is that the claim that He created speech within Himself can be refuted without adopting the position of either the Kullābiyyah or the Karrāmiyyah. It has become clear that what subsists in His essence cannot be created, since it comes about through His will and power, whereas anything created must have an act of creation. His very act of speaking through His will and power is not an act of creating that speech; rather, through that speaking He creates other things, and an act of creation cannot create itself.

What demonstrates the falsity of the position of the “Kullābiyyah” is that speech can occur only through His will and power, whereas they say that He speaks without His will or power. They say that He speaks without His will or power.

As for the “Karrāmiyyah,” they say that He began speaking after not having done so. This entails that He previously lacked an attribute of perfection, that something came into being without a cause, and that His essence became the locus of a kind of temporal occurrence after not having been so—as the “Karrāmiyyah” allege. This is false.

This is what the early generations refuted by arguing that whatever subsists in Him in the way of speech, will, and action must be either an attribute of perfection or an attribute of deficiency. If it is a perfection, He would have remained deficient until that perfection arose in Him. If it is a deficiency, He would have become deficient after having been perfect.

This argument does not rule out will and speech subsisting in Him as kinds through one instance after another. That entails only that individual instances of will and speech come into being, not that the kind comes into being; and the kind has always been

---

## Page 2764

eternal, and He has always been characterized by speech and will. This is an attribute of perfection, so He has always possessed perfection and always will, unlike the claim that He began to will and speak after not having done so.

If it is asked in this connection, “Is an individual instance of will, speech, or action a perfection or a deficiency?” the answer is:

It is a perfection at the time it occurs, but would be a deficiency if it occurred before then. For example, His calling to Moses was a perfection when Moses came; had He called to him before that, it would have been a deficiency, from which Allah is exalted. Moreover, individual temporal occurrences cannot be eternal, and where something cannot be eternal, its absence in eternity is not a deficiency. Rather, the deficiency being denied must consist in the absence of something whose existence is possible—more precisely, something whose existence is possible and whose existence is better than its absence.

Thus, the absence of something is not a deficiency unless these two conditions are met: its absence is possible, and its existence is better than its absence. If its absence is impossible—as with the absence of a partner or child—this is praiseworthy and an attribute of perfection. If its absence is possible, then its absence is preferable, as with the things He did not create: not creating them was more perfect than creating them, just as creating what He did create was more perfect than not creating it.

Accordingly, whatever temporal occurrences come to exist, whether within His essence or separate from Him, their existence at the time they exist is perfection, and their absence at the time they are absent is perfection. Their absence at the time they exist, or their existence at the time they are absent, would be a deficiency from which Allah—glorified and exalted is He—is far removed.

The distinction between temporal occurrences as a kind and their individual instances has thus become clear. If the kind had come into being within His essence after not having existed, it would follow that He became perfect after having been deficient, or deficient after having been perfect.

---

## Page 2765

Furthermore, whatever comes into being must have a cause. Individual instances can come into being because other things precede them that can serve as causes. But if the entire kind is supposed to have been nonexistent and then to have come into being, this would entail its coming into being without a cause requiring it to do so, which is impossible.

Moreover, concerning this “kind,” either He has always been capable of it, or He became capable after not having been so. If He was capable of it, its existence was possible, not impossible; thus, its nonexistence cannot be categorically asserted. If He was not capable of it, this would entail power coming into being without a cause, a change in power, and a transition from impossibility to possibility without a cause. Individual instances are different: a particular instance was impossible until something occurred that made it possible; or it was possible, but wisdom required its existence to follow those other things. As for the kind, if it is said to have come into being, no particular time could be singled out for this, since in absolute nonexistence no time can be conceived as distinguishable from another.

“Furthermore,” the kind is likewise possible for Him by virtue of His existence, and it depends on nothing beyond Him, whether proceeding from Him or from another. Whatever is possible and depends only on His essence must exist by virtue of His essence existing, as with His life, knowledge, power, and His other attributes. This establishes that these attributes must be eternal as a kind, and that the kind is inseparable from His essence, even if individual instances are said to come into being.

On this basis, it may be said that attributes which come into being do not subsist in His essence. That is, no kind of attribute that comes into being subsists in Him: speech is an attribute, and will is an attribute, but these attributes do not begin to exist in Him, nor does any kind among these attributes. Rather, He has always possessed speech and will, even if there come into being

---

## Page 2766

individual instances of each attribute—that is, His willing of this particular occurrence and this particular individual. The attribute itself has always existed.

On this basis, it may be said: Even if He were to create “speech” within His essence, or originate speech within His essence, or if His speech were something that comes into being or is originated, speech itself—that is, this attribute and its kind—is neither something that comes into being, nor originated, nor created. As for particular speech, “such as the Quran,” it is not created, either within His essence or outside His essence. Rather, He spoke it by His will and power, and it comes into being within His essence.

May it be said that He originated it within His essence? There are two views, the sounder of which is that this may be said, as Allah Most High says:

“No new reminder comes to them from their Lord.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah brings about whatever He wills of His command, and among what He has newly ordained is that you must not speak during prayer.”

Al-Bukhārī devoted a chapter to this in his Sahīh, on a subject supported by the Book and the Sunnah.

This differs from creating something. Neither reason, revelation, nor language provides any basis for a person to call the actions and speech that subsist in him his own creation, saying, “I created that.” Rather, he says, “I acted and spoke.” He may also say, “I brought about these words and actions,” as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Beware of newly introduced matters, for every innovation is misguidance.”

He also said:

“Medina is a sanctuary between ‘Ayr and Thawr. Whoever introduces an innovation there or shelters an innovator incurs the curse of Allah, the angels, and all people.”

Although what he means here by “introducing” is narrower than bringing something about in the general sense of performing an action

---

## Page 2767

, he means only someone who introduces there an innovation contrary to what has been established as Sunnah and prescribed. Crimes are termed ahdāth (occurrences), and by ihdāth (bringing about) they mean initiating something that did not previously exist. Examples of this usage include:

“Allah brings about whatever He wills of His command.”

“No new reminder comes to them from their Lord.”

They call something “created” only when it is separate from its maker, as in His saying:

“And when you fashioned from clay the form of a bird.”

When they describe someone’s speech as “created” and “fabricated,” they mean that it is false and invented, as in His saying:

“And you fabricate falsehood.”

## Page 2768

Section

The arguments advanced by the philosophers and speculative theologians concerning “the temporal origination of the world” support only the position of the early Muslim generations and the imams. As for the “philosophers,” their argument establishes only that He has always acted, just as the argument of the “Ash'arīs” establishes only that He has always spoken. Both groups argue for the beginningless existence of the particular entity in question using evidence that does not entail this conclusion.

As for the “speculative theologians,” their principal argument is that whatever is never free of temporal events has a beginning, or that whatever does not precede temporal events has a beginning. Each of these propositions is correct when understood in a particular sense and points to the truth. Whatever does not precede bounded temporal events that have a beginning must itself have a beginning. This is evident to sound reason and agreed upon by rational people. Thus, anything known to have existed after an event that has a beginning, or alongside an event that has a beginning, necessarily also has a beginning. The same applies to whatever is never free of these temporal events.

Furthermore, whatever is never free of temporal events while depending upon them has a beginning. Whatever is never free of temporal events brought about within it by something else has a beginning. Indeed, whatever depends upon temporal events in any way has a beginning. Whatever has events brought about by something else subsisting in it has a beginning. Whatever depends upon something other than itself has a beginning. And whatever has temporal events subsisting in it has a beginning.

---

## Page 2769

This refutes the position of the “philosophers” who maintain that the celestial sphere is beginningless, such as Aristotle and his followers. “Aristotle” says that it needs the First Cause in order to resemble it. Proclus, Ibn Sīnā, and others like them say that it is His effect—that is, necessitated by Him—and that the First is its efficient cause. Thus, they all say that it depends upon something other than itself, while temporal events subsist in it and it has never been free of them. Yet they say that it is beginningless. This position is false.

“Ibn Sīnā” says that it is contingent, admitting both existence and nonexistence, while temporal events subsist in it, yet that it is eternal and beginningless. This is false. Its dependence upon another precludes its being necessarily existent in itself, for whatever is necessarily existent in itself cannot depend upon another. If it is not necessarily existent in itself, then it is contingent, admitting both existence and nonexistence. In that case, it must have been brought into existence, for several reasons.

One reason is that whatever is contingent and admits both existence and nonexistence can only be something brought into existence. By contrast, that which is beginningless, whose nonexistence is impossible, does not admit both existence and nonexistence.

Another reason is that if, besides being dependent, it has temporal events brought about within it by another, this indicates that the other exercises control and domination over it: temporal events are brought about within it, and it cannot ward them off. Whatever stands in such subjection in relation to another neither exists through itself nor is self-sufficient; nor is it unassailable or independent in itself. Anything of this kind can only be something made and subject to a Lord, and must therefore have been brought into existence.

Furthermore, if it is never free of the temporal events that another brings about within it, and did not precede them, but rather they have always accompanied it, this indicates that throughout its existence it stands in subjection in relation to another and is under its control; this indicates

---

## Page 2770

that it is always dependent upon that other. This refutes the position of the speculative theologians who say, “It depends upon Him only when it is brought into existence.” It likewise refutes the position of the philosophers who say, “It depends upon Him for its continued existence, despite being beginningless and never having been brought into existence.”

The correct conclusion is that it was brought into existence and depends upon Him both when it comes into existence and throughout its continued existence. The fact that temporal events brought about by another occur within it—or that temporal events occur within it while it is dependent—indicates that it was brought into existence. By contrast, the occurrence within it of temporal events that it itself brings about entails neither its dependence nor its having been brought into existence.

For this reason, the Companions would mention that the occurrence of temporal events in the world indicates that it is subject to a Lord, as we have discussed elsewhere. Whatever is subject to a Lord has been brought into existence. Everything other than Allah has temporal events brought about within it by another and is dependent upon another.

Every celestial sphere is moved by another, so its motion is brought about within it by another. The encompassing sphere sets them all in motion, yet its motion differs from theirs. Thus, a new relation arises within it without its choosing, while they are independent in their own motion and do not depend upon it for that. Hence, it cannot be their lord. The sun, the moon, and the stars are moved by another; all are subjected to His command.

## Page 2771

Section

We have already mentioned two principles:

First: The scriptural and rational arguments they cite in support of their doctrines actually support the position of the early generations and what the Quran and Sunnah teach. They do not support the innovations through which they have contradicted the Quran and Sunnah.

Second: The arguments they cite establish the opposite of what they intend and demonstrate the falsity of their position. This is a distinct matter: an argument supporting a position they do not hold is one thing; its establishing the opposite of their position and demonstrating its falsity is another.

This occurs in the arguments of both the philosophers and the speculative theologians. Examples among the philosophers include their arguments for the beginninglessness of the world or some part of it. They have argued from the four kinds of causes: efficient, final, material, and formal. Their principal argument concerns the efficient cause: it is impossible for Him to become an agent after not having been one; therefore, He must always have been acting. This is the chief argument relied upon by their later thinkers, such as Ibn Sīnā and others like him. I believe it was transmitted from Proclus.

Aristotle and his followers, however, do not employ this argument, since, in their view, He is not an agent. Rather,

---

## Page 2772

they argued from the necessary beginninglessness of time and motion—the argument from the formal cause—and from the necessary beginninglessness of matter. For everything that comes into being is preceded by the possibility of its existence, and this possibility must have a substrate. Thus, everything that comes into being is received by matter capable of receiving it. As for the “final cause,” it is of the same kind as the “efficient cause.”

The response to them is that these arguments support only the position of the early generations and the leading scholars, as explained above, and also demonstrate the falsity of their own position.

As for the beginninglessness of “agency”—meaning that He has always been acting—the response is: This expression is ambiguous. By an agent, you mean one whose effect coexists with him in time. If He is an agent in this sense, His effect must coexist with Him, and His action cannot come later. This is your principal argument. Yet an agent, according to rational people generally, your predecessors, and even yourselves outside this discussion, is one who does something and thereby brings it into being. Understood in this sense, the effect cannot coexist with Him. Rather, everything He brings about must come after Him. Nothing He brings about, therefore, shares His beginninglessness; everything other than Him comes into being.

People then take two approaches here.

“Some” say that everything He brings about must come after Him, and that He must remain inactive before subsequently acting. This is the position of the adherents of innovated speculative theology among the religious communities—the Jahmiyyah, the Mu'tazilah, and those who follow their path. This denial contradicts continuous agency and therefore contradicts what those arguments entail.

“The second” approach is to say that He has always been bringing one thing into being after another. Everything other than Him thus comes into being after not having existed, while He alone possesses beginninglessness and eternity. He is “the First,” beginningless and eternal, with nothing else sharing this with Him; and He has always been bringing one thing into being after another.

---

## Page 2773

It may therefore be said to them:

The arguments you advance for the necessary beginninglessness of “agency” invalidate your own position just as they invalidate that of the adherents of innovated speculative theology. For if they established continuous agency in the sense you claim, it would follow that nothing could come into being in the world. According to you, an effect must coexist in time with its efficient cause, and everything other than the First is His effect. Everything other than Him would therefore coexist with Him, so nothing could come into being in the world. This contradicts observation and reason, is false by the agreement of all humanity, and runs contrary to sense perception and rational understanding.

Furthermore, if an effect must coexist in time with its cause, then whenever anything comes into being, an infinite number of other things must come into being simultaneously with it, none preceding another. This amounts to affirming the existence of an infinite number of causes, which is likewise false according to clear reason and the agreement of rational people. Nor is there any difference here between the impossibility of this concerning the cause itself and its impossibility concerning one of its conditions. Just as it is impossible for an infinite number of causes themselves to come into being at a single instant whenever anything comes into being, the same applies to the conditions that complete the cause, for these constitute one of its two components. An infinite number cannot therefore exist at a single instant in either component. This is agreed upon among people.

As for the dispute over “the existence of an infinite succession,” part of their argument has thus fallen away. Their argument does not yield what they claimed; rather, it entails “the other position”: that the agent has always been bringing one thing into being after another. In that case, every effect comes into being after not having existed. This is the very opposite of their position. Indeed, this is among the strongest arguments supporting what the Messengers conveyed: that Allah

---

## Page 2774

is the Creator of all things. For this establishes that nothing is beginningless except Allah, and that everything other than Him comes into being after not having existed, whether it is called an intellect, a soul, a body, or anything else. This is unlike the argument advanced by the adherents of innovated speculative theology to establish that things came into being. For they said:

“Even if it were sound, it would establish only that bodies came into being. Yet we have established the existence of entities other than intellects, and the ‘speculative theologians’ have offered no proof that these do not exist.”

Later thinkers, such as al-Shahrastānī, al-Rāzī, and al-Āmidī, agreed with them on this. They claimed that the speculative theologians had no proof negating these intellectual substances, and that their argument for bodies having come into being did not encompass them. Consequently, those who claimed to answer them with “the overwhelming reply” fell into the contradiction mentioned earlier.

It has thus become clear that the very argument they advanced demonstrates the falsity of both their own position and that of the speculative theologians. It also establishes, by a sound and unassailable demonstration, that everything other than Allah came into being and that He alone is beginningless. Thus it has become clear—all praise belongs to Allah—that their principal argument for the beginninglessness of the world establishes only the opposite of their position: that everything other than Allah came into being. To Allah belong all praise and gratitude.

As for the “argument” they advanced to establish that motion and time have always existed, and that this kind could not have had a beginning—an argument relied upon by Aristotle and his followers—they may be told:

This does not establish the beginninglessness of any particular motion or its time, nor of any particular moving thing. It therefore does not establish what they seek to prove: the beginninglessness of the celestial sphere, its motion, and its time;

---

## Page 2775

rather, it demonstrates the opposite of their position. For motion must have a mover, and all motions ultimately lead back to a first mover. They concede this. That first mover, from which the motion of everything else proceeds, must either be in motion or not be in motion. If it is not in motion, this entails motion proceeding from something that is not in motion, which contradicts sensory experience and reason.

For an effect must correspond to its cause. If the effect comes into being successively, its cause cannot remain in one unchanged state. As you yourselves have said, nothing can come into being from such a cause after not having existed. Indeed, continuous coming into being from such a cause is even more clearly impossible than a new occurrence proceeding from it, for the former entails more instances of the impossible than the latter.

For if it is said, “It is known by plain reason that, for anything that was not acting, a cause must arise that necessitates its acting; and that if an agent remains in the same state it was in before acting, it will do nothing and nothing will come into being from it,” the reply to them is:

This very truth, known by plain reason, entails that nothing can come into being from that cause at a later time which did not exist at an earlier time, unless some new factor has arisen in the cause itself. If nothing new arises in it, nothing new comes into being from it. Thus, to maintain that things continually come into being from it without anything new arising in it is to maintain that impossibilities continually occur. For whenever anything comes into being, the essence is turned, at the moment of its occurrence, into what it was before its occurrence. Previously, it was impossible for that thing to come into being from it; so now, likewise, it remains impossible for that thing to come into being from it.

---

## Page 2776

Or it may be said:

It did not bring it into being before, so it does not do so now. Thus, whenever anything comes into being, the cause remains as it was before. Before that thing came into being, the cause was not bringing it into being; indeed, doing so was impossible. Likewise, at the time when it is supposed to come into being, its coming into being must be impossible.

Their most accomplished thinkers have acknowledged this as a necessary consequence, as Ibn Rushd, al-Rāzī and others have stated. They have acknowledged that something changing coming into being from something unchanging runs counter to the judgment of rational thinkers. Ibn Sīnā recognized this.

## Page 2777

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—was asked:

What do the esteemed scholars—may Allah be pleased with them all—say in response to the specious argument advanced by the Muʿtazilah in denying the divine attributes? They claim that “the Creator’s attributes are not additional to His essence,” arguing as follows:

Either His existence depends upon a particular attribute, such that supposing its nonexistence entails His nonexistence, or it does not. If it does, then His existence depends upon that attribute, and He becomes a composite of parts, whose existence is possible only through all those parts together. A composite, however, has a cause. If His existence does not depend upon that attribute, and supposing its nonexistence does not entail His nonexistence, then it is accidental, and an accident has a cause. Both are impossible with respect to Allah. The only remaining conclusion, therefore, is that the Creator’s attributes are not additional to His essence—which is what they seek to prove.

He replied—may Allah be pleased with him:

Praise be to Allah. The Quran and the Sunnah establish that Allah, glorified be He, possesses knowledge, power, mercy, will, might, and other attributes. For He, the Most High, says:

“They encompass nothing of His knowledge.”

And He says:

“But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He has sent it down with His knowledge.”

And He says:

“Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of Power, the Firm.”

And He says:

“And might belongs to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers.”

And He says:

“Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge.”

---

## Page 2778

And in the hadith of seeking Allah’s guidance, recorded in the Sahīh:

“O Allah, I seek Your guidance through Your knowledge, and I ask You to grant me ability through Your power, and I ask You of Your immense bounty.”

In the hadith of Shaddād ibn Aws, recorded in the Sunan, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“O Allah, by Your knowledge of the unseen and Your power over creation, keep me alive as long as life is better for me, and cause me to die when death is better for me.”

And in an authentic hadith:

“No, by Your might!”

Examples of this are numerous. It is also recorded in the Sahīh that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, questioned the man who recited “Say, ‘He is Allah, One’” in every unit of prayer while leading others. The man replied, “I love it because it is a description of the Most Merciful.” The Prophet said, “Tell him that Allah loves him.” Thus, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, approved his calling it a description of the Most Merciful. There are also numerous other reports to this effect.

These texts establish that words conveying information about Allah constitute a description of Him. Describing means making something manifest and clear to sight or hearing, as when jurists speak of a garment that reveals the skin or does not reveal it.

Allah Most High says:

“He will repay them for their descriptions.”

And He says:

“Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“A woman must not describe another woman to her husband as though he were looking at her.”

Here, ‘depicting’ means describing. Examples of this are numerous.

The word sifa (‘description’) is a verbal noun: one says wasaftu al-shay’a, asifuhu (‘I described something; I describe it’), with the verbal nouns wasf and sifa. Similarly, wa‘ada (‘he promised’) has the verbal nouns wa‘d and ‘ida (‘promising’), and wazana (‘he weighed’) has wazn and zina (‘weighing’).

They also apply a verbal noun to the object of the action. Thus, they call a created thing khalq (‘creation’), and say, ‘a dirham of the ruler’s minting.’ Accordingly, when the One being described is said to encompass all things in mercy and knowledge, the meaning attributed to Him through these words is called an attribute. Mercy, knowledge and power are therefore called attributes in this sense. This is the reality of the matter.

---

## Page 2779

Many of the Mu‘tazilites and others like them maintain that wasf (‘description’) and sifa (‘attribute’) refer only to verbal statements, without any meanings subsisting in the eternal Essence. Many theologians who affirm the divine attributes distinguish between wasf and sifa, saying that wasf is the verbal statement, whereas sifa is the meaning subsisting in the one described. Discerning scholars, however, know that each of these two terms is sometimes applied to the statement and sometimes to the meaning. The Quran and Sunnah explicitly affirm the existence of such meanings as knowledge, power and others, as we have already explained.

As for the word dhāt (‘essence’), it is, in Arabic, the feminine form of dhū (‘possessor of’). This form is used in a genitive construction with common nouns as a means of describing something by them. Thus one says, ‘a person possessed of knowledge, wealth and honour,’ referring to his actual being; or ‘an entity or self possessed of knowledge, power, authority,’ and the like.

It may also be joined to proper names, as in Dhū ‘Amr and Dhū al-Kalā‘, and in ‘Umar’s statement: ‘The wealthy one is Bilāl, together with his kin.’

When they found that Allah said in the Quran:

‘You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself,’

‘Allah warns you of Himself,’

and ‘He has prescribed mercy for Himself,’

they described this Self, saying: ‘A Self possessed of knowledge, power, mercy, will,’ and the like. They then omitted the noun being described and made the descriptive word definite, saying al-dhāt (‘the essence’). It is a later coinage, not an ancient term. It does occur in the speech of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the Companions, but with a different meaning, as in the words of Khubayb recorded in Sahīh al-Bukhārī:

---

## Page 2780

“And that is for Allah’s sake; and if He wills,
He will bless the limbs of a body torn apart.”

In the Sahīh, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is reported to have said:

“Abraham told only three lies, all of them for Allah’s sake.”

Abū Dharr said: “We are all fools for Allah’s sake.” Others have said: “We have suffered for Allah’s sake.” The meaning is on Allah’s side and in His cause—that is, for Allah’s sake and seeking His Face. The Self is not what is meant here. Similar expressions occur in the Quran:

“So fear Allah and set right relations among yourselves,”

and:

“He knows what is within the hearts.”

These refer, respectively, to the condition and circumstances pertaining to your mutual relations, and to His knowledge of the thoughts and the like that dwell within hearts. Thus, the word dhāt in the speech of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the Companions, and in pure Arabic usage, carries this meaning. The theologians and others subsequently applied it to the “Self” for the reason explained above: it possesses the attributes. Thus, when they say “the Essence,” they are saying “that which possesses the attributes.”

A report transmitted both with and without attribution to the Prophet states:

“Reflect on Allah’s blessings, but do not reflect on Allah’s Essence.”

If this wording, or something similar, is authentically established from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and his Companions, then their speech does contain the application of the word dhāt to the Self, as later scholars use it.

Once this principle is established, it remains “like motion.” Its persistence has been disputed, as has that of taste, colour and smell; most rational thinkers hold that it may persist. In their view, these accidents cannot validly be used to infer that the body came into existence;

---

## Page 2781

so it is all the more clear that Allah’s attributes cannot validly be used to infer that the One possessing them came into existence. Moreover, “this argument” for the world’s having come into existence requires lengthy examination, for which this is not the place.

The same response may also be given to the philosophers. There is no doubt that He is the Originator of the world and the cause of its existence, and they ascribe to Him certain things concerning intellect and providence which they must affirm. Thus, the same reasoning applies to what the adherents of the Book and Sunnah affirm as applies to what all schools must affirm. His reality has been established through necessary knowledge and conclusive proofs, and they agree on this. It has also been established that He is self-subsisting and is not of the same kind as other self-subsisting things, whether spirits or bodies. Since they agree that He is self-subsisting and is not of the same kind as other bodies and spirits, likewise the attributes that belong to Him in His own right are not of the same kind as those belonging to other things.

If it is supposed that an originated accident inhering in a substance proves that the substance came into existence, this does not entail that everything subsisting in another is an accident unless it also entails that everything self-subsisting is a substance. For if someone may refrain from calling some self-subsisting things substances, he may likewise refrain from calling some things that subsist in another accidents. Indeed, declining to call enduring qualities accidents accords more closely with linguistic usage. If, however, someone calls everything that subsists in another an accident, he may then call everything self-subsisting a substance.

---

## Page 2782

“In that case,” inferring from an accident or attribute having come into existence that its substance or bearer has likewise come into existence does not entail that every accident or attribute proves that its substance or bearer came into existence. If that followed, their claim that all substances and bodies came into existence would be invalid, since, on this supposition, the One without beginning would fall within this general category. Indeed, even the claim that any substance or body is contingent would be invalid.

The answer has thus become clear through two approaches.

The first has two aspects: counterargument and holding the opponents to the implications of their position; and demonstrating contradiction and invalidating their argument. These two aspects show that this specious argument is invalid according to the principles of all people on earth, and intrinsically invalid as well. For its truth entails its own negation, and anything whose truth entails its negation is intrinsically false.

The second approach consists in resolving the difficulty and clarifying the matter, as explained above.

As for the second specious argument—the argument concerning “composition,” which is shared by the philosophers and the Muʿtazilites, whereas the first is exclusively Muʿtazilite—the Muʿtazilites regard His most distinctive attribute as His being without beginning, and affirm that everything other than Him came into existence. The philosophers regard His most distinctive attribute as His necessarily existing in His own right, and hold that everything other than Him is contingent. They do not acknowledge coming into existence from nonexistence, and they maintain that the “composition” they describe entails a dependence that precludes His being necessarily existent in His own right.

---

## Page 2783

The answer to this, too, has two approaches. The first comprises two methods: counterargument and demonstrating contradiction. The second consists in resolving the difficulty.

As for the first, they affirm that He is knowing and powerful, necessarily existent in His own right, and the producer of what is other than Him. It is self-evident that the concept of His being knowing differs from the concept of His producing other things. If His essence is composed of these meanings, the “composition” they allege necessarily follows; and if these meanings are accidental to His essence, the “dependence” they allege necessarily follows. In short, whatever they say concerning these matters is what the adherents of the Book and the Sunnah say concerning knowledge and power.

As for “demonstrating contradiction”: if the One necessarily existent in His own right is not distinguished from anything else by a positive attribute, then there is no necessarily existent being. If there is no necessarily existent being, no impossibility follows from composition. For they deny these meanings only because affirming them entails “composition,” which in turn entails the negation of necessary existence. Yet this is contradictory: denying these meanings itself entails denying necessary existence. How, then, can they deny them in order to affirm it?

The explanation is that the One necessarily existent in His own right is real, existent, knowing, powerful, and active; and a contingent being may also be existent, knowing, powerful, and active. What they share is not merely a word, but intelligible meanings known self-evidently.

If what they share entails what distinguishes them, then the necessarily existent has become contingent, and the contingent necessarily existent. If it does not entail it, then the necessarily existent has something by which He is distinguished from

---

## Page 2784

the contingent—something other than these shared meanings. He thus has an aspect of commonality and an aspect of distinction; and this, according to them, is an impossible “composition.” If this composition entails the nonexistence of the necessarily existent, then the existence of the One necessarily existent in His own right entails His nonexistence. This is contradictory. This “compelling demonstration” thus establishes that their argument is internally contradictory, just as it has been established that, on their own principles, it is countered by what they themselves affirm.

As for the answer that resolves the difficulty, we say:

“Composition,” as understood by human reason and in human language, is the composition of an existing thing from parts distinguishable from one another. This is the composition of a body from its parts, such as a human being’s composition from organs and humours, a garment’s composition from its parts, or a drink’s composition from its ingredients. It makes no difference whether one part is distinct from the other, as a hand is distinct from a foot, or diffused throughout it, as bile is diffused in blood and water in milk.

The “logicians,” however, speak of species as composed of genus and differentia, as a human being is composed of animality and rationality: that is, composed of what it shares with the other species and what distinguishes it from other species. They also divide attributes into the “essential,” from which essences are composed—namely, genus and differentia—and the “accidental,” namely, the common accident and the distinctive property. The essence composed of the shared and distinguishing elements is then the “species.”

We say: this “composition” is a mental construct with no existence outside the mind, just as the “essence of the species,” insofar as it is universal, has no existence outside the mind. Rather, the very

---

## Page 2785

realities outside the mind contain neither external universality nor external composition. As we said concerning “the nonexistent,” it is a thing in the mind, not outside it, since it is an object of knowledge and will. A human being existing outside the mind does not contain distinct entities, some constituting animality, others rationality, others the capacity for laughter, and others sensory perception. Rather, the intellect apprehends in him a meaning whose counterpart is also found in another species, and therefore says that he possesses a shared meaning. It also apprehends a meaning peculiar to him, then combines the two meanings and says: “He is composed of them.” Yet when it apprehends these two meanings in him, it does not apprehend either as distinct and separate from the other. Likewise, when it apprehends existence, necessary existence, self-subsistence, and the sustaining of others, it does not apprehend any of these meanings as separate and distinct from the others.

An even clearer example is that the taste, colour, and smell inhering in a body are not distinguished from one another by occupying different locations; rather, the senses distinguish between these realities. This kind of “composition” is therefore unlike the composition of a body from its parts and humours: parts are not like accidents. We do not dispute calling this composite, for that is merely a verbal dispute. The point, however, is that this composition is not of the kind that human beings understand through their original innate disposition, such that the term “parts” may be applied to it.

Once this is understood, there are two approaches to resolving the difficulty, just as there were two approaches to refuting the argument.

(The first is that we do not concede that there is any composition from parts whatsoever. Rather, it is an essence that subsists

---

## Page 2786

in itself and necessarily entails its inseparable attributes, without which it cannot exist. The attributes of a thing are not its constituent parts or portions, distinct from one another or from the thing itself, such that it could properly be said to be composed of them or not composed of them. Affirming or denying composition presupposes a conception of it, and no such conception applies here.

The second answer is that, even supposing this were called composite, it would entail neither contingency nor origination. For what is known through reason and revelation is that it is impossible for the Lord, Most High, to depend upon His creation. Rather, He has no need of any of the worlds. It is known that He is Ever-Living and Self-Subsisting, that His holy Self subsists in itself and exists in its own right, and that He is One, the Self-Sufficient Master, needing nothing beyond Himself. His existence and self-sufficiency are not derived from another. Rather, He has always been and will always remain, in Himself, the True One, the Self-Sufficient Master, the Self-Subsisting Sustainer. Could it therefore be said that He depends upon Himself or needs Himself because His Self subsists only in Himself? What is said of His “attributes,” which are included in what is meant by His Self, is the same as what is said of His Self.

Thus, if it is said that His attributes are essential to Him, and that He needs them, this is equivalent to saying that He needs Himself, for His essential attributes are those without which His Self cannot be.

Likewise, if we say that His essence necessitates His existence, that He necessarily exists in Himself, or that He Himself entails the necessity of His existence, someone might object: “It follows that He is an effect, and an effect is dependent.” He would be answered: “The cause here is not something other than the effect. What is denied is His dependence upon another and His being the effect of anything besides Himself. As for His subsisting in Himself, that is true.”

---

## Page 2787

Furthermore, as for these expressions that suggest an unsound meaning, whether they are used with the correct meaning in view or not used at all, neither course does any harm, provided the correct meaning is known and cannot be refuted. This profound point deserves careful attention, for it dispels illusory doubts that have led many people astray.

When we say that “essences” are brought into being, we mean essences existing in external reality, on the basis that the existence of each thing in external reality is identical to its essence. For an externally existing thing is not something other than its existence. It is this externally existing thing that depends upon another, whether it is simple or composite.

A composite existing in external reality does not depend upon an agent because it is composite, but because its reality is dependent and its very being is inescapably needy. It has no subsistence, existence, or actual being except from its Lord. For this same reason, a simple thing depends upon the Maker just as a composite does. As for the “essences” known to the intellect, whether simple or composite, they depend upon an agent only insofar as a servant’s knowledge must have a cause—not because a composite depends upon its parts.

It has thus become clear to you that a composite does not depend upon its parts, either in the mind or in external reality, except in the same sense that a simple thing depends upon itself. A part of a composite is therefore equivalent to the simple thing itself, and each depends upon something else in external reality.

If it is legitimate to say, “It depends upon itself,” then it is legitimate to say, “It depends upon its attribute or its part.” If the former is not legitimate, neither is the latter. Thus, neither the attribute of a thing nor the part of a composite is

---

## Page 2788

anything other than the equivalent of the thing itself, whose essence cannot subsist without that attribute or part. There is nothing in our statement, “It depends upon itself,” that negates its being necessarily existent in itself; the same applies here.

Thus, the flaw in each of the two premises has become clear: that attributes entail composition, and that composition entails dependence upon another. Since each premise is false, this argument is invalid in its entirety. Allah knows best. May Allah send blessings upon Muhammad, his family, and all his Companions.

In addressing you, we praise Allah, besides whom there is no god. He is worthy of all praise and has power over all things. I write to you—may Allah bestow His kindness upon you in this world and the Hereafter, raising you thereby to lofty ranks in goodness and well-being—amid blessings and mercy from Allah, and well-being encompassing us and all our brethren. in what it has done.

A person therefore says, ‘Surely I am not one of these?’—although he is one of them.” These were his words, or something close to them.

Let your heart, then, find relief from the scorching heat of this awareness. It is a well-trodden path followed by servants of Allah whom His witnesses on earth unanimously acknowledged to have held a lofty station with Him. Indeed, a greater measure of this awareness is generally beneficial, so long as it does not lead to resentment of what has been decreed, despair of Allah’s relief, or a weakening of hope. May Allah Most High take you into His care and not leave you in the charge of anyone besides Him.
