## Page 2792

As for your request concerning the four grounds that necessitate interpreting speech figuratively rather than literally, I shall summarize the discussion I had with someone on this subject—the discussion I recounted to you and whose account you requested. Allah willing, it benefited him and others, notwithstanding the additions, omissions, and alterations in this account.

Someone said to me:

“If we wish to follow the path of safety and silence—the way by which we remain safe—we say what al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: ‘I believe in Allah and in what has come from Allah, according to Allah’s intent; and I believe in Allah’s Messenger and in what has come from Allah’s Messenger, according to the intent of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’ But if we follow the path of inquiry and careful investigation, then the truth lies with those speculative theologians who interpret the verses and hadiths concerning the divine attributes nonliterally.”

I replied:

“What al-Shāfiʿī said is true, and every Muslim must believe it. Whoever believes it and makes no statement contradicting it follows the path of safety in this world and the Hereafter. But when a person investigates and examines the matter closely, he finds that all the nonliteral interpretations through which the speculative theologians oppose the people of hadith are false, and becomes certain that the truth lies with the people of hadith, both outwardly and inwardly.”

He was taken aback by this and said:

“Would you like the people of hadith to debate this?”

We therefore arranged a day to meet. Among the matters we discussed was that the principal issues on which the later speculative theologians who profess to follow al-Ashʿarī differed with the people of hadith were three:

---

## Page 2793

describing Allah as being high above the Throne;
the question of the Quran;
and the question of interpreting the divine attributes nonliterally.

I said to him:

“Let us begin with the question of interpreting the divine attributes nonliterally, for this is the fundamental issue, and the remaining questions depend upon it.”

I also said to him:

“The position of the people of hadith—the early generations, comprising the first three generations, and those of later generations who followed their path—is that these hadiths are to be accepted as they have come, believed in, and affirmed as true. They must be safeguarded against nonliteral interpretation that leads to negating the attributes, and against specifying their manner in a way that leads to likening Allah to His creation.

“More than one scholar who has reported the consensus of the early generations—including al-Khattābī—has stated their position in general terms: these hadiths are understood according to their apparent sense, without specifying how the attributes are or likening them to those of creation. This is because what is said concerning the attributes follows from what is said concerning the divine essence, adhering to the same pattern and principle. Thus, just as affirming the divine essence means affirming its existence, not specifying how it is, so too affirming the attributes means affirming their existence, not specifying how they are. We therefore say that He has a hand and hearing, but we do not say that hand means power or that hearing means knowledge.”

I then said to him:

“Some people say, ‘The position of the early generations is that the apparent sense is not intended,’ and say, ‘We agree that the apparent sense is not intended.’ This expression is erroneous—either in both wording and meaning, or in wording but not in meaning—because ‘the apparent sense’ has come to be used for two different things:

---

## Page 2794

the first is to say that the hand is a limb like the limbs of created beings; that the apparent sense of anger is the heart’s boiling in pursuit of vengeance; and that the apparent sense of His being in heaven is that He is like water in a vessel. Undoubtedly, anyone who says that these meanings and similar attributes of created beings and qualities of things brought into existence are not intended in the Quranic verses and hadiths has spoken truthfully and rightly. For Ahl al-Sunnah do not disagree that nothing resembles Allah Most High, whether in His essence, His attributes, or His actions. Indeed, most of Ahl al-Sunnah, both among the scholars of our school and others, declare those who liken Allah to His creation and those who ascribe a body to Him to be disbelievers.

However, this person has erred in supposing that this is the apparent sense of these verses and hadiths, and in attributing to the early generations something they never said. For ‘the apparent sense of speech’ is what first comes to a sound mind when someone understands the language in question. This sense may be apparent from the established meanings of the words alone, or from the context. Yet ‘these meanings’—created characteristics that cannot possibly apply to Allah Most High—are not what first comes to the minds of believers. Rather, they regard the hand as they regard knowledge, power, and the divine essence. Our knowledge, power, life, speech, and similar attributes are accidents indicating that we came into existence, and Allah—glorified be He—cannot possibly be described as having their like. Likewise, our hands, faces, and similar things are bodies that have also been brought into existence, and Allah Most High cannot possibly be described as having their like.

Yet no one among Ahl al-Sunnah has said that, when we affirm that Allah has knowledge, power, hearing, and sight, ‘the apparent sense is not intended,’ and then explained that apparent sense in terms of our own attributes. Likewise, it is impermissible to say that the apparent sense of the hand and face is not intended, for there is no difference between those of our attributes that are bodies and those that are accidents inhering in bodies.

---

## Page 2795

Whoever says that the apparent sense of any of His names or attributes is not intended has erred. For with every name by which Allah Most High is called, the apparent sense applicable to a created being is not intended of Him. Thus, this person’s statement would imply that all His names and attributes convey meanings contrary to their apparent sense. The unsoundness of this is evident.

(The second meaning is that these attributes are indeed the attributes of Allah—glorified and exalted be He—in a manner befitting His majesty. They relate to His holy essence as the attributes of anything relate to its essence. Thus, knowledge is understood to be an attribute intrinsic to the one who possesses it, with its own distinctive characteristics; the same applies to the face.

It must not be said that He has no need of these attributes, for they necessarily belong to His essence. “God,” the One worshipped—glorified be He—is the One to whom all these attributes rightfully belong. Our purpose here is not to discuss matters with those who deny the attributes altogether, but with those who affirm some of them.

Likewise, regarding “His action,” we know that creation means bringing things into existence from nothing, although we do not specify the manner of that act. Nor does it resemble our actions, for we act only out of a need to act, whereas Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy.

Similarly, the “essence” is known in general terms, although it does not resemble created essences. None but He knows what He is, and its modality cannot be grasped. This, then, is the apparent meaning conveyed when these attributes are used without qualification, and this is how they must be understood.

---

## Page 2796

Thus, the believer knows the implications and effects of these attributes, which is what he is meant to know. He knows that Allah has power over all things; that Allah encompasses all things in knowledge; that the entire earth will be in His grasp on the Day of Resurrection and the heavens will be rolled up in His right hand; and that the believers will gaze upon the face of their Creator in Paradise, experiencing a delight beside which all other pleasures pale—and other such matters. Likewise, he knows that he has a Lord, a Creator, and One whom he worships, without knowing the full reality of any of this.

Indeed, this is the utmost extent of created beings’ knowledge: they know things in certain respects but do not encompass their full reality. Their knowledge of themselves is of this kind.

I said to him, “Is it permissible, then, to say that ‘the apparent meaning is not intended,’ when understood in this sense?”

He replied, “That is not possible.”

I said to him, “If someone says that the apparent meaning is not intended, meaning that the attributes of created beings are not intended, we say to him: ‘You are correct in your meaning but mistaken in your wording. Your wording suggests religious innovation and gives the Jahmiyyah a means of achieving their aim. You could instead have said: These attributes are to be left as they have come, according to their apparent sense, while knowing that Allah Most High’s attributes are not like those of created beings, and that He is exalted and holy, free of anything that would imply that He has a beginning or is deficient.’

“But whoever says that ‘the apparent meaning is not intended’ according to the second interpretation—which is what the Jahmiyyah and their followers among the Muʿtazilah, some Ashʿarīs, and others intend—has erred. Now, the closest of these ‘Jahmiyyah,’ the Ashʿarīs, say that He has seven attributes: life

---

## Page 2797

, knowledge, power, will, speech, hearing, and sight. They deny all other attributes. Some add only ‘the hand’ to these; others suspend judgment on denying the remaining attributes, while their extremists categorically deny them.

As for the ‘Muʿtazilah’, they deny the attributes altogether while affirming the corresponding predicates. For most of them, these amount to His being All-Knowing and All-Powerful. As for His having will and speech, they regard these as attributes that arise in time, express relations, or consist in negations. They are the closest of all people to the ‘Sabian philosophers’ among the Romans and those Arabs and Persians who followed their path, who claimed that all attributes amount to a negation, a relation, or a combination of negation and relation. All these people are misguided and reject the messengers. Whoever Allah has granted knowledge of what the messengers brought and penetrating insight, and who understands the true basis of these people’s views, knows with certainty that they deviate from the truth concerning His names and signs, and that they have rejected the messengers, the Scripture, and that with which His messengers were sent.

Hence they used to say: ‘Religious innovations spring from unbelief and lead back to it.’ They would also say: ‘The Muʿtazilah are the effeminate counterparts of the philosophers, and the Ashʿarīs are the effeminate counterparts of the Muʿtazilah.’

Yahyā ibn ʿAmmār used to say: ‘The Muʿtazilah are the male Jahmiyyah, and the Ashʿarīs are the female Jahmiyyah.’ They meant those Ashʿarīs who deny the attributes known through revelation. As for any of them who adheres to the book al-Ibānah, which al-Ashʿarī composed toward the end of his life, and has not openly expressed a position contradicting it, such a person is counted among Ahl al-Sunnah. Nevertheless, identifying oneself by affiliation with al-Ashʿarī is itself a religious innovation

---

## Page 2798

, especially since this creates a favorable impression of everyone who claims that affiliation and opens doors to evil. The discussion concerns those who deny the apparent meaning of the attributes as understood in this sense.

I said to him:

When Allah describes Himself with an attribute, or His Messenger describes Him with it, or the believers—whose guidance and understanding the Muslims unanimously acknowledge—describe Him with it, diverting it from its apparent meaning, which befits the majesty of Allah, glorified be He, and from the literal meaning understood from it, to a hidden meaning contrary to its apparent meaning and a figurative sense incompatible with its literal meaning, requires four things:

First: The expression must admit of that figurative usage. The Quran, the Sunnah, and the speech of the early generations are in the Arabic language, and nothing in them may be understood in a manner contrary to Arabic usage or to the usage of all languages. That figurative sense must therefore be one that the expression can convey. Otherwise, anyone advancing falsehood could interpret any expression as whatever meaning occurred to him, even if it had no basis in the language.

Second: He must have evidence requiring the expression to be diverted from its literal meaning to its figurative meaning. Otherwise, when an expression is used literally in one sense and figuratively in another, all rational people agree that it may not be understood figuratively without evidence requiring that departure. If he claims that departing from its literal meaning is necessary, he must provide decisive evidence, whether rational or scriptural, requiring that departure. If he claims that departing from its literal meaning is the more likely interpretation, he must provide evidence favoring the figurative reading.

Third: The evidence requiring that departure must be free of countervailing evidence. Otherwise, if Quranic evidence or evidence grounded in faith establishes that the literal meaning is intended, it is impermissible

---

## Page 2799

to abandon it. If that evidence is a conclusive text, no consideration is given to what contradicts it; if it conveys an apparent meaning, the competing evidence must be weighed.

(Fourth:
When the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, says something while intending a meaning contrary to its apparent and literal meaning, he must explain to the Muslim community that he does not intend its literal meaning but a figurative one, whether or not he specifies that figurative meaning. This is especially so in discourse concerning knowledge, where what is required of them is belief and knowledge rather than bodily action. For Allah, glorified and exalted be He, made the Quran a light, guidance, clarification for humanity, and a healing for what is in their hearts. He sent the messengers to explain to people what had been revealed to them, to judge between them concerning their disagreements, and so that people would have no argument against Allah after the messengers.

Moreover, this “Messenger,” an unlettered Arab, was sent with the most eloquent of languages and the clearest speech and expression. Those of his community who learned from him possessed the deepest knowledge, were the most sincere in their concern for the community, and explained the Sunnah most clearly. Thus, neither he nor they could use words while intending something contrary to their apparent meaning without providing evidence that precludes understanding them according to that apparent meaning.

This evidence may be readily apparent rational evidence, as in His saying:

“She has been given of all things.”

Everyone knows through reason that this means she was given the kinds of things that someone like her would be given. Likewise, in the words:

“Creator of all things,”

the listener knows that the Creator is not included in this general statement. Or it may be clear scriptural evidence, such as the indications in the Quran and Sunnah that divert certain expressions from their apparent meanings.

It is not permissible for him to refer them to obscure evidence that only a few individuals can deduce, whether scriptural or rational. For if he uses words that convey a particular meaning and repeats them a number of times

---

## Page 2800

—many times over—and addresses all people with them, including the intelligent and the dull-witted, those versed in religion and those who are not, requiring them to ponder that discourse, understand it, reflect upon it, and believe what it entails, but then requires them not to believe anything of its apparent meaning because some obscure evidence, discernible only to a few individuals, indicates that its apparent meaning was not intended, this would constitute deception and obfuscation. It would be the opposite of clarification and the very contrary of guidance, resembling riddles and puzzles more than guidance and explanation. How much more so if that discourse indicates its apparent meaning far more strongly than the obscure evidence indicates that this meaning was not intended? And what if that obscure evidence is merely a specious argument with no basis in reality?

The man conceded these points to me.

I said:

Let us discuss one of the attributes and make our discussion of it a model to follow, taking the attribute of the “Hand” as our example. Allah Most High says:

“The Jews say, ‘Allah’s Hand is shackled.’ May their hands be shackled, and may they be cursed for what they have said! Rather, both His Hands are outstretched; He spends however He wills.”

And He, Most High, said to Iblīs:

“What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two Hands?”

And He, Most High, says:

“They have not accorded Allah His true worth. On the Day of Resurrection, the earth in its entirety will be in His grasp, and the heavens will be rolled up in His Right Hand.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Blessed is He in whose Hand is dominion.”

And He says:

“In Your Hand is all good. Indeed, You have power over all things.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Do they not see that We have created livestock for them from what Our Hands have made, and that they own them?”

---

## Page 2801

And references to the “Hand” are established in the Sunnah through mass-transmitted reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

What is understood from this discourse is that Allah Most High has two Hands, peculiar to Him and belonging to His Essence, in a manner befitting His majesty; that He, glorified be He, created Adam with His Hand, unlike the angels and Iblīs; that He, glorified be He, grasps the earth and rolls up the heavens with His Right Hand; and that “both His Hands are outstretched.” Their being outstretched means abundant generosity and bountiful giving, since giving and generosity usually involve opening and extending the hand, whereas withholding involves drawing the hand up to the neck. Such expressions have thus become literal in customary usage: when one says, “He is open-handed,” an actual hand is understood, while the apparent sense conveys generosity and miserliness. As Allah Most High says:

“Do not keep your hand shackled to your neck, nor extend it to its utmost extent.”

People also say, “So-and-so is tight-fingered,” and “He is open-fingered.”

I said to him:

If someone claims that He does not have a hand of the same kind as the hands of created beings, and that His Hand is not a bodily organ, this is true. But if he claims that He has no Hand beyond the seven attributes, he is asserting falsehood. He must therefore go through those four stages of argument.

As for the “first,” he says that “hand” can mean a favor or a gift, naming something after its cause, just as rain and vegetation are called “sky.” Examples include their saying, “So-and-so has done him many favors,” and the words of Abū Tālib when he could not find the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“O Lord, return my rider Muhammad to me …
[Return him, my Lord] and bestow a favor upon me.”

---

## Page 2802

and the words of ‘Urwah ibn Mas‘ūd to Abū Bakr on the day of al-Hudaybiyah:

“Were it not for a favor you did me, which I have not yet repaid, I would have answered you.”

“Hand” may also mean power, naming a thing after what causes it, since power moves the hand. People say, “So-and-so has a hand in such-and-such.” Another example is what “Ziyād” said to Mu‘āwiyah: “I have held Iraq with one of my hands, while my other hand remains free.” He meant that controlling Iraq’s affairs took half his power.

Another example is His saying:

“In whose hand is the marriage tie.”

Marriage is contracted through spoken words; the meaning is simply that he has authority over it.

They may also attribute an action to the hand to attribute it to the person himself. Since most actions are performed with the hand, mentioning the hand came to indicate that someone performed an action himself. Allah Most High says:

“Allah has certainly heard the words of those who said, ‘Allah is poor, while we are rich’”

—down to His words—

“That is for what your hands have sent forth.”

That is, what you yourselves have sent forth, for some of what they sent forth consisted of words they spoke. Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“If only you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve, striking their faces and their backs”

—down to His words—

“That is for what your hands have sent forth.”

The Arabs say, “Your own hands tied it, and your own mouth inflated it,” rebuking anyone who brings trouble upon himself, because this was first said to someone who had acted with his own hands and mouth.

(I said to him:

We do not deny any of these usages in the Arabic language in which the Quran was revealed. Those who figuratively interpreted the divine attributes, distorting words from their proper places and deviating concerning His names and signs, interpreted His saying:

“Rather, both His Hands are outstretched,”

and His saying:

“What I created with My two Hands,”

along these lines

---

## Page 2803

, drawing on all these usages. They said: What is meant is His blessing—that is, the blessing of this world and the blessing of the Hereafter. They also said: “By His power.” They further said: The expression is an indirect reference to generosity itself, without there actually being a hand; rather, this expression has become a literal designation for giving and generosity.

His words:

“What I created with My two Hands”

mean: “I Myself created it,” even if there is no actual hand.

I said to him: “Are these, then, their interpretations?”

He replied: “Yes.”

I said to him: Let us, then, examine what we have already set out:

(The first point: The expression “two hands,” in the dual form, has not been used to mean either blessing or power. For the Arabs use the singular to mean the plural, as in His saying:

“Indeed, man is in loss.”

They also use the plural to mean the singular, as in His saying:

“Those to whom the people said, ‘Indeed, the people’”

and the plural to mean two, as in His saying:

“The hearts of you both have inclined.”

But using the singular to mean two, or the dual to mean one, has no basis. These expressions denote number and are explicit in their meanings; they cannot be used figuratively. One cannot say, “I have a man,” meaning two men, or “I have two men,” meaning the class as a whole. A singular noun can denote a class, and a class encompasses an indefinite range of individuals. Likewise, a plural noun carries the sense of a class, and a class is instantiated by even a single individual.

Thus, His words:

“What I created with My two Hands”

cannot mean power, because power is a single attribute, and the dual cannot be used to express the singular. Nor can they mean blessing, because Allah’s blessings are beyond counting, and blessings beyond counting cannot be expressed using the dual form.

---

## Page 2804

Nor can it mean “what I Myself created,” for when they intend this meaning, they ascribe the action to the hand, thereby associating the hand with the action, as in His words:

“For what your two hands have sent forth,”

and:

“For what your hands have sent forth.”

This also includes His words:

“Livestock, among the things Our Hands have made.”

But when He ascribes the action to the agent and connects the verb to the hand through the preposition bi (“with”), as in His words:

“What I created with My two Hands,”

this explicitly states that He performed the action with His two Hands. Thus, one cannot say to someone who has spoken or walked, “You did this with your two hands,” although one may say, “Your two hands did this.” Simply saying “You did it” suffices to attribute the action to its agent. If an actual action performed with the hand were not intended, the additional wording would be entirely superfluous and serve no purpose.

In the speech of Arabs or non-Arabs, you will not find—if Allah Most High wills—an eloquent speaker saying, “I did this with my two hands,” or “So-and-so did this with his two hands,” unless he actually did it with his two hands. It cannot mean that he has no hand, or that he has a hand but the action was performed without it. This established distinction makes clear where expressions are figurative and where they are literal. It also makes clear that, on purely linguistic grounds, these verses admit no figurative interpretation whatsoever.

He said to me: “But they have used the dual in place of the singular in His words, ‘Cast him into Hell, you two,’ although the address is only to one.”

I said to him: This is not conceded. Rather, concerning His words, “Cast, you two,” it has been said that the agent takes the dual form because the action is repeated twice, the meaning being: “Cast! Cast!” It has also been said that the address is to the driver and the witness. Whoever says that it addresses one person says that a person has two companions with him: one on his right and the other on his left

---

## Page 2805

and so he says, “My two friends! My two friends!” He then addresses them in this way even when they are not present, as though addressing two people who are present. Thus, according to this interpretation, His words,

“Cast, you two,”

address two whose presence is assumed. This therefore provides no evidence whatsoever.

I said to him:

(The second point: Suppose that “hand” may mean an actual hand, or power or favor, or that mentioning it may serve as an indirect expression for the action. Yet what requires us to depart from its literal meaning?

If you say, “Because a hand is a bodily member, and that is impossible for Allah, glorified is He,” I reply: This and similar arguments establish that He cannot be described as having a hand of the same kind as the hands of created beings. There is no doubt about this. But why could He not have a “Hand” befitting His Essence, to which attributes of perfection belong just as they belong to His Essence?

He said: “Neither reason nor revelation establishes that this is impossible.”

I said: Since this is possible, and it is the word’s literal meaning, why should the word be diverted from that meaning to a figurative one? Whatever evidence the opponent adduces to show that He cannot be described by what the term denotes—provided that the evidence is sound—we concede that the meaning proper to a created being is excluded in His case. The word’s literal and apparent meaning, however, is a “Hand” befitting the Creator, just as knowledge and power befit Him—indeed, just as essence and existence do.

(The third point:

I said to him: Have you come across anything in Allah’s Book, in the Sunnah of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or reported from any of the imams of the Muslims, stating that the intended meaning of “hand” is other than its apparent meaning, or that its apparent meaning is not intended? Or is there any verse in Allah’s Book that rules out describing Him

---

## Page 2806

as having a Hand, by any clear indication—or even a subtle one?

For the most that someone straining to make this argument can cite is His saying:

“Say: He is Allah, the One,”

and His saying:

“There is nothing like Him,”

and His saying:

“Do you know of any equal to Him?”

These verses indicate only the negation of corporeality and resemblance to created beings. As for denying a Hand befitting His Majesty, nothing in these words indicates that in any way whatsoever. Likewise, does reason clearly indicate that the Creator has no “Hand” whatsoever—neither a “Hand” befitting His Majesty nor a “hand” like those of created beings? Does reason indicate this at all, even in some subtle way?

If, then, neither revelation nor reason contains anything that rules out an actual Hand altogether—and if any supposed contrary evidence rests only on subtle arguments, even according to those advancing it, while in reality it is merely a fallacious objection—can the Quran and Sunnah be filled with references to the Hand: that Allah Most High created with His Hand, that “His two Hands are outstretched,” and that dominion is in His Hand, with countless such references in the hadith, yet Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and those in authority fail to explain to people that neither the literal nor the apparent meaning of these words is intended? Must “Jahm ibn Safwān” then arise after the age of the Companions has passed to explain to people what was revealed to them through their Prophet, followed in this by “Bishr ibn Ghiyāth” and all those accused of hypocrisy who followed their path?

How could our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, teach us everything, even “how to relieve ourselves,” and say, “I have left nothing that brings you nearer to Paradise without telling you of it, nor any

---

## Page 2807

thing that keeps you away from the Fire without telling you of it,” and, “I have left you upon a clear path, whose night is like its day; none will deviate from it after me except one who is doomed”—then leave the Book revealed to him and his radiant Sunnah full of statements whose apparent meaning, according to the opponent, likens Allah to creation and ascribes corporeality to Him, such that believing their apparent meaning is misguidance—without explaining or clarifying this? How could the early generations say, “Leave them as they have come,” if their figurative meaning is what is intended, yet this is something the Arabs do not understand? Are the descendants of the Persians and Romans then more knowledgeable about the Arabic language than the descendants of the Emigrants and the Helpers?

(The fourth point):

I said to him: “I shall present clear, decisive, and evident proofs demonstrating to you that Allah truly has ‘two Hands.’

“Among these is His favoring Adam in a manner that required the angels to prostrate to him and refrain from treating him arrogantly. If what was meant were that He created him by His power, through His favor, or merely that his creation was attributed to Him, then Iblīs and all created beings would share this with him.”

He said to me: “Something may be attributed to Allah as a mark of honor, as in His saying, ‘Allah’s she-camel,’ and the House of Allah.”

I said to him: “Such attribution is not an honor unless the thing attributed to Him possesses a quality that distinguishes it from others. Had the she-camel and the House not possessed clear signs distinguishing them from all other she-camels and houses, they would not have merited this attribution. The same applies here: attributing the creation of

---

## Page 2808

Adam to Him on the grounds that He created him with His two Hands necessarily means that He truly did create him with His two Hands, whereas He created these others by His command, “Be,” and they come into being, as the transmitted reports state.

Another point is that when the Arabs say, “In his hand is dominion,” or, “Your two hands made it,” two things are involved:

(First) Affirming the hand.

(Second) Attributing dominion or action to it.

The second frequently involves figurative usage. As for the first, however, they use such expressions only of a kind of being that truly has a “hand.” They do not speak of the “hand” of desire or the “hand” of water. Suppose, then, that His words, “In His Hand is dominion,” are understood to mean “by His power.” Even so, such figurative language is used only of one who truly has a hand.

The difference between His words, exalted is He, “what I created with My two Hands,” and His words, “what Our Hands have made,” is twofold:

(First): In the former, He attributes the act to Himself and explains that He created him with His two Hands; in the latter, He attributes the act to the hands.

(Second): In Arabic usage, a plural form may stand in place of the dual when there is no risk of confusion, as in His words, exalted is He:

“As for the man and woman who steal, cut off their hands”—that is, their two hands.

And His words:

“For your hearts have indeed deviated”—that is, your two hearts.

The same applies to His words, “what Our Hands have made.”

As for the Sunnah, the evidence is exceedingly abundant, such as his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: “Those who act justly will be with

Allah, on pulpits of light, to the right of the Most Merciful—and both His Hands are right Hands—those who act justly in their judgments, with their families, and in whatever is entrusted to their care.” Narrated by Muslim.

## Page 2812

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section:

The objector said concerning the Most Beautiful Names:

“‘The Light, the Guide’: ‘the Light’ must certainly be interpreted figuratively, for light is a quality that inheres in what is corporeal, and it is the opposite of darkness. The True One—glory be to Him—is far above having an opposite. Were He light, it would not be permissible to attribute it to Himself in His words:

‘The likeness of His light’

for this would amount to attributing a thing to itself, which is impermissible.

“Regarding His words:

‘Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth,’

the Quran commentators said that this means the Guide of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth. This interpretation, however, is weak, because mentioning ‘the Guide’ after it would then be repetitive. It has also been said that He illuminates the heavens with the stars, or with clear proofs and compelling arguments. Light is a subtle, transparent body, so it cannot be predicated of Allah.

“Figurative interpretation is reported from Ibn ‘Abbās, Anas and Sālim. This refutes his claim that figurative interpretation negates the apparent meaning and has not been transmitted from the early generations. Were He truly light—as those who liken Allah to His creation maintain—there would necessarily be perpetual illumination, night and day.

---

## Page 2813

And His words:

‘Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of good tidings and a warner,
and as one who invites to Allah, by His permission, and as an illuminating lamp.’

It is well known that he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was not a lamp in the familiar sense. Rather, he was called a lamp because of the guidance he brought; the clarity of his proofs was like an illuminating lamp. It is also reported from Ibn ‘Abbās, in another narration, and from Abū al-‘Āliyah and al-Hasan that this means the Illuminator of ‘the heavens and the earth’: their sun, moon and stars.

Among the sayings of those who know Allah is this: ‘The Light’ is He who illuminates the hearts of the sincere with belief in His oneness and illuminates the inmost hearts of those who love Him with His support. It has also been said: He is the One who gives life to the hearts of those who know Him through the light of knowing Him, and to the souls of His worshippers through the light of worshipping Him.”

(The answer): This statement and others like it do not constitute an objection to our position. Rather, it marks the beginning of their diminished respect for him, owing to what he supposes our position entails, or what he supposes we say in the manner he has described.

Allah Most High has said:

“Avoid much suspicion; indeed, some suspicion is sinful.”

And the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the falsest of speech.”

When a statement attributes to others views that are false according to reason and revelation, and then refutes those views, this constitutes falsehood and injustice. We seek refuge in Allah from that. Yet, despite its injustice towards us, if only it were sound and coherent discourse! We would then waive our claim against him, and people could benefit from the knowledge it contained. But it contains distortion of Allah’s Book, deviation concerning His verses and Names, and falsehood, injustice and transgression that infringe upon Allah’s rights. Even if we waive our own claim, Allah’s right rests with Him, not with anyone else.

---

## Page 2814

And we shall set forth what is appropriate here in fulfilment of Allah’s rights and in defence of His Book and His religion. For the statements he has cited contain contradictions and flaws that I doubt he can keep track of, in several respects.

First: At the beginning, he said, “Light is a quality inhering in corporeality.” Then, at the end, he said, “A subtle, transparent body.” Thus, at the beginning he described it as an accident and an attribute, but at the end as a body—a self-subsisting substance.

Second: He reported that the Quran commentators interpreted this as meaning “the Guide,” and questioned that interpretation. Yet, at the end, he mentioned that among the sayings of those who know Allah is that “the Light” is He who illuminates the hearts of the sincere with belief in His oneness, illuminates the inmost hearts of those who love Him with His support, and gives life to the hearts of those who know Him through the light of knowing Him. This is precisely the meaning of “the Guide,” which he initially questioned. Thus, he first questions it, then presents it as a saying of “those who know Allah”—an expression that holds powerful sway over hearts. In fact, it is merely a saying of certain shaykhs who engage in a kind of exhortation that lacks rigorous examination.

Shaykh Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān included in Haqā’iq al-tafsīr various allusions: some are sound and beneficial statements; some are fabrications falsely attributed to their purported speakers, such as those transmitted from Ja‘far and others; and some are invalid, rejected reports.

The “allusions of the Sufi shaykhs” fall into two categories. One consists of allusions pertaining to spiritual states—those they make with their hearts. This is what distinguishes them, but this is not the place to discuss it. The other consists of allusions connected with words, such as those they derive from the Quran

---

## Page 2815

and the like. Such allusions involve drawing parallels and reasoning by analogy: relating cases not explicitly addressed in a text to those that are, much as jurists do when drawing parallels and reasoning by analogy in legal rulings. Here, however, this is employed in encouragement and warning, the merits of deeds, the ranks of men, and similar matters. If an “analogical allusion” constitutes a valid analogy, it is good and acceptable. If it resembles a weak analogy, it receives the same judgment. But if it distorts words by taking them out of their proper contexts and interprets them contrary to their true meaning, it belongs to the same category as the discourse of the Qarmatians, the Bātiniyyah, and the Jahmiyyah. Reflect carefully on this, for I have explained it in “The Principle of Allusions.”

(The third aspect)

Another contradiction is that he said this interpretation was transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbās, Anas, and Sālim, yet he mentioned only three interpretations.

(The first)

He is the Guide of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth. Yet he deemed this interpretation weak. If this weak interpretation is what was transmitted, then what a fruitless endeavour! For in everything he has said up to this point, he has transmitted nothing from the early generations except this interpretation, which he himself has deemed weak and discredited.

If, however, what was transmitted from these three is that He illuminates the heavens with the heavenly bodies, then he has contradicted himself in another respect. He subsequently mentioned that another report from Ibn ‘Abbās, as well as reports from Abū al-‘Āliyah and al-Hasan, states that He illuminates them with the sun, moon, and stars. This entails that what was initially transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbās and the other two must differ from what was transmitted from him in another report and from those not mentioned alongside him in the first.

---

## Page 2816

And if the meaning is that He illuminated it with compelling arguments and proofs, then he has contradicted himself, for this is precisely the meaning of “the Guide”: His establishing proofs and arguments is part of His guidance. Yet he has deemed this interpretation weak. I do not know which is more astonishing: his presenting two interpretations, one of which falls within the meaning of the other, or his deeming the questioner’s interpretation weak, which entails deeming both interpretations weak—without realizing that he has rejected both. One must therefore understand the meanings of the interpretations one transmits and recognize that what one dismisses as weak must not be the very thing one has extolled.

(The fourth aspect)

It has become clear that he has transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbās, Anas, and Sālim only the interpretation he deemed weak, or something included within it. If their interpretation was “the Guide,” he explicitly declared it weak. If it was “the One who establishes proofs,” this falls within the meaning of “the Guide.” If it was “the One who illuminates through the heavenly bodies,” he presented that as a separate interpretation. If it was what he related from certain people of spiritual insight, that too falls within the meaning of “the Guide.” Since he has acknowledged the weakness of what he related from Ibn ‘Abbās, Anas, and Sālim, it provides no argument against us. Thus, regarding what he has related from “the early generations,” either he is reporting falsely or he is making a false allegation in declaring it weak. In either case, it provides no argument against us.

(The fifth aspect)

He has shown disrespect towards the early generations by attributing to them an interpretation he deems weak. He has presented them to people as having engaged in figurative interpretation, seeking thereby to establish an argument for figurative interpretation in general, even though he has acknowledged the weakness of this particular interpretation. Whoever advances an argument that he himself has declared weak, without realizing that he has done so, has shot himself with his own arrow. Whoever shoots the arrow of transgression will be struck down by it:

“Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.”

(The sixth aspect)

His statement: This refutes his claim that “figurative interpretation sets aside the apparent meaning

---

## Page 2817

and was not transmitted from the early generations.” I have not made this statement. Even if I had, he has transmitted only what he himself knew to be weak, and weak evidence refutes nothing. These points demonstrate his inconsistency and his attribution to us of statements we have not made.

As for “demonstrating the unsoundness of the argument,” we say: Regarding his statement, “It must certainly be interpreted figuratively,” we concede neither that it must be interpreted figuratively nor that, even if this were obligatory, its obligation would be certain. Rather, the vast majority of Muslims do not interpret this name figuratively. This is the position of those who follow the early generations and of the majority of those who affirm the divine attributes among the theologians, jurists, Sufis, and others. It is also the position of Abū Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb, who mentioned it in al-Sifāt (The Attributes) and refuted the Jahmiyyah’s figurative interpretation of “the name Light.” He is the master of the Ash‘arī theologians who affirm the divine attributes—their earliest master. Abū Bakr ibn Fūrak reported this from him in his book Maqālāt Ibn Kullāb (The Doctrines of Ibn Kullāb), as did al-Ash‘arī. Neither attributed its figurative interpretation to anyone other than the Jahmiyyah, who are condemned by common agreement. This is also the position of Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī, which he mentioned in al-Mūjaz (The Epitome).

As for his statement that this occurs among the Most Beautiful Names, the hadith in which it is mentioned is the report of al-Tirmidhī. He narrated the Most Beautiful Names in his Jāmi‘ through al-Walīd ibn Muslim, from Shu‘ayb, from Abū al-Zinād, from al-A‘raj, from Abū Hurayrah. Ibn Mājah also narrated them in his Sunan through Mukhallad ibn Ziyād al-Qatawānī, from Hishām ibn Hassān, from Muhammad ibn Sīrīn, from Abū Hurayrah. Those versed in hadith have agreed that these two narrations are not the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Rather, each consists of the words of some of the early generations. Al-Walīd related these names from some of his Syrian teachers, as is explicitly explained in some transmission routes of his hadith.

---

## Page 2818

For this reason, the particular names in the two versions transmitted from him differ: one narration includes names in place of those mentioned in the other. Those who compiled them would sometimes mention one name and sometimes another. They and others believed either that the Most Beautiful Names whose enumeration leads to Paradise were not a fixed set—rather, whoever enumerates ninety-nine of Allah’s names will enter Paradise—or that, even if they were a fixed set, two names with the same meaning could substitute for one another, such as al-Ahad (the One and Only) and al-Wāhid (the One).

Thus, the narration of Hishām ibn ‘Ammār from al-Walīd ibn Muslim, from him, as transmitted by ‘Uthmān ibn Sa‘īd, has “al-Ahad” in place of “al-Wāhid,” and “al-Mu‘tī (the Giver)” in place of “al-Mughnī (the Enricher),” the latter two being close in meaning. Al-Walīd lists these names after narrating the hadith from Khulayd ibn Da‘laj, from Qatādah, from Ibn Sīrīn, from Abū Hurayrah.

Hishām then said: “Al-Walīd also narrated to us, saying that Sa‘īd ibn ‘Abd al-‘Azīz had narrated the same to him. He said, ‘All of them are in the Quran: “He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity” …’” The list follows the one given by al-Tirmidhī, but al-Tirmidhī narrated it through Safwān ibn Sālih, from al-Walīd, from Shu‘ayb. Ibn Abī ‘Āsim also narrated it, and his list differs from al-Tirmidhī’s in some places.

All this makes clear that these names are material appended to and interpolated into the hadith from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in some transmission routes; they are not his words. For this reason, “others” compiled a different list, deriving the names from the Quran. Among them were Sufyān ibn ‘Uyaynah, Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others, as I mentioned in my discussion of this subject long ago. All this implies that, in their view, these names admit of substitution;

---

## Page 2819

for the overwhelming majority of Muslims hold that Allah’s names are more than ninety-nine.

They—including al-Khattābī—said: In his statement,

“Allah has ninety-nine names; whoever enumerates them,”

the numerical restriction applies to the names described as being these particular names. Thus, the clause,

“Whoever enumerates them will enter Paradise,”

qualifies the ninety-nine. It is not an independent sentence, but occupies the accusative position grammatically. It may, however, be understood as an independent sentence without changing the meaning. The sense is: Allah has names numbering this many; whoever enumerates them will enter Paradise. This is like someone saying, “I have a hundred slaves whom I have set aside for emancipation, and a thousand dirhams which I have set aside for Hajj.” The numerical restriction applies to what bears this qualification, not to the total number possessed. For he did not say, “Allah’s names are ninety-nine.”

He said: This is supported by his words in the hadith narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad:

“O Allah, I ask You by every name belonging to You with which You have named Yourself, or which You have revealed in Your Book, or taught to any of Your creation, or kept exclusively with Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen.”

This indicates that Allah has more than ninety-nine names, which some believers enumerate.

Furthermore, the numerical specification in his statement,

“Allah has ninety-nine,”

is comparable to the Exalted’s words,

“Nineteen.”

When they considered them few, He said:

“And none knows the soldiers of your Lord except Him.”

It is all the more fitting, then, that none but He should know His names. Even if the former statement had been made on its own, it would imply the exclusion of any additional names only through the restrictive implication of a specified number. This is weaker than the restrictive implication of a qualifying attribute, and the disagreement over it is well known. Nevertheless, the view we favor is that singling something out for mention—once grounds for general inclusion are present—does imply

---

## Page 2820

that the ruling applies exclusively to it. For departing from the requirement of general inclusion in favor of singling something out—unless this is intended to restrict the ruling to it—would mean disregarding the grounds for general inclusion without any countervailing consideration, which is impossible.

Thus, in his statement,

“Allah has ninety-nine,”

giving this number may serve purposes other than restricting the total to it. (Among these) is his mention that enumerating them leads to Paradise. Had he stated the first sentence independently and followed it with the second as a separate sentence, that would have been perfectly sound. How much more so when speech is presumed to be connected rather than disconnected, making the conditional sentence a qualifying clause rather than an independent sentence. This is the preferable grammatical interpretation in Arabic, alongside the evidence already mentioned.

For this reason, he said:

“He is One and loves what is odd-numbered.”

His love for this indicates that it relates to enumeration: that is, He loves for this number of His names to be enumerated. If Allah’s names exceed ninety-nine, it is possible that enumerating any ninety-nine names leads to Paradise, without restriction to a particular set. This provides a basis for their view, although many people understand these to be specific names.

Among the latter, some say that there are only ninety-nine names in all. This is the view of Ibn Hazm and a group of others. Most of them, however, say: Even if Allah has more names, those for whose enumeration Paradise has been promised are a specific set.

In any event, identifying these names individually is not part of the Prophet’s own words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as those knowledgeable about his hadith agree. Rather, various lists have been transmitted from the early generations, including the one mentioned by al-Tirmidhī and others besides it.

With this understood, regarding his inclusion of “the Light, the Guide” among His Most Beautiful Names, if someone were to challenge him

---

## Page 2821

over whether this is authentically established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he would have no proof. Yet this does occur in authentic hadiths, such as the report in the two Sahīh collections from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say:

“O Allah, to You belongs all praise. You are the Light of the heavens and the earth and all who are in them.”

The hadith continues. In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Dharr said:

“I asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘Have you seen your Lord?’ He replied, ‘Light—how could I see Him?’ Or he said, ‘I saw light.’”

Thus, what occurs in the Quran and authentic hadith is “Light” in a construct phrase, as in His words:

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth,”

or “the Light of the heavens and the earth” and all who are in them.

As for his statement, “Since light is an inhering quality,” we say: Created light is perceptible to the senses and needs no explanation of its nature. It is, however, of two kinds: concrete entities and accidents.

“Concrete entities” include the very body of fire wherever it may be—the light of a lamp, of the lamp enclosed in glass, and the like. This is the light Allah used in His parable. Another example is the moon, for Allah called it a light, saying:

“He made the sun a radiance and the moon a light.”

There is no doubt that fire is a subtle, transparent body.

“Accidents” include the rays of the sun, moon, and fire that fall upon polished bodies and other surfaces. When a lamp is in a room, it illuminates the room’s various sides. That light and those rays falling upon the walls, ceiling, and floor constitute an accident: a quality inhering in a body.

It may be said that the attribute inhering in fire, the moon, and the like is not light, in which case the term would apply at one time to the substance and at another to an attribute. Hence daylight is called light, as He says

---

## Page 2822

—exalted is He:

“and made darkness and light.”

Hence night is called darkness and day light, for both are accidents, although it has also been said that they are two substances. This is not the place to discuss that at length. It is thus clear that the term “light” encompasses both categories. The objector first gave the definition of an “accident,” then the definition of a “body,” thereby contradicting himself. It seems that he took this from my words but failed to understand how the two usages are reconciled. Likewise, the term “truth” applies to the essence of Allah, exalted is He, and to His holy attributes, as in the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“You are the Truth, Your word is the truth, Paradise is real, Hell is real, the prophets are true, and Muhammad is true.”

As for the objector’s statement, “Light is the opposite of darkness, and the Truth is far too exalted to have an opposite,” he is told:

You have not understood the meaning of the opposite that is denied of Allah. An “opposite” can mean something that precludes the existence of the other, as is said of mutually opposed accidents such as blackness and whiteness. People say, “Two opposites cannot coexist,” and, “The coexistence of two opposites is impossible.” According to many, this opposition occurs only among “accidents”; there is no such opposition among “concrete entities.” On this understanding, it is inadmissible to say either “Allah has an opposite” or “He has no opposite.” Others hold that opposition can be conceived among concrete entities. Allah, exalted is He, undoubtedly has no opposite that could prevent His being and existence. Rather, He is the All-Subduing, the Victor who cannot be overcome.

An “opposite” may also mean one who opposes His command and judgment, even though that opponent does not prevent His essence from existing. Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever’s intercession prevents the enforcement of one of the prescribed punishments of

---

## Page 2823

Allah has thereby opposed Allah in His command.” Narrated by Abū Dāwūd. Calling someone who opposes His command and judgment an “opposite” is like calling him an “enemy.” In this sense, Allah has many enemies and opponents. According to the first interpretation, however, there is undoubtedly nothing in reality that stands in opposition to Allah. Rather, such opposition occurs in the minds of the unbelievers: falsehood is the opposite of truth, and lying is the opposite of truthfulness. Thus, any belief about Allah that attributes to Him something from which He is exalted is contrary to sound faith in Him.

As for his statement:

“Light is the opposite of darkness, and the Truth is far too exalted to have an opposite,”

he is told:

The living is the opposite of the dead, and the knowledgeable is the opposite of the ignorant. One who hears, sees, and speaks is the opposite of one who is deaf, blind, and mute. Likewise, all the other names by which Allah is named have opposites, but He is exalted above being called by those opposites. Far exalted is Allah above being dead, powerless, needy, or anything of that kind.

As for the existence of a creature of His characterized by the opposite of one of His attributes—such as someone who is dead, ignorant, needy, or unjust—there are many such creatures. Indeed, most of His names have opposites found among existing beings. Such beings are not called “opposites of Allah”; rather, they are said to possess attributes opposite to Allah’s attributes. For incompatibility between attributes applies only within one and the same subject, not across two different subjects. Thus, for one characterized by death, life is incompatible with that state; and for one characterized by life, death is incompatible with that state.

---

## Page 2824

And Allah, exalted is He, cannot be darkness or be characterized by darkness, just as He cannot be dead or be characterized by death. This objector has used the word “opposite” equivocally, without distinguishing between an opposite whose existence would be incompatible with the existence of the Truth, His attributes, and His actions; something among His creatures characterized by the opposite of His attributes; and something that opposes His commands and prohibitions. The first kind of opposite is impossible, whereas the other two occur frequently. Neither, however, is called an “opposite of Allah,” for possessing an attribute opposite to His attributes does not mean standing in opposition to Him.

Those who said, “Light is the opposite of darkness,” meant that the two cannot coexist in one and the same entity. They did not say that one thing cannot be characterized as light while another is characterized as darkness. Let anyone possessed of reason reflect on this denial of Allah’s attributes and this confusion.

As for his statement:

“If He were light, it would not be permissible to ascribe light to Himself in His words, ‘The likeness of His light,’”

there are two ways to answer this.

(First) We say: The texts of Allah’s Book and the Sunnah of His Messenger have named Allah the Light of the heavens and the earth. They have stated that Allah is light, and have also stated that He veils Himself with light. These, then, are three lights mentioned in the texts. The first has already been discussed.

(As for the second), it occurs in His words:

“And the earth will shine with the light of its Lord,”

and in His words:

“The likeness of His light,”

and in the report narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh from ‘Abdullāh ibn ‘Amr, who related a statement by

---

## Page 2825

the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah created His creation in darkness and cast upon them some of His light. Whoever was reached by that light was guided, and whoever it missed went astray.”

Another instance is his supplication at Tā’if, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“I seek refuge in the light of Your Face, by which the darkness is illuminated and the affairs of this world and the Hereafter are set right, lest Your displeasure descend upon me or Your wrath befall me.”

This was narrated by al-Tabarānī and others.

Another instance is the statement of Ibn Mas‘ūd:

“With your Lord there is neither night nor day. The light of the heavens comes from the light of His Face.”

Another instance is his statement in the report narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh from Abū Mūsā, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stood among us and delivered four statements, saying: ‘Allah does not sleep, nor is it befitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the balance. The deeds of the night are raised to Him before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the deeds of the night. His veil is light—or fire. Were He to remove it, the radiance of His Face would burn all of His creation that His sight reaches.’”

This hadith mentions His veil. The narrator’s uncertainty between the words “fire” and “light” does not affect this, for pure fire of this kind, through which He spoke to Moses, may be called both fire and light. Likewise, Allah called the flame of a lamp light. This differs from dark fire, such as the fire of Hell, which is not called light.

There are thus three categories:

“Illumination without burning”: pure light, such as that of the moon.

“Burning without illumination”: dark fire.

“That which is both fire and light”: such as the sun and the flames of lamps in this world, which are described in both ways. Since this is so, it is valid for Him to be

---

## Page 2826

the Light of the heavens and the earth, and for light to be ascribed to Him, without the light ascribed to Him being identical to Him.

(The second approach)

It may be said: This objection applies to you as well; it is not confined to those who call Him by the name He has given Himself and explained. Whether you say “Guide,” “Illuminator,” or something else, the one named “Light” is the Lord Himself, not the light ascribed to Him.

When you say, “He is the Guide, so His light is guidance,” you make one of the two lights a self-subsisting entity and the other an attribute. Those who call Him Light say the same. Since the objection applies to both positions and their proponents, singling out one of them as contradicting his own position is injustice and obstinacy in argument, or ignorance and deviation from the truth.

As for the views he has mentioned, there is no doubt that people have expressed more views on this matter than he has cited. The true and false reports, and the correct and mistaken opinions, circulating among the Muslim community are beyond anyone’s reckoning but Allah’s. Discussions of “the interpretation of Allah’s names, attributes, and speech” contain such quantities of sound and worthless material that none but the Lord of all worlds can reckon them. What matters, however, is truth, knowledge, and religion.

Long ago, in one of my writings addressed to a distinguished person, I wrote:

Knowledge is what is established by evidence, and beneficial knowledge is what the Messenger brought. What matters, then, is that we speak on the basis of knowledge: authenticated transmission and rigorous investigation. Anything else—even if some people embellish such things—is merely painted earthenware; otherwise, it is sheer falsehood, like what he has mentioned concerning this verse and others. These books that many people call “books of Quranic commentary” contain much

---

## Page 2827

commentary consisting of reports falsely attributed to the early generations and pronouncements about Allah and His Messenger based on mere opinion—indeed, on nothing more than a specious analogical or literary argument.

He has not named the commentators whose views he cites. Even so, he has challenged their position on false grounds. These commentators interpreted “Light” in the verse as “the Guide”; they were not interpreting “Light” among Allah’s Most Beautiful Names or in the hadith transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. His grounds for challenging their position are therefore invalid. We have mentioned this only to expose his inconsistency and show that none of the arguments he advances against us could persuade anyone of sound understanding, for inconsistency is the first stage of unsoundness. This interpretation has indeed been advanced by a group of commentators.

As for its being authentically attributable to Ibn ʿAbbās or anyone else, we have not established that.

It is well known that the “books of Quranic commentary” contain many fabricated reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, transmitted through al-Kalbī from Abū Sālih and through others. Reports must therefore be authenticated before they can serve as proof. One should consult the “books of Quranic commentary” in which transmitted reports are carefully scrutinized, such as the commentary of Muhammad ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī, who transmits the statements of the early generations with their chains of transmission—and set aside the commentaries of Muqātil and al-Kalbī. Earlier works include the commentaries of Baqī ibn Makhlad al-Andalusī, ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Ibrāhīm Duhaym al-Shāmī, ʿAbd ibn Humayd al-Kashshī, and others, if one does not go further back to the commentaries of Imam Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and other imams. These are the most knowledgeable people on earth concerning authentic Quranic interpretations transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and reports from the Companions and Successors, just as they are the most knowledgeable concerning the Prophet’s hadith, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and reports from the Companions and Successors on foundational principles, subsidiary matters, and other branches of knowledge.

---

## Page 2828

But if he establishes a principle on mere personal opinion and makes it a general rule, this will gain acceptance only among those ignorant of the evidence and unversed in the issues. It is through such transmitted reports—whose truth is not distinguished from falsehood—and such rational arguments—whose correctness is not distinguished from error—that those among the people of the East who went astray did so in foundational principles, subsidiary matters, jurisprudence, and Sufism.

How fitting that this should arise in connection with the verse of Light, in which Allah Most High says:

“And he to whom Allah has not granted light—for him there is no light.”

We ask Allah to grant us light.

We then say: Some commentators have explained His words,

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth,”

as meaning the Guide of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth. This interpretation neither undermines our position nor contradicts what we have said. They offered it when explaining the verse in which “Light” occurs in a possessive construction; they did not offer it as an explanation of “Light” without qualification, as you claim it occurs in the hadith. How can the two be equated?

Moreover, the statement of some of the early generations that He is the Guide of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth does not preclude His being Light in Himself. In their explanations, the early generations commonly mention some of the attributes of what a name denotes, or some of its types. This does not negate the other attributes of the entity so named—indeed, the two attributes may be inseparable—but the remaining types are not included in the particular type mentioned.

We have established this more than once in the preceding principles. Whoever reflects upon it will realize that most statements of the early generations concerning Quranic interpretation agree rather than conflict. An example is their explanation of

“the straight path”:

some say that it is Islam; another says that it is the Quran; and another, that it is the Sunnah

---

## Page 2829

and the community; another says that it is the path of servitude to Allah. These are all inseparable descriptions of it, not divergent ones. Calling it by these names is like referring to the Quran and the Messenger by their various names—indeed, it is comparable to Allah’s Most Beautiful Names.

An example of the “second” is His saying, Most High:

“Among them are those who wrong themselves, those who are moderate, and those who are foremost in good deeds.”

A particular category among them may thus be mentioned, although the term “servant” encompasses them all. The one who wrongs himself neglects some obligations; the moderate one fulfills them; and the one foremost in good deeds draws near to Allah through voluntary acts after fulfilling the obligatory ones.

People engage in this according to their respective approaches to explanation and translation, illustrating the particular kind and the general category to make the meaning easier for the listener to grasp. It is like a non-Arab asking, “What is bread?” and being told, “This,” while someone points to a loaf. What is intended is the general category, not that particular loaf. Much of the early generations’ Quranic interpretation is of this kind: it is a form of teaching.

Thus, explaining

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth”

as meaning the Guide of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth is correct. One meaning of His being the Light of the heavens and the earth is that He guides their inhabitants. But it is not known that they excluded every other meaning. As for the claim that this was their intent, it is established that Ibn Masʿūd said:

“With your Lord there is neither night nor day; the light of the heavens comes from the light of His Face.”

The reports already cited from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—concerning the light of His Face, together with the narration mentioning “light,” are sufficient. This therefore establishes a meaning other than guidance.

---

## Page 2830

Allah has also declared in His Book that the earth will shine with the light of its Lord. If it shines with His light, how could He not be light? This light cannot be attributed to Him merely on the grounds of creation, ownership, and special selection—as in His words, “Allah’s she-camel,” and similar expressions—for several reasons.

First: Light is never attributed to Allah when it is an attribute of independently existing entities. The lamps in this world are not called “Allah’s light,” nor are the sun and moon. Rather, one says, as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said:

“With your Lord there is neither night nor day; the light of the heavens comes from the light of His Face.”

In the supplication transmitted from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—it says:

“I seek refuge in the light of Your Face, by which the darkness is illuminated and the affairs of this world and the Hereafter are set right.”

Second: Created lights, such as the sun and moon, illuminate the earth in this world, and there is no light that is not among Allah’s creations. Likewise, saying that He is the Illuminator of the heavens and the earth does not contradict His being light. Every illuminator is light, so the two descriptions are inseparable.

Moreover, Allah Most High likened His light in the believers’ hearts to the light in a lamp: it is light in itself and illuminates other things. If His light in people’s hearts is both light and illuminating, then He Himself is all the more entitled to these descriptions. It is known that everything that is light also illuminates.

As for the statement, “It means the One who illuminates the heavens with the stars”: if its proponent means that this is among the meanings of His being the Light of the heavens, and that he intends thereby that there is not, in His being the Light of

---

## Page 2831

the heavens and the earth, any meaning other than this, then his claim is false; for Allah has declared that He is the Light of the heavens and the earth, whereas the light of the stars does not reach throughout the heavens and the earth.

Moreover, He said:

“The likeness of His light is that of a niche containing a lamp.”

He thus gave a likeness of His light present in the believers’ hearts. This establishes that the light in the believers’ hearts—the light of faith and knowledge—is intended by the verse. He did not apply this likeness to the physical light of the stars. This also answers what he cited from Ibn ʿAbbās in another narration, and from Abu al-ʿĀliya and al-Hasan—though proof of the transmission’s authenticity must first be demanded, and the report from Ibn ʿAbbās is probably weak. For they included this among the meanings of light. But to claim that they understood His words,

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth,”

to mean nothing other than illumination by the sun, moon, and stars is certainly false. The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“You are the Light of the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them.”

It is known that the blind have no share in that illumination, nor does anyone screened from it by a barrier. The dead have no share in it, nor do the inhabitants of Paradise, for Paradise has neither sun nor moon. Indeed, it has been related that the inhabitants of Paradise distinguish night from day by lights appearing from the Throne, just as the sun appears to the people of this world. Those lights are therefore distinct from the sun and moon.

As for his statement, “It has been said: through proofs and arguments,” this is part of the meaning of “the Guide.” We have already discussed his statement: “This invalidates his assertion that interpretation involves setting aside the apparent meaning and has not been transmitted from

---

## Page 2832

the early generations.” These words have been falsely attributed to me. Their author’s inconsistency has already been established, as has the fact that he cited nothing from the early generations except reports whose weakness he himself acknowledged.

What I now state and write—although I did not write it in my earlier responses, but have often stated it in gatherings—is that no disagreement has been transmitted from the Companions concerning the interpretation of any of the Quranic verses about Allah’s attributes. I have examined the Quranic commentaries transmitted from the Companions and the hadiths they narrated, consulting as many large and small works as Allah Most High has willed—more than a hundred commentaries. To this very moment, I have not found a report from any Companion interpreting any verse or hadith concerning the attributes contrary to its commonly understood meaning. Rather, their statements affirming and establishing these meanings, and explaining that these are attributes of Allah, contradict the claims of those who reinterpret them in ways that Allah alone can enumerate. Likewise, those who transmit and recount their statements relate a great deal of this.

To complete this point: I have found no disagreement among them except concerning passages such as His words, Most High:

“On the Day when a shin is laid bare.”

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and a group of others that what is meant is hardship—that Allah will lay bare the hardship of the Hereafter. It is related from Abū Saʿīd and another group that they counted this among the attributes, on account of the hadith narrated by Abū Saʿīd in the two Sahih collections.

There is no doubt that the apparent meaning of the Quran does not indicate that this is one of the attributes, for He said:

“On the Day when a shin is laid bare.”

The word “shin” is indefinite in an affirmative statement. He did not attribute it to Allah, nor did He speak of

---

## Page 2833

His shin. Since it is not made definite by attribution to Him, it does not evidently denote one of His attributes without further evidence. Such an interpretation is not a departure from the apparent meaning. Rather, that consists in diverting a verse from what it indicates, conveys, and is ordinarily understood to mean. Yet many of these people assign an expression a meaning it does not convey, then seek to divert it from that meaning and call this interpretation. This is mistaken on two counts, as we have explained more than once.

As for his statement:

“If He were truly light—as those who liken Him to creation falsely claim—there would necessarily be illumination continuously, night and day.”

We accept the implication of this statement of his. Those who liken Allah to creation say that He is light like the sun, whereas Allah Most High says:

“There is nothing like Him.”

He is not like any light, just as His essence is not like any other essence. Yet what the objector has mentioned is an argument against him, for He may be light that He veils from His creation, as stated in the hadith:

“His veil is light—or fire. Were He to remove it, the splendour of His Face would burn everything in His creation that His sight reaches.”

There is, however, an error in the attribution here: assigning this view to those who liken Allah to creation. It is also among the views of the Jahmiyyah, who deny the divine attributes, such as al-Marīsī. He used to say that He is light, although he was a leading figure among the Jahmiyyah. If, however, by those who liken Allah to creation he means those who affirm that Allah is truly light, then everyone who affirms the attributes is, in his view, guilty of likening Him to creation. This is “the language of the pure Jahmiyyah”: they describe everyone who affirms the attributes as someone who likens Allah to creation.

We have already mentioned that Ibn Kullāb, al-Ashʿarī, and others stated that denying that He is light in

---

## Page 2834

Himself is the view of the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah, and that both affirmed that He is light. They and their leading followers established this position—how much more so the scholars of hadith and the imams of the Sunnah! Foremost among these believers in Allah and His names and attributes is the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, answered this very question raised by the objector when he said:

“His veil is light. Were He to remove it, the splendour of His Face would burn everything in His creation that His sight reaches.”

He thus explained that He is screened from created beings by His veil of light, so that the splendour of His Face does not reach them. Were He to remove that veil, the splendour of His Face would burn everything in His creation that His sight reaches. This veil, which prevents that splendour from burning them, clarifies the issue raised here.

As for what he cited from Ibn ʿAbbās in the other narration, it refers to certain forms of perceptible light. What he cited from the words of those who know Allah concerns some aspects of His guidance of His servants. These are simply particular examples, presented according to the needs of those being addressed. As we have mentioned, it was the practice of the early generations to explain such matters by mentioning particular instances as illustrations suited to their audience’s needs, not as exhaustive or restrictive definitions.

It has thus become clear that all the statements he cited come back to two meanings of His being the Light of the heavens and the earth. None of this indicates that He is not light in Himself.
