## Page 2835

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-ʿAbbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah Most High be pleased with him—was asked about the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The Black Stone is Allah’s right hand on earth,”

and his saying:

“Indeed, I feel the breath of the Most Merciful from the direction of Yemen,”

and the words:

“Then He rose over the Throne,”

and:

“Allah’s hand is above their hands,”

and:

“And be patient with your Lord’s judgement, for you are under Our eyes.”

He replied—may Allah have mercy on him:

As for the first hadith, it has been narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through a chain of transmission that is not established as authentic. The well-known report is instead from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said:

“The Black Stone is Allah’s right hand on earth. Whoever clasps it and kisses it, it is as though he has shaken hands with Allah and kissed His right hand.”

Anyone who reflects on the transmitted wording will see that it presents no difficulty except to someone who has not reflected on it. For he said, “Allah’s right hand on earth,” qualifying it with the words “on earth.” He did not say simply, “Allah’s right hand,” without qualification. A qualified expression does not carry the same force as an unqualified one.

He then said:

“Whoever clasps it and kisses it, it is as though he has shaken hands with Allah and kissed His right hand.”

It is well known that the thing being likened is distinct from that to which it is likened. This explicitly shows that the person clasping it has not actually clasped Allah’s right hand at all, but

---

## Page 2836

has been likened to someone who shakes hands with Allah. Thus, both the beginning and the end of the hadith make clear that the Stone is not one of Allah’s attributes, as everyone of sound reason knows. Rather, it explains that just as Allah Most High has appointed for people a House around which they perform circumambulation, He has appointed for them something to touch, so that this serves the same purpose as kissing the hands of persons of high rank. By customary practice, this brings the person kissing the hand closer and confers honour upon him. Allah and His Messenger do not speak in a way that misleads people; rather, people must be shown clearly what they should guard against. The hadith thus makes clear what rules out likening Allah to His creation.

As for the second hadith, the words “from Yemen” clarify its intended meaning. Yemen has no special connection with Allah’s attributes that would warrant such a supposition. Rather, from there came those whom He loves and who love Him, concerning whom He said:

“Whoever among you turns away from his religion, Allah will bring forth a people whom He loves and who love Him.”

It has been narrated that when this verse was revealed, he was asked who these people were, and he said that they were the people of Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī. Authentic hadiths have also been transmitted, such as his saying:

“The people of Yemen have come to you; their hearts are more tender and more gentle. Faith is Yemeni, and wisdom is Yemeni.”

These were the people who fought the apostates and conquered the cities. Through them, the Most Merciful relieved the believers of their distress. Anyone who confines this to Uways has strayed far from the intended meaning.

As for the verse, it is widely reported that Mālik ibn Anas was asked about it. The questioner said to him: “‘The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.’ How did He rise over it?” Mālik bowed his head until he was overcome by

---

## Page 2837

sweat. Then he said:

“Rising over the Throne is known; its manner is unknown. Belief in it is obligatory, and asking about its manner is an innovation. I consider you nothing but an innovator.” He then ordered that the man be removed, and he was taken out.

The statements of all the leading imams of religion—such as Ibn al-Mājishūn, al-Awzā‘ī, al-Layth ibn Sa‘d, Hammād ibn Zayd, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others—convey the same meaning as Mālik’s statement: we do not possess knowledge of the manner of the divine attributes. Knowing the manner of an attribute depends on knowing the manner of the one who possesses it. If the manner of the One possessing the attribute is unknown, the manner of His attribute cannot be known.

When the believer is kept clear of the path of distortion and denial of the divine attributes, and the path of likening Allah to His creation, he follows the straight path. For the Book, the Sunnah and consensus establish what is also known through reason: that Allah Most High—

“There is nothing like unto Him”

—has no likeness in His essence, His attributes or His actions. It is therefore impermissible to describe Him with anything peculiar to created beings, for He possesses the utmost perfection and is free from every deficiency. He, glorified be He, has no need of anything besides Himself, whereas everything besides Him stands in need of Him. Whoever claims that the Quran indicates such creaturely characteristics has made a false claim about the Quran. Nothing in the words of Allah, glorified be He, entails describing Him in this way.

Rather, a person may be led astray by his own faulty understanding, reading into the words of Allah and His Messenger meanings from which Allah, glorified be He, must be declared free. Yet the way one who upholds falsehood treats the words of Allah and His Messenger is as it has been said:

Many a critic finds fault with sound words,
Yet the fault lies in his own unsound understanding.

---

## Page 2838

Scholars must make clear that Allah Most High’s attributes are free of the deficiencies that the ignorant imagine in them, and that the words of Allah and His Messenger do not imply any such deficiency. They must also explain that the Quran is clarification, guidance and healing. If anyone nevertheless goes astray through it, that is due to his own negligence. As the Most High says:

“And We send down of the Quran that which is healing and mercy for the believers, but it increases the wrongdoers only in loss.”

And He says:

“Say, ‘For those who believe, it is guidance and healing.’ But those who do not believe have deafness in their ears, and it is blindness for them.”

---

## Page 2839

The shaykh, imam and eminent scholar, Shaykh al-Islām Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-'Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. I bear witness that none is worthy of worship except Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. May Allah bless him and his family and grant him abundant peace.

The hadith concerning “the believers’ seeing their Lord in Paradise on a day corresponding to Friday in this world” was narrated by Abū al-Hasan al-Dāraqutnī in his book on the vision of Allah. We know of no one who has compiled more on this subject than is found in the works of Abū Bakr al-Ājurrī and the hadith master Abū Nu'aym al-Asbahānī. Al-Dāraqutnī narrated it from Anas as traced back to the Prophet, and from Ibn Mas'ūd as a report stopping at him. Ibn Mājah also narrated it from Ibn Mas'ūd as traced back to the Prophet.

As for the hadith of Anas, al-Dāraqutnī narrated it through five or six chains of transmission, most of which state:

“The vision will take place at a time corresponding to Friday prayer in this world.”

Some versions explicitly state:

“Women will see Him on the festivals.”

As for the hadith of Ibn Mas'ūd, in all its chains of transmission—whether traced back to the Prophet or stopping at Ibn Mas'ūd—

---

## Page 2840

this is stated explicitly; and the chain of transmission of Ibn Mas'ūd’s hadith is stronger than all the other chains on this subject. Abū 'Abd Allāh ibn Battah also narrated it in al-Ibānah through another chain from Anas, stronger than the others. It includes the words:

“That is at the time corresponding to your departure from Friday prayer.”

Abū Ahmad ibn 'Adī narrated it through Sālih ibn Hayyān, from Ibn Buraydah, from Anas, but I do not know its wording. Abū 'Amr al-Zāhid narrated it through another chain whose wording I cannot recall. Abū al-'Abbās al-Sarrāj also narrated it: 'Alī ibn Ashyab narrated to us; Abū Badr narrated to us; Ziyād ibn Khaythamah narrated to us, from 'Uthmān ibn Muslim, from Anas ibn Mālik. This version does not contain the addition. Abū Ya'lā al-Mawsilī narrated a similar report in his Musnad, from Shaybān ibn Farrūkh, from al-Sa'q ibn Hazn, from 'Alī ibn al-Hakam al-Bunānī, from Anas, but I do not know its wording.

Abū Bakr al-Bazzār, Abū Bakr al-Khallāl and Ibn Battah narrated it from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yamān as traced back to the Prophet. This version does not mention the addition, but states at the end:

“Every seven days, they will have twice what they had before.”

He said: This is what Allah says in His Book:

“No soul knows what delights are kept hidden for them as a reward for what they used to do.”

Al-Ājurrī and Ibn Battah also narrated it from Ibn 'Abbās as traced back to the Prophet. It includes the words:

“Those seated nearest to Him are those who hasten most to Him on Friday and set out earliest.”

It also has another chain from Abū Hurayrah. Al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah narrated it through 'Abd al-Hamīd ibn Abī al-'Ishrīn, from al-Awzā'ī, from Hassān ibn 'Atiyyah, from

---

## Page 2841

Abū Hurayrah. Al-Tirmidhī said:

“This is a hadith that we know only through this chain.”

Suwayd ibn ‘Amr narrated something of this from al-Awzā‘ī. They said: Suwayd ibn ‘Abd al-‘Azīz also narrated it from al-Awzā‘ī. He said: He said: “A hadith from Sa‘īd.” Its meaning has also been narrated from Ka‘b al-Ahbār as his own statement, including the substance of the additional wording.

The basic hadith concerning the “marketplace of Paradise” was narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh, but he did not mention seeing Allah in it. Most of these hadiths, when their chains are considered individually, are open to criticism, whether mild or severe. Yet their number and the many routes through which they are transmitted make it highly probable that they are genuine; indeed, this may establish their authenticity with certainty. Moreover, statements agreeing with this have been transmitted from the “Companions” and the “Successors.” Such matters cannot be asserted on the basis of personal opinion; they can only be stated on the basis of received revelation.

Al-Dāraqutnī narrated through an authentic chain from Ibn al-Mubārak: Al-Mas‘ūdī informed us, from al-Minhāl ibn ‘Amr, from Abū ‘Ubaydah, from ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, who said:

“Hasten to Friday prayer, for Allah will appear before the people of Paradise every Friday on a mound of camphor. Their nearness to Him will correspond to their haste in attending Friday prayer in this world.”

He also narrated through an authentic chain to Shabābah ibn Sawwār, from ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Mas‘ūdī, from al-Minhāl ibn ‘Amr, from Abū ‘Ubaydah ibn ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, from ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, who said:

“Hasten to Friday prayer, for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will appear before the people of Paradise every Friday on a mound of white camphor, and they will be near

---

## Page 2842

to Him in proportion to their haste in attending Friday prayer in this world. He will then bestow upon them an honor they had never seen before.”

He said: No one used to precede ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd to Friday prayer. One day, however, he arrived to find that two men had preceded him. He said: “Two men, and I am the third! Indeed, Allah blesses the third.”

Ibn Battah also narrated it through this route with an authentic chain, adding:

“Then they return to their families and tell them of the honor He has newly bestowed upon them—something they had never seen before.”

This is a sound chain of transmission, deemed sound by al-Tirmidhī and others. It is said that Abū ‘Ubaydah did not hear directly from his father. Nevertheless, he knew his father’s circumstances well and received the reports concerning him from his father’s leading companions. This was a recurring practice of ‘Abd Allāh—may Allah be pleased with him—and would therefore have been well known among his companions, with many recounting it. None of ‘Abd Allāh’s companions was suspected of falsely attributing reports to him, such that one might fear that such a person was the intermediary. For this reason, people have relied on his son’s narrations from him as evidence, even though it is said that he did not hear directly from his father.

This has also been narrated from Ibn Mas‘ūd through another route. Ibn Battah narrated it in al-Ibānah with an authentic chain from al-Walīd ibn Muslim, from Thawr ibn Yazīd, from ‘Amr ibn Qays, reaching ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, who said:

“Allah will appear before the people of His Paradise every Friday on a mound of white camphor. Their nearness to Him will correspond to their haste in attending Friday prayer. He will then grant them life and honor such as they had never seen before.”

It has also been narrated from Ibn Mas‘ūd through “a third route.” Sa‘īd narrated it in his Sunan: We were told by

---

## Page 2843

Faraj ibn Fadālah, from ‘Alī ibn Abī Talhah, from Ibn Mas‘ūd, who used to say:

“Set out early for Friday prayers in this world, for Allah appears before the people of Paradise every Friday on a mound of white camphor. Their nearness to Him will correspond to how early they set out for Friday prayer in this world.”

What Ibn Mas‘ūd reported is something known only to a prophet or someone who received it from a prophet. This establishes that Ibn Mas‘ūd received it from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. He cannot have received it from the People of the Book, for several reasons:

(First): The Companions were forbidden to affirm the truth of what the People of the Book told them. It is therefore inconceivable that Ibn Mas‘ūd—may Allah be pleased with him—would relate something reported by the Jews as religious instruction and base a ruling upon it.

(Second): Ibn Mas‘ūd—may Allah be pleased with him—in particular was among the Companions most vehement in censuring those who took reports from the People of the Book. May Allah be pleased with them all.

(Third): Friday prayer was prescribed only for us, and attending it early is prescribed only in our revealed law. It is therefore unlikely that such a report was received from earlier prophets. It is also unlikely that a Jew would relate such a virtue of this community, when they are described as concealing knowledge, withholding it, and envying this community.

Ibn Mājah also narrated it in his Sunan through another route, tracing it back to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, from ‘Alqamah, who said:

“I went with ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd to Friday prayer, and he found that three men had arrived before him. He said: ‘The fourth of four! Yet the fourth of four is not far behind. I heard the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him,

---

## Page 2844

say: “People will be seated near Allah on Friday according to the order in which they went to Friday prayer: first, second, and third.”’ Then he said: ‘The fourth of four! Yet the fourth of four is not far behind.’”

This hadith is among those the scholars have cited as evidence that going early to Friday prayer is recommended. They have also included this meaning among the interpretations of His words:

“And the foremost will be the foremost.”

Some of them said: “Those who are foremost in attending Friday prayers in this world will be foremost on the Day of Increase in the Hereafter”—or words to that effect, for I do not presently recall the exact wording. This is supported by the Prophet’s statement, peace and blessings be upon him, recorded in the two Sahīh collections:

“We are the last, but will be the foremost on the Day of Resurrection, although they were given the Scripture before us and we were given it after them. This was their day, concerning which they differed, but Allah guided us to it. Thus, the people follow us in this regard: the Jews tomorrow and the Christians the day after tomorrow.”

Our precedence over them in the Hereafter is thus attributed to our having been given the Scripture after them, then being guided to the truth concerning which they differed, until we came to precede them in worship. Just as we preceded them in worship in this world, we shall precede them in receiving His honour in the Hereafter.

As for the hadith of Anas—the best-known of the hadiths concerning what will take place on Friday in the Hereafter, including visiting Allah, seeing Him, and going to the market of Paradise—the most authentic report from him is what Muslim narrated in his Sahīh, from Hammād ibn Salamah, from Thābit, from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“In Paradise there is a market which they will visit every Friday. A north wind will blow, sweeping over their faces and clothes, and they will increase in beauty and loveliness. Their families will say to them: ‘By Allah, you have increased in beauty and loveliness since we parted!’ They will reply: ‘And you, by Allah, have increased in beauty and loveliness since we parted!’”

---

## Page 2845

This report states only that they visit the market, where they increase in beauty and loveliness, and that their families likewise increase in beauty and loveliness during their absence, even though they have not visited the market of Paradise.

If additional details found in some hadiths but not others are unacceptable, and are instead treated as a kind of contradiction, then no hadith concerning seeing Allah on Friday should be accepted in this discussion. None of those reports can match this hadith of Anas, for it alone, among all these reports, was included by the compilers of the Sahīh collections. Indeed, one might argue: if seeing Allah were exclusive, and the increase in the faces’ beauty and loveliness resulted from it, he would have mentioned that in this hadith. One might even argue that its apparent meaning is that their increased beauty and loveliness resulted only from the wind blowing over their faces and clothes.

If, however, the proper position is to say that the additional details in those hadiths do not contradict this report—even though this one is more authentic—because preference is given to one report over another only when they conflict, whereas, if one hadith relates something and another provides an additional detail that does not contradict it, that detail has the standing of an independent report, then this is indeed correct.

This is not the issue over which jurists differed when asking whether an addition to a scriptural text constitutes abrogation. That question concerns only legal rulings: commands, prohibitions, permissions, and their related matters. For example, Allah Most High says:

“As for the woman and the man guilty of unlawful sexual intercourse, flog each of them with a hundred lashes.”

And the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“For the unmarried with the unmarried: one hundred lashes and a year’s banishment.”

He also said to another man:

“Your son is liable to one hundred lashes and a year’s banishment.”

Here the scholars differed over whether this addition abrogates His words:

“As for the woman and the man guilty of unlawful sexual intercourse, flog each of them.”

The majority, however, hold that it does not constitute abrogation. This is the correct view, as established in the appropriate discussion.

---

## Page 2846

As for one report containing additional details beyond another in “purely factual reports,” Muslims have not differed over the fact that this does not constitute abrogation, and that an addition is not rejected if it does not contradict the original report. If a man were to say, “I saw a man,” and then say, “I saw an intelligent man,” or “a learned man,” the two statements would not contradict one another. Thus unrestricted and qualified wording, and wording with or without additions, are treated differently in “prescriptive matters” and in “factual matters.”

That being so, it may be said: Other hadiths relate that the “market” comes after “seeing Allah, glorified be He,” just as people customarily disperse throughout the land and seek Allah’s bounty in this world after visiting Allah and turning to Him on Friday. This hadith’s mention of “their faces increasing in beauty and loveliness” does not imply that this results solely from the wind, for their wives have also increased in beauty and loveliness without sharing in that wind. Rather, the wind may have brought them a further increase beyond what they had already attained. It is also possible that this hadith gives an abbreviated account of what the other hadiths relate: that the cause of the increase is “seeing Allah Most High,” together with what accompanies it.

On this understanding, it is possible that “their believing wives” have seen Allah in their homes in Paradise, and that this “seeing” brought them increased beauty and loveliness—if seeing Him is the cause, as other hadiths explicitly explain. This is just as, in their earthly lives, the men would go to the mosques and turn to Allah there, while the women would turn to Allah in their homes through the noon prayer. The men increase in light in this world through this prayer, and the women likewise increase in light through their prayer, each according to their own measure. Allah, glorified be He, is not distracted by one affair from another; rather, every servant

---

## Page 2847

sees Him privately, at one and the same time, as related in several hadiths. Indeed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that each person can see one of His creations—the moon—privately whenever he wishes. With this clarified, we say:

Of “the hadiths containing details additional to this hadith,” some mention seeing Allah on Friday without relating its degree to Friday prayer in this world, as in Abū Hurayrah’s hadith about the market in Paradise. Others state that, on Friday in the Hereafter, people will sit near Allah in positions corresponding to when they set out for Friday prayer in this world, without mentioning seeing Him—as in the previously cited hadith of Ibn Masʿūd traced back to the Prophet. Still others mention both matters, and these constitute the majority of the hadiths.

The hadiths that mention “seeing Allah alone,” without relating its degree to Friday prayer, are not inferior to those that include this detail, either in number or in the strength of their chains of transmission. Rather, those that include this detail are more numerous, and some have stronger chains of transmission than those other reports. Even if those other reports were more numerous, and this additional detail were transmitted through only one chain comparable to theirs, its acceptance or rejection would be governed by the same ruling as the report to which it adds, since there is no contradiction.

Even supposing that some of these reports, but not others, became well known among “some of the general public” who hear hadiths from storytellers or critics, or among some who read hadiths without taking care to distinguish between them, this would carry no weight whatsoever. How many things are widely known among the general public—indeed, among many jurists, Sufis, and speculative theologians, or

---

## Page 2848

most of them—yet discerning hadith authorities regard them as having no basis; indeed, they may declare with certainty that they are fabricated. Conversely, how many things are well known among “those versed in hadith”—indeed, transmitted among them through numerous independent chains—yet most ordinary people, and even many scholars who have not devoted attention to hadith, have never heard them, or have heard them only at a distant remove. They either deny them or doubt them. Moreover, they have not mastered them as a scholar masters his discipline, as a grammarian masters grammar or a physician medicine. Even if they have retained something of them, it is merely a word here and a word there, which neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger. Such knowledge cannot be relied upon, nor can Allah’s religion be soundly maintained through it, nor does it discharge the community’s obligation to preserve the knowledge conveyed by prophethood and understand it. Imām Ahmad said: “Knowledge of hadith and understanding it are dearer to me than memorizing it.”

I shall now mention corroborating reports for what I have stated.

Al-Dāraqutnī narrated in his Book of the Vision of Allah—among the first reports he included in the section on Anas—through the following chain: Ahmad narrated to us; Sulaymān narrated to us; Muhammad ibn ʿUthmān ibn Muhammad narrated to us; Marwān ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us; Nāfiʿ Abū al-Hasan, the client of Banū Hishām, narrated to us; ʿAtāʾ ibn Abī Maymūnah narrated to us, from Anas ibn Mālik, who said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘On the Day of Resurrection, the believers will see their Lord, Mighty and Majestic. Those among them who have seen Him most recently will be those who see Him every Friday. Believing women will see Him on the Day of Eid al-Fitr and the Day of Sacrifice.’”

Al-Dāraqutnī also narrated, through a group of trustworthy transmitters, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawh al-Madāʾinī:

---

## Page 2849

Sallām ibn Sulaymān narrated to us: Warqā’, Isrā’īl, Shu‘bah, and Jarīr ibn ‘Abd al-Hamīd—all of them—said: Layth narrated to us, from ‘Uthmān ibn Humayd, from Anas ibn Mālik, who said: I heard the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say:

“Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to me carrying in his palm something like a white mirror, with something like a black speck on it. I asked, ‘What is this in your hand, Gabriel?’ He replied, ‘This is Friday.’

“I asked, ‘What is Friday?’ He replied, ‘There is good in it for you.’ I asked, ‘What will there be for us in it?’ He replied, ‘It will be a festival for you and your people after you, and the Jews and Christians will follow you.’ I asked, ‘What do we have in it?’ He replied, ‘There is an hour in it during which, whenever Allah’s servant asks Him for something allotted to him, He gives it to him; and if it is not allotted to him, He stores up for him something greater in his Hereafter.’

“I asked, ‘What is this speck on it?’ He replied, ‘It is the Hour. We call it the Day of Increase.’ I asked, ‘What is that, Gabriel?’ He replied, ‘Your Lord has prepared a valley in Paradise containing dunes of white musk. When Friday comes, He, Mighty and Majestic, descends from ‘Illiyyīn upon His seat. The seat is surrounded by seats of light, and the prophets come and sit on those seats. The seat is also surrounded by pulpits of light and gold, adorned with jewels. Then the foremost in truthfulness and the martyrs come and sit on those pulpits. Then the inhabitants of the chambers descend from their chambers and sit on those dunes.

“‘Then He, Mighty and Majestic, reveals Himself to them and says, “I am the One who has fulfilled My promise to you and perfected My favour upon you. This is the place where I honour you, so ask Me.” They ask Him until they have exhausted their wishes. He then opens to them what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever imagined. This lasts as long as it takes you to disperse after the Friday prayer. Then He, Mighty and Majestic, ascends upon His seat, and the prophets, the foremost in truthfulness, and the martyrs ascend with Him, while the inhabitants of

---

## Page 2850

chambers return to their chambers. These are of white pearl, green emerald, and red ruby, with chambers and doors of the same material, rivers flowing through them, spouses and servants within them, and fruit hanging low. Nothing do they long for more than Friday, when they may gaze still more upon their Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and receive still greater honour from Him.’”

Ibn Battah also narrated this hadith in similar wording from al-Qāfilānī: Muhammad ibn Ishāq al-Sāghānī narrated to us: ‘Abd Allāh ibn Muhammad ibn Abī Shaybah narrated to us: ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from Layth, from ‘Uthmān, from Anas. His version includes:

“Then their Lord, Exalted is He, reveals Himself to them and says, ‘Ask Me, and I shall give you.’ They ask Him for His pleasure. He says, ‘My pleasure has brought you into My abode and granted you My honour, so ask Me, and I shall give you.’ They ask Him for His pleasure, and He calls them to witness that He is pleased with them. He said: Then He opens to them what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever imagined. He said: This lasts as long as it takes you to disperse after the Friday prayer. Then He ascends, and the prophets, the foremost in truthfulness, and the martyrs ascend with Him, while the inhabitants of the chambers return to their chambers.”

He then related the remainder.

This chain establishes that this hadith was indeed transmitted from Layth ibn Abī Sulaym, thereby removing the objection concerning Sallām ibn Sulaym, since all the narrators preceding Layth in this second chain are leading authorities. As for the first chain, it seems to leave some misgiving, because Sallām narrated it from a group of well-known transmitters, and ‘Abd Allāh ibn Rawh al-Madā’inī narrated it from him. Assessments of this Sallām have differed. Ibn Ma‘īn once said, “There is nothing wrong with him.” Abū Hātim said, “He is truthful, and his hadith are acceptable.”

On another occasion, Ibn Ma‘īn was asked about him: “Is he trustworthy?” He replied, “No.” Al-‘Uqaylī said, “His narrations are not corroborated by other transmitters.”

---

## Page 2851

Since the hadith has been transmitted through that sound chain, the grounds for blaming him fall away.

Al-Dāraqutnī also narrated it through this chain by a third route, from al-Hasan ibn ‘Arafah: ‘Ammār ibn Muhammad, the nephew of Sufyān al-Thawrī, narrated to us, from Layth ibn Abī Sulaym, from ‘Uthmān, from Anas ibn Mālik, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Gabriel came to me, holding in his palm something like a white mirror, with something like a black spot in it.”

He related the hadith in wording similar to what preceded, but did not mention: “That lasts as long as it takes you to disperse after the Friday prayer.” This strengthens the conclusion that the hadith has a basis in transmission from Layth. The omission of the additional wording does not undermine it, for neither the additions nor the omissions of ‘Ammār ibn Muhammad ibn Abī Ukht Sufyān may be relied upon as proof. We have mentioned his narration only as corroboration.

This hadith states that it is the righteous who return to their families. As for the prophets, the foremost in truthfulness, and the martyrs, they do not return at that time. It contains nothing either affirming or denying that women see Allah.

Abū al-‘Abbās Muhammad ibn Ishāq al-Sarrāj also narrated it: ‘Alī ibn Ashyab narrated to us: Abū Badr narrated to us: Ziyād ibn Khaythamah narrated to us, from ‘Uthmān ibn Muslim, from Anas ibn Mālik, who said:

“One day, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was late coming out to us. When he came out, we said, ‘You have kept us waiting.’ He replied, ‘Gabriel came to me, holding in his palm something resembling a white mirror, with a black spot in it. He said, “This is Friday; it holds good for you and your nation. The Jews and Christians sought it, but missed it.” I asked, “O Gabriel, what is in this black spot?” He said, “This is the hour on Friday which no servant encounters, asking Allah for some good from his allotted share, except that

---

## Page 2852

Allah grants it to him, stores up its equivalent for him on the Day of Resurrection, or averts an equivalent evil from him. Friday is the best of days in Allah’s sight, and the people of Paradise call it the Day of Increase.”

I asked, “O Gabriel, what is the Day of Increase?”

He said, “In Paradise there is a spacious valley whose soil is white musk. Allah descends to it every Friday, and His seat is set in place. Then pulpits of light are brought and placed behind it, and the angels gather around it. Seats of gold are then brought and set in place. The prophets, the foremost in truthfulness, the martyrs, and the believers who dwell in the chambers then come and sit down. Allah smiles at them and says, ‘Ask.’ They say, ‘We ask for Your good pleasure.’ He says, ‘I am pleased with you, so ask.’ They ask for what they desire, and He grants them what they request many times over. He also grants them what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever imagined.

“Then He says, ‘Have I not fulfilled My promise to you and perfected My favor upon you? This is the abode of My honor.’ Then they return to their chambers, coming back every Friday.”

I asked, “O Gabriel, what are their chambers made of?”

He said, “Of a white pearl, a red ruby, and a green chrysolite, with their doors fashioned from the same material. Their spouses are within them, and their rivers flow continually.”’”

Abū Ya‘lā al-Mawsilī narrated a similar report in his (Musnad), from Shaybān ibn Farrūkh, from al-Sa‘q ibn Hazn, from ‘Alī ibn al-Hakam al-Bunānī, from Anas. I did not have its wording at hand.

Al-Dāraqutnī also narrated it through ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Hamīm al-Rāzī: And ‘Amr ibn Qays narrated to us, from Abū Shabībah, from ‘Āsim, from ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Umayr Abū al-Yaqzān, from Anas. He also narrated it through Ishāq ibn Sulaymān al-Rāzī: ‘Anbasah ibn Sa‘īd narrated to us, from ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Umayr, from Anas ibn Mālik, in wording similar to the preceding account, without mentioning the additional wording.

---

## Page 2853

Ibn Battah also narrated, with a sound chain of transmission to al-Aswad ibn ‘Āmir, who said: It was related to me from Sharīk, from Abū al-Yaqzān, from Anas, concerning the words, “And with Us is more,” that he said: “He manifests Himself to them every Friday.”

Al-Dāraqutnī also narrated it through Muhammad ibn Hātim al-Missīsī: Muhammad ibn Sa‘īd al-Qurashī narrated to us; Hamzah ibn Wāsil al-Minqarī narrated to us; Qatādah ibn Di‘āmah narrated to us—I heard him say: Anas ibn Mālik narrated to us, saying: “While we were gathered around the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he said, ‘Gabriel came to me holding the white mirror.’” He then related the preceding hadith at greater length. It contains wording that reconciles the hadith of Anas in Sahīh Muslim with the other hadiths, including: “It remains so until the time corresponding to their dispersal after the Friday prayer.”

It was also transmitted through another chain, narrated by Abū ‘Umar Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Wāhid al-Zāhid, known as Ghulām Tha‘lab: Muhammad ibn Ja‘far ibn Abī al-Dumayk al-Marwazī narrated to us; Salamah ibn Shabīb narrated to us; Yahyā ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Harrānī narrated to us; Dirār ibn ‘Amr narrated to us, from Yazīd al-Raqāshī, from Anas ibn Mālik. He related the hadith at greater length than the preceding versions. I did not have its wording at hand, but I think it contains the aforementioned addition. This chain of transmission is weak because of Yazīd al-Raqāshī and Dirār ibn ‘Amr, but it is considered alongside the preceding reports.

It was also transmitted through another chain from Anas, narrated by Abū Hafs ibn Shāhīn: Ja‘far ibn Muhammad al-‘Attār narrated to us; my grandfather, ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Hakam, narrated to us: I heard ‘Āsim Abū ‘Alī say: I heard Humayd al-Tawīl say: I heard Anas ibn Mālik say: “I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say, ‘Indeed, Allah manifests Himself to the people of Paradise every day upon

---

## Page 2854

a mound of white camphor.’” It has been said that Ja‘far, his grandfather, and ‘Āsim are unknown narrators. This does not preclude adducing the report as counterevidence.

Al-Dāraqutnī also narrated it with a sound chain of transmission to al-‘Abbās ibn al-Walīd ibn Mazīd: Muhammad ibn Shu‘ayb informed me; ‘Umar, the freedman of ‘Afrah, informed me, from Anas ibn Mālik, with wording similar to the preceding narrations. It includes: “After their departure from the Friday gathering, He opens up for them what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.” Thus, this has been narrated from Anas through several transmitters, and most of their narrations mention the addition, as noted above.

As for the hadith of Hudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with him, Abū Bakr al-Khallāl narrated it from Yazīd ibn Jumhūr: Al-Hasan ibn Yahyā ibn Kathīr al-‘Anbarī narrated to us; my father narrated to us, from Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mubārak, from al-A‘mash, from Abū Wā’il, from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yamān, who said: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Gabriel came to me holding in his palm a mirror like the clearest and finest of mirrors.’” He related the hadith with additional material beyond what preceded. It contains other wording, but he did not mention the aforementioned addition.

Abū Bakr al-Bazzār also narrated it: Muhammad ibn Ma‘mar and Ahmad ibn ‘Amr al-‘Usfūrī narrated to us, saying: Yahyā ibn Kathīr al-‘Anbarī narrated to us, from Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mubārak, from al-Qāsim ibn Mutayyab, from al-A‘mash, from Abū Wā’il, from Hudhayfah. He related the hadith, which includes: “Then Allah reveals to the bearers of the Throne that they should open the veils between Him and them. The first thing they hear from Him, Exalted is He, will be: ‘Where are My servants who obeyed Me in the unseen, without having seen Me, and believed

---

## Page 2855

My messengers and followed My command? Ask Me, for this is the Day of Increase.’ They all say with one voice: ‘We are content, so be pleased with us.’—Then the account returns to His words—‘O people of Paradise, had I not been pleased with you, I would not have admitted you to My Paradise. This is the Day of Increase, so ask Me.’ They all say with one voice: ‘Our Lord, show us Your Face so that we may look upon it.’ Allah then removes the veils and manifests Himself to them. They are enveloped by such light from Him that, had Allah not decreed that they would never die, they would be consumed by it. Then they are told: ‘Return to your dwellings,’ and they return to their dwellings. There is one such day in every seven days: that is the Day of Increase.”

As for the hadith of Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him, it has been narrated through more than one sound chain in (the book of al-Ājurrī) and the works of Ibn Battah and others, from Abū Bakr ibn Abī Dāwūd al-Sijistānī: My uncle Muhammad ibn al-Ash‘ath narrated to us; Ibn Jisr narrated to us; my father, Jisr, narrated to us, from al-Husayn, from Ibn ‘Abbās, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“The people of Paradise see their Lord, Exalted is He, every Friday amid sands of camphor. Those seated closest to Him are those who hasten most eagerly to the Friday prayer and set out earliest in the morning.”

This explicitly states the additional detail under discussion.

As for the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah narrated it through ‘Abd al-Hamīd ibn Abī al-‘Ishrīn: Al-Awzā‘ī narrated to us; Hassān ibn ‘Atiyyah narrated to us, from Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyab, who met Abū Hurayrah. Abū Hurayrah said: “I ask Allah to bring us together in the marketplace of Paradise.”

Sa‘īd asked: “Is there a marketplace there?”

He replied: “Yes. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, informed me that when the people of Paradise enter it, they take up their dwellings

---

## Page 2856

there according to the merit of their deeds. Then, at a time corresponding to Friday in this world, they are granted permission to visit their Lord. He brings forth His Throne for them and manifests Himself to them in one of the gardens of Paradise. Pulpits of light, pearls, rubies, chrysolite, gold and silver are set out for them. Those of the lowest rank—though none among them is lowly—sit upon dunes of musk and camphor. They do not consider those seated on chairs to have better seats than theirs.”

Abū Hurayrah said: “I asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, will we see our Lord, Mighty and Majestic?’

“He replied, ‘Yes. Do you have any doubt about seeing the sun, or the moon on the night when it is full?’

“We said, ‘No.’

“He said, ‘Likewise, you will have no doubt about seeing your Lord, Blessed and Exalted. No one in that gathering—meaning, no man—will be left without Allah addressing him directly. He will even say to a man among them: “O so-and-so, son of so-and-so, do you remember the day you said such-and-such?”—reminding him of some of his acts of betrayal in this world.

“‘The man will say, “My Lord, did You not forgive me?”

“‘He will reply, “Indeed. It is through the vastness of My forgiveness that you have attained this station.”

“‘While they are thus gathered, a cloud will cover them from above and rain down upon them perfume whose fragrance they have never encountered before. Our Lord will say, “Rise and go to the honours I have prepared for you, and take whatever you desire.”

“‘We will then come to a marketplace surrounded by angels, containing things the like of which eyes have never seen, ears have never heard, and hearts have never imagined. Whatever we desire will be carried for us; nothing there is bought or sold. In that marketplace, the people of Paradise will meet one another.’

“He said, ‘A man of high rank will approach and meet someone of a lower rank—though none among them is lowly—who will be dazzled by the clothes he is wearing. Before their conversation has ended, something finer still will appear to him. This is because no one should experience sorrow there. Then we will return to our dwellings, and our wives will come out to meet us

---

## Page 2857

and say, “Welcome! You have returned more beautiful than when you left us.”

“He will reply, ‘Today we sat with our Lord, the Compeller, and it is only fitting that we should return as we have.’”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “This is a singular hadith; we know it only through this route. Suwayd ibn ʿAmr also narrated part of it from al-Awzāʿī.”

I say: Ibn Battah narrated this hadith in (al-Ibānah) through authentic chains of transmission from Abū al-Mughīrah ʿAbd al-Quddūs ibn al-Hajjāj, from al-Awzāʿī; and from Muhammad ibn Kathīr, from al-Awzāʿī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sālih, who said: “Al-Hiql related to me, from al-Awzāʿī, who said: ‘I was informed that Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib met Abū Hurayrah and said: “I ask Allah to bring us together in the marketplace of Paradise.”’” He then related the hadith as cited above.

This shows that the hadith is reliably preserved from al-Awzāʿī. In those narrations, however, he named the person who related it to him, whereas in the remaining, latter narrations he did not name him. Allah knows best.

The implication of this hadith is that their wives were not with them at the Friday gathering in the Hereafter or in its marketplace. However, it does not rule out their having seen Allah in their dwellings. The men attributed their increased beauty and splendour to sitting with the Compeller, and the women shared in this increase in beauty and splendour, as previously mentioned in the most authentic hadiths.

---

## Page 2858

Section

What prompted me to write this was that, some time ago, a jurist asked me on behalf of the women of his household: “Will believing women see Allah in the Hereafter?”

I answered with what came to mind at the time: that the apparent meaning of the evidence is that they will see Him. I mentioned that Abū Bakr had narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that they would see Him on the Eids; that the hadiths concerning seeing Allah encompass all believers, men and women alike, as do the scholars’ statements; and that the reasoning underlying the matter supports this, according to my examination of the evidence. I also mentioned other points that do not come to mind at present.

It had occurred to me, concerning the report from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the reason for this was that the regular, communal occasions of “seeing Allah” in the Hereafter correspond to the regular congregational prayers. Since men have been prescribed to gather every Friday in this world to remember Allah, converse intimately with Him, behold Him with their hearts, and delight in meeting Him in prayer, He has appointed for them a gathering every Friday in the Hereafter to converse intimately with Him, behold Him directly, and enjoy meeting Him.

Likewise, since the established Sunnah directs women to go out for Eid—even young maidens and menstruating women—and believing women generally used to go out for Eid during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, their Eid of seeing Allah in the Hereafter was made to correspond to their Eid in this world.

---

## Page 2859

What further supported this understanding for me was the report recorded in the two Sahīh collections from Jarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī, who said:

“We were sitting with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when he looked at the moon on the night of the full moon and said: ‘You will see your Lord just as you see this moon, with none of you deprived of seeing Him. So, if you can avoid being prevented from offering a prayer before sunrise and a prayer before sunset, then do so.’ Then he recited: ‘And glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting.’”

This is among the most authentic hadiths on earth, received with acceptance and unanimously acknowledged by hadith scholars and all other adherents of the Sunnah.

I observed that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, informed the believers that they would see their Lord, then followed this with his words:

“So, if you can avoid being prevented from offering a prayer before sunrise and a prayer before sunset, then do so.”

It is well known that when a ruling follows an attribute, or an attribute follows a ruling, linked by the particle fa (“so”), this indicates that the attribute is the cause of the ruling. This is especially so because mere temporal succession is impossible here: seeing Allah is mentioned in the hadith before the exhortation to observe the two prayers, yet that vision occurs in the Hereafter, whereas the exhortation occurs before it, in this world.

By “immediate succession,” grammarians do not mean that the wording of the second item comes after the first, for this occurs with or without fa, and with all the other conjunctions. Rather, they mean that what is expressed second occurs immediately after what is expressed first. Thus, when you say, “Zayd stood up, then ʿAmr,” this conveys that ʿAmr’s actual standing occurred immediately after Zayd’s—not merely that the speaker uttered the second expression immediately after the first. This is well established among jurists in the principles of jurisprudence, and is understood from

---

## Page 2860

the Arabic language. If someone says, “This is a righteous man, so honour him,” it is understood that his righteousness is the reason for the command to honour him. Thus, if we subsequently saw another righteous man, one could say, “The same applies: this man too is righteous, so will you not honour him?” If he does not do so, the ruling must have failed to apply because of some countervailing consideration; otherwise, this would be regarded as a contradiction.

Likewise, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There is not one of you but that his Lord will speak to him, with neither a gatekeeper nor an interpreter between him and Him. He will look to his right and see only what he has sent ahead; he will look to his left and see only what he has sent ahead; and he will look before him and find the Fire facing him. Whoever among you can shield himself from the Fire, even with half a date, should do so. If he cannot, then with a kind word.”

It is understood that his exhortation here to guard against the Fire is because they will face it when meeting their Lord, even if there is another cause for it.

Likewise, when Ibn Masʿūd said:

“Hasten to the Friday prayer, for Allah will reveal Himself to the people of Paradise every Friday upon a mound among the mounds of camphor. Their nearness to Him will correspond to how eagerly they hastened to the Friday prayer in this world.”

People understood from this that seeking this reward is the reason for the command to hasten to Paradise.

Likewise, if someone were to say, “Tomorrow the ruler will judge between the people or distribute shares among them, so whoever wishes should attend,” it would be understood that the command to attend is so that one may receive one’s share of his judgment or distribution. This is clear.

Furthermore, this attribute that gives rise to the ruling “sometimes constitutes a cause that precedes

---

## Page 2861

the ruling both logically and in actual existence, as in His words:

‘As for the male and female thief, cut off their hands.’”

“At other times,” its outcome precedes the ruling in knowledge and intention, but follows it in actual existence. For example, you might say, “The ruler will attend tomorrow.” If he does attend, his attendance will have been conceived and intended before the command to attend with him, even though it takes place after that command. This is called the final cause; jurists call it the wisdom underlying the ruling. It causes the intention to enact its ruling, while its ruling causes its actual realization.

Sometimes a “causal explanation” is expressed in terms of the actual beneficial outcome itself, making it appear that the cause follows its effect. In reality, however, the cause is seeking and desiring that outcome. Seeking and desiring well-being precede seeking the measures taken to achieve it, whereas those measures precede well-being itself in actual existence. There are many similar examples, as in the statements:

“When you recite the Quran, seek refuge.”

“When you rise for prayer, wash.”

Likewise, one says, “When you perform Hajj, take provisions.”

Thus, the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “You will see your Lord; so if you can avoid being prevented from observing two prayers,” continuing to “then do so,” imply that steadfastly observing them here is for the sake of seeking this vision, and that steadfast observance is a cause of this vision. This does not preclude such observance from bringing another reward for whose sake it is commanded, or from being a cause of that reward; nor does it preclude the vision from having another cause. For a single ruling may have several causes, and a single cause may give rise to several rulings.

The same applies to most hadiths promising reward, such as his words:

“Whoever prays two units of prayer without conversing during them with

---

## Page 2862

himself will have his past sins forgiven. Whoever performs Hajj to this House, neither engaging in obscenity nor committing sin, will return free of sins as on the day his mother bore him.” And his words:

“A woman must not be married to a man who is already married to her paternal or maternal aunt, for if you do that, you will sever your ties of kinship.”

These and similar statements imply that offering those two units of prayer is a cause of forgiveness, as is an accepted Hajj, even though forgiveness has other causes.

This meaning is further supported by Allah’s words:

“Do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face.”

This supplication has been interpreted as referring to the Fajr and ‘Asr prayers. Since Allah has stated that they seek His Face through these two prayers, and has stated in this hadith that they will look upon Him, the exhortation to observe these prayers accords with this: whoever seeks His Face will look upon His Face—blessed and exalted is He.

When this is considered alongside the earlier point that Friday prayer is a cause of seeing Him at its corresponding time, as is the Eid prayer, it is fitting that these two prayers—the finest prayers, whose times are the finest times—should likewise be such a cause. Thus, it is fitting that prayer, which is the finest of deeds, and particularly the finest prayers offered at the finest times, should be a cause of the finest rewards at the finest times.

This is especially so given the hadith of Ibn ‘Umar narrated by al-Tirmidhī through Isrā’īl, from Thuwayr ibn Abī Fākhitah, who said: I heard Ibn ‘Umar say:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘The lowest-ranking inhabitant of Paradise is one who can see his gardens, spouses, delights, servants, and couches over a distance of a thousand years’ journey. The most honoured of them before Allah is one who looks upon His Face morning and evening.’ Then the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited: ‘Faces that Day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.’”

---

## Page 2863

Al-Tirmidhī said: “This hadith has been transmitted through several routes from Isrā’īl, from Thuwayr, from Ibn ‘Umar, traced back to the Prophet. ‘Abd al-Malik ibn Abjar transmitted it from Thuwayr, from Mujāhid, from Ibn ‘Umar, as a statement of Ibn ‘Umar himself. ‘Ubayd Allah al-Ashja‘ī also transmitted it from Sufyān, from Thuwayr, from Mujāhid, from Ibn ‘Umar as his own statement, without attributing it to the Prophet.”

Al-Tirmidhī also said: “We know of no one who mentioned Mujāhid in its chain other than Thuwayr.”

I believe it has been said, concerning His words:

“And they will have their provision therein, morning and evening,”

that this provision includes looking upon Allah. A hadith traced back to the Prophet has been transmitted concerning this. Al-Dāraqutnī narrated it in *The Vision*: Abū ‘Ubayd Qāsim ibn Ismā‘īl al-Dabbī narrated to us; Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Marzūq al-Basrī narrated to us; Hāni’ ibn Yahyā narrated to us; Sālih al-Misrī narrated to us, from ‘Abbād al-Minqarī, from Maymūn ibn Siyāh, from Anas ibn Mālik, who related that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, taught him to recite this verse:

“Faces that Day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.”

He said: “By Allah, He has not abrogated it since He revealed it. They visit their Lord, blessed and exalted is He, and are given food and drink, perfumed, and carried. The veil between Him and them is lifted, and they look upon Him, and He, mighty and majestic, looks upon them. This is His saying: ‘And they will have their provision therein, morning and evening.’”

Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī included this hadith in *Fabricated Reports* and said: “This is not authentic. Its chain includes Maymūn ibn Siyāh. Ibn Hibbān said: ‘He alone transmits objectionable reports from well-known narrators; his reports cannot be used as evidence when he is their sole transmitter.’ It also includes Sālih al-Misrī, of whom al-Nasā’ī said: ‘He is abandoned as a hadith transmitter.’”

I say: As for Maymūn ibn Siyāh, both al-Bukhārī and al-Nasā’ī transmitted reports through him, and Abū Hātim al-Rāzī said of him: “Trustworthy.” These three considerations suffice. It is also reported that Ibn Ma‘īn said of him:

---

## Page 2864

“Weak.” But Ibn Ma‘īn says this of more than one trustworthy narrator. As for Ibn Hibbān’s remarks, they introduce an innovation into the criticism of narrators.

The preceding hadith of Ibn ‘Umar promises the highest-ranking among them the vision “morning and evening.” The Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, made the morning and evening prayers a means of “seeing Allah,” and the Friday prayer a means of “seeing Allah” at its corresponding time. Together with the connection between prayer and the vision, these considerations strongly suggest that these two prayers are a means of seeing Allah at their corresponding times in the Hereafter. Allah knows best the reality of the matter.

This was what had occurred to me. Since women share with men in performing the deed that brings about the reward, they share with them in its reward. Where there was no shared participation in the Friday prayer, there was likewise no shared participation in looking upon Allah in the Hereafter; where there was shared participation in the Eid prayer, there was shared participation in its reward.

Then, a long time later, this “question” came up in discussion. I had forgotten what I had mentioned initially—not merely part of it—and the discussion prompted me to mention what I had said at first. I was told: “The hadith indicates that these two prayers constitute part of the cause of seeing Allah, not the whole cause. The evidence is that someone who performs them but does not perform the noon and afternoon prayers does not deserve the vision.”

I was also told: “The hadith indicates that the two prayers are a cause in general, so these two prayers could be a means of seeing Allah on Friday. Indeed, has it not been said that the highest-ranking person in Paradise is one who sees Him twice? How, then, can those who consistently observe these two prayers be the highest-ranking among them?”

I replied: The apparent meaning of the hadith indicates that these two prayers are the cause of this

---

## Page 2865

“vision,” in accordance with the principle concerning women that I mentioned earlier. Yet a cause may fail to produce its effect because of an impediment, without this undermining its causal force, as with the other hadiths promising reward. For when he said:

“Whoever performs the two prayers in the cool hours will enter Paradise,”

and, “Whoever does such-and-such will enter Paradise,” he indicated that the deed in question is a cause of entering Paradise, even if its consequence fails to follow because of unbelief or sinful disobedience. Whoever abandons the noon prayer, commits fornication, steals, or does something similar is sinfully disobedient; and a sinfully disobedient person is not entitled to the promise of entering Paradise, just as an unbeliever is not.

The same applies to hadiths of warning. When it is said, “Whoever does such-and-such will enter the Fire,” the stated consequence does not apply to someone who repents, someone who performs good deeds that erase bad deeds, and others. There may also be another cause of seeing Allah. Thus, its being a cause does not preclude its consequence from being prevented by an impediment, nor does it preclude another cause of seeing Allah from existing.

Furthermore, I say: whether performing the remaining obligatory duties is part of the cause or a condition for this cause makes little difference; the dispute is merely verbal. Our discussion concerns only someone who has fulfilled the remaining conditions of the promise and is free of its impediments.

Nor may it be said, “Being female is an impediment to receiving the promise, or being male is a condition.” If evidence from revelation indicated this, just as it indicates that performing the remaining obligatory duties is a condition, we would accept it. But mere possibility does not justify setting aside what the wording entails and requires. Rather, once the general scope of the wording and of the underlying rationale is established, their consequence must be applied unless evidence indicates otherwise. It has not been established that being male is a condition or that being female is an impediment, just as the wording does not indicate that being Arab or non-Arab, black or white, has any bearing on this.

---

## Page 2866

Likewise, the hadith indicates that “those who take a middle course” share with “the foremost” in seeing Allah, although the foremost surpass them in rank and reward; alternatively, its meaning encompasses both groups equally. In this respect, it is evidence that these two prayers are a cause of seeing Allah. The existence of a cause entails the existence of its effect unless a condition is absent or an impediment arises. Establishing such conditions and impediments requires evidence.

As for the objection concerning these two prayers being a cause of seeing Allah in general—even if only on Friday—the response is: this does not rule out women seeing Him in general, even if on a day other than Friday. That is precisely what we seek to establish.

Furthermore, taken together, all the hadiths mentioned above indicate that the vision occurs at the time corresponding to when the deed was performed in this world. Thus, if it is said that the vision occurs morning and evening, and that its cause is the morning and afternoon prayers, this plainly supports what we have said. What we claim is an apparent meaning, not certainty.

As for the argument that “seeing Allah twice” is reserved for the highest-ranking inhabitants of Paradise, whereas not everyone who performs these two prayers belongs to that rank, this does not refute what we have stated. These two possibilities are conceivable, and the evidence can be interpreted accordingly; but Allah knows best which of them actually occurs.

The cause may be performing these two prayers as Allah has commanded, inwardly and outwardly—not the prayer performed by most people. Consider the hadith of ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, who reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “A man may finish his prayer with only a quarter of it recorded for him, only a fifth, only a sixth—until

---

## Page 2867

he said: a tenth of it.” Reported by Abū Dāwūd. Accepted prayer is a cause of reward, and accepted prayer is that which is recorded for the person who performs it. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that some worshippers have only part of their prayer recorded for them. Such a worshipper is therefore not entitled to the reward earned by someone whose prayer Allah accepts and records in full. On this understanding, scarcely anyone would fall within the scope of the hadith except those of consummate truthfulness and a few others—and among women, too, are those of consummate truthfulness.

It is also possible that someone whose voluntary prayers make up for deficiencies in his obligatory prayers falls within the scope of the hadith, as stated in the hadith reported by Abū Hurayrah from the Prophet:

“Voluntary prayers will make up for deficiencies in obligatory prayers on the Day of Resurrection.”

On this understanding, most worshippers who faithfully observe their prayers would qualify, and these would be the highest-ranking inhabitants of Paradise. For most of Muhammad’s community, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, do not faithfully observe the prayers: some delay certain prayers beyond their appointed times; some omit certain obligatory elements of their prayers; and some abandon certain prayers altogether. The other nations before us had no share in these two prayers.

Even if it were said that everyone who performs these two prayers and enters Paradise, whatever his condition, having been forgiven, receives this reward, that would be within Allah’s power, and the hadith would not rule it out. For the most it says is that such a person is among the highest-ranking inhabitants of Paradise. Being higher or lower is relative. Thus, the inhabitants of the three Gardens may rightly be described as ranking above the inhabitants of the remaining five Gardens. The same may also be said

---

## Page 2868

of most of the inhabitants of Paradise: they rank above those beneath them. Some of this, however, is open to question, and Allah knows best the reality of the matter. The point is that this does not negate what we have stated. All this, moreover, assumes that the hadith mentioning “twice” could serve as counterevidence to the proof we have presented. It cannot do so, however, because of the discrepancies in its chain of transmission.

When the question of “women seeing their Lord in the Hereafter” arose again, I presented several arguments. I shall set them out, noting the objections raised against me and the points left unchallenged, so that the matter becomes clear. I say: the proof that women will see Him is that the texts stating that believers will see Him in the Hereafter include women in both their wording and their meaning. Nothing requiring their exclusion has been advanced against this general scope. We must therefore accept the evidence, which stands free of any counterevidence of comparable strength.

If we were asked, “What is the proof that Persians will see Allah?” or “that tall men will see Allah?” or “What is the proof that Abyssinian women will emerge from the Fire?”, a general statement of this kind would be entirely sufficient, unless its scope were specifically restricted. It should also be understood that an established general statement that admits of no restriction is almost conclusive in its inclusiveness; indeed, it may be conclusive.

As for the “general texts,” these include the report in the two Sahīh collections from Abū Hurayrah that the people said:

“O Messenger of Allah, will we see our Lord on the Day of Resurrection?”

He said: “Do you have any doubt about seeing the moon on the night when it is full, with no clouds obscuring it?”

They said: “No, O Messenger of Allah.”

He said: “Then do you have any doubt about seeing

---

## Page 2869

the sun when no clouds obscure it?”

They said, “No.”

He said: “You will see Him just as clearly. The people will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection, and He will say, ‘Whoever worshipped anything, let him follow it.’ Some will follow the sun, some will follow the moon, and some will follow false deities. This community will remain, including its hypocrites. He will come to them in a form other than His form which they recognize. They will say, ‘We seek refuge in Allah from you. We shall remain here until our Lord, Mighty and Majestic, comes to us. When our Lord, Mighty and Majestic, comes, we shall recognize Him.’ He will then come to them in His form which they recognize and say, ‘I am your Lord.’ They will say, ‘You are our Lord.’ He will call them, and they will follow Him. The bridge will be laid across the midst of Hell, and my community and I will be the first to cross. None but the messengers will speak that day, and the messengers’ supplication that day will be, ‘O Allah, grant safety! Grant safety!’” He went on to relate the hadith.

The two Sahīh collections also report from Abū Sa‘īd, who said:

“We said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, will we see our Lord on the Day of Resurrection?’

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Yes. Do you have any difficulty seeing the sun at midday when the sky is clear and there are no clouds? Do you have any difficulty seeing the moon on the night when it is full, when the sky is clear and there are no clouds?’

“They said, ‘No, O Messenger of Allah.’

“He said, ‘You will have no more difficulty seeing Allah, Blessed and Exalted, on the Day of Resurrection than you have seeing either of them. When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will proclaim, “Let every community follow what it used to worship.” All those who worshipped anything other than Allah—idols or objects of worship set up for them—will fall into the Fire, until none remain but those who worshipped Allah, whether righteous or wicked, and those other than the People of the Book.’”

He then related the passage of the hadith concerning the summoning of the Jews and Christians, until he said:

“Until none remain but those who worshipped Allah, whether righteous or wicked, Allah will come to them in a lower form than that in which they had seen Him. He will say, ‘What are you waiting for? Every community is following what it used to worship.’ They will say, ‘Our Lord, we parted from the people in this world when we were most in need of them, and did not

keep their company.’ He will say, ‘I am your Lord.’ They will say, ‘We seek refuge in Allah from you. The word “people” encompasses both groups, and both groups will be gathered. The scope of this general wording may not be restricted—or, even if such restriction were permissible, the case for it would be weak—because women outnumber men. It is authentically established that women constitute the majority of the inhabitants of the Fire. It is also authentically established that every man in Paradise will have two human wives, besides the wide-eyed maidens. Thus, women outnumber men in Paradise, just as they do in the Fire, making women the greater number overall. General wording may not be understood to cover only the minority of instances while excluding the majority without an accompanying contextual indication. That would be misleading and inept expression, far beneath the speech of the Lawgiver.

Then his statement that it will be said, “Whoever worshipped anything, let him follow it,” is a description expressed in one of the formulations that

## Page 2871

encompass both men and women. The meaning is also general: a person follows what he worshipped because he worshipped it in this world, and this reason applies to both groups.

The words, “When He comes, we shall recognize Him,” together with his statement, “He will then come to them in His form which they recognize and say, ‘I am your Lord.’ They will say, ‘You are our Lord.’ Then He will call them,” explain what we mentioned at the beginning of the hadith: that they will see their Lord as they see the sun and the moon.

Concerning those who prostrate, he said, “Everyone who used to prostrate to Allah of his own accord will be permitted by Allah to prostrate.” The word “whoever” encompasses both men and women. Thus, everyone who has prostrated sincerely to Allah, whether man or woman, will have prostrated to Allah and seen Him on these three occasions.

This is not the place to explain matters relating to the repeated prostration, the change of form, or other matters one might seek to understand. Our purpose here is simply to establish the point we set out to address. Both hadiths also tell of their crossing the Bridge and of some people falling into the Fire

and included in it words from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) indicating that Jābir heard the entire account from him. The same applies to his statements:

“There is not one of you but that his Lord will be alone with him, just as each of you is alone with the moon.”

“Every one of you will be spoken to by his Lord, with neither a doorkeeper nor an interpreter between him and his Lord.”

There are other authentic and good hadiths explicitly stating that all people, male and female, share in these matters: “being called to account,” “seeing Allah,” “being alone with Him,” and “being spoken to by Him.”

The same applies to the hadiths about “seeing Him—glorified be He—in Paradise,” such as the report Muslim narrated in his Sahih from Suhayb, who said:

“The Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said, ‘When the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire have entered the Fire, a caller will proclaim, “O people of Paradise, Allah has made you a promise which He wishes to fulfil for you.” They will say, “What is it? into Paradise and saved us from the Fire?” Then the veil will be lifted, and they will look upon Allah. Nothing they have been given will be dearer to them than looking upon Him. This is the increase.’”

His words, “When the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire have entered the Fire,” encompass men and women, for the term “people” includes both sexes. Moreover, it is known that women are among the people of Paradise.

His words, “O people of Paradise, Allah has made you a promise which He wishes to fulfil for you,” address all the people of Paradise who have entered it and have been promised their reward. This includes all morally accountable women.

Likewise, their words, “Has He not made our scales heavy, brightened our faces, admitted us, and fulfilled His promise?” encompass both sexes.

In his words, “Then the veil will be lifted, and they will look upon Him,” the pronoun refers back to those previously mentioned, encompassing both sexes. The verse cited also provides a further proof, for Allah, glorified be He, says:

It is known that women are among those who do good. His subsequent words, “Those are the inhabitants of Paradise,” imply that the inhabitants of Paradise consist exclusively of those people. Since women are among the inhabitants of Paradise, they must be included among “those.” That word refers to those who will receive the best reward and more. Women must therefore be included among those who will receive the best reward and more. This also entails that everyone who belongs to the inhabitants of Paradise has been promised the “increase beyond the best reward,” which is looking upon Allah, glorified be He. No one may be excluded from this without evidence.

No particular time has been specified for this “seeing Him shared by all.” It may occur immediately after they enter Paradise, before they settle into their dwellings. Allah knows best when that will be.

## Page 2875

Likewise, the passages of the Book that indicate seeing Allah, such as His words:

divide humanity into categories—the humanity mentioned in His words:

The apparent sense is that faces fall into these two categories. Similarly, His words:

also divide them into these two categories. Thus, anyone whose face is not among the gloomy faces will be among those whose faces are radiant and looking upon their Lord. How could it be otherwise, when it is established in the hadith that women increase in beauty and loveliness just as men do at the appointed times of looking upon Allah?
