have been interpreted as referring to seeing Allah, as have His words:

“Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss, looking on from their couches.”

All of this encompasses both men and women.

Know that scholars have differed concerning “masculine plural forms, both explicit nouns and pronouns,” such as “the believers” and “the righteous.” The question is whether women are included when such wording is used without qualification, or whether they are included only where there is evidence. There are two views:

(The better-known view among our scholars and those who agree with them is that women are included. This is based on the Arabic convention that, when males and females are mentioned together, the masculine form takes precedence. We also know from the Lawgiver’s manner of address that it encompasses both groups, with women included through this predominance of the masculine form. In short, the Arabs sometimes use these plurals for males alone and sometimes for both males and females.

---

## Page 2876

and we know from the Lawgiver’s practice that His unqualified address follows the second pattern. By “unqualified,” we exclude qualified expressions such as His words:

“the believing men and believing women.”

Some who hold this view maintain that, in Arabic itself, such wording encompasses both groups when used without qualification.

The second view is that women are included only where there is evidence. Nevertheless, both sides agree that the Quranic verses concerning “legal rulings,” “promises of reward,” and “warnings of punishment” encompass both groups, even when expressed in the masculine form. Some proponents of this view say that both groups are included because revelation uses the wording to refer to both, even though the unqualified expression does not itself encompass them. This amounts to the first view.

Others say that they are included because we know from the religion that both groups are equal with respect to these rulings. Thus, they are included just as we are included in what was addressed to the Messenger, and just as the rest of the Muslim community is included in what was addressed to one of its members, even though the wording itself does not encompass anyone other than the addressee.

The substance of this view is that an expression particular in form is used generally, with a “literal meaning established by convention,” whether that convention is specific or general. Some may call this a manifest analogy that undermines any ruling contrary to it. Most, however, do not call it “analogy.” Rather, the equality of the addressee and others is already known, so we understand an address to him as an address to everyone else. Even if we supposed that the address did not apply to him because of something peculiar to him, this would not entail that it did not apply to others.

“Analogy” involves extending a ruling from one case to another. Here, however, no ruling has been extended; rather, the ruling is established for everyone together. It is more akin to extending the address conveying the ruling, not the ruling itself.

---

## Page 2877

On either view, then, the masculine plural forms support this conclusion, just as expressions such as “whoever,” “people of,” “people,” and the like unquestionably do.

Know that there is a second kind of indication here: generality of meaning, which is stronger than generality of wording. Allah says:

“No soul knows what joy is kept hidden for them as a reward for what they used to do.”

This “joy” has been interpreted as seeing Allah, among other things. This implies that seeing Him is a reward for their deeds. Men and women share in the deeds by which men have merited Paradise. Seeing Allah is not restricted to those who undertake activities peculiar to men, such as rulership and—according to the majority—prophethood, and the like. Rather, among the men who will see Him are those who have done nothing peculiar to men, but have confined themselves to their obligations, such as prayer, zakat, and other duties. These are shared by both groups.

Likewise, Allah says:

“Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss, looking on from their couches.”

Righteousness is the cause of this reward, and righteousness is shared by both sexes. Likewise, whenever seeing Allah is linked to a designation such as faith, this implies that it is the cause of that reward, and thus encompasses both groups.

It was through this line of reasoning that the leading scholars argued that the disbelievers will not see their Lord. They said: Since the disbelievers are veiled from Him because of His displeasure, this indicates that the believers will see Him because of His pleasure. It is well known that believing women differ from the disbelievers in what earned the latter His displeasure and exclusion from seeing Him, and share with believing men

---

## Page 2878

in that by which they have earned His pleasure and the direct vision of Him. Thus, their seeing Him is established through both direct and converse reasoning. This is a vast subject; unless we bring it to a close, it will have no end.

If it is objected: “The indication afforded by general wording is weak, for it has been said that most general expressions are subject to qualification. It has also been said that there is no general expression except His statement, ‘And He has knowledge of all things.’ Some have even denied altogether that general expressions indicate generality.”

We reply: As for generality established through meaning and reason, no one in the Muslim community has denied its evidentiary force, so far as I know—indeed, no rational person has. Nor can it be denied, unless perhaps someone among the strict literalists, who disregard meanings, adopts the position of denying it. Yet these people do not deny generality of wording; rather, it is their mainstay. Nor do they deny the generality of the meanings conveyed by general expressions. They may, however, deny that the generality of abstract meanings can be understood from another person’s speech.

We therefore know of no one who has denied both kinds of generality: that of wording and that of meaning. We have established generality through both together. There thus remains common ground concerning generality of meaning, which cannot be denied in principle. Whoever denies it closes off his own means of establishing judgments concerning numerous things. Indeed, he deprives his reason of its most distinctive property: making universal judgments. We have established generality on this basis. Scholars have, in fact, differed over whether generality of this kind admits qualification, holding two well-known views.

As for generality of wording, this too has never been denied by any leading scholar or by any group with an established school of thought

---

## Page 2879

in scholarship. Nor did anyone deny it during the first three generations. Its denial arose only after the second century and became widespread after the third. The principal cause of its denial was that some who affirmed the possibility of divine pardon, among both Ahl al-Sunnah and the Murji’ah, found themselves at a loss when those who insist on the fulfilment of divine threats—the Wa'īdiyyah—confronted them with the general wording of the verses and hadiths containing such threats. This drove them to deny generality in language and revelation. In resorting to this denial, they were like someone seeking refuge from scorching ground in a fire.

Had they only found the sound reply to the Wa'īdiyyah—that a threat, though general and unrestricted in one verse, is qualified and restricted in another, in keeping with sound principles; and that it is more appropriate to allow pardon for the person threatened, even if specifically identified, thereby restricting the unrestricted threat—or other such replies! This is not the place to expound upon that, for scholars have established generality through arguments too extensive to mention here.

Indeed, it may be said that the knowledge that generality is conveyed by its linguistic forms is self-evident from language, revelation, and customary usage. Those who deny it are a small group who may deny self-evident truths or be deprived of knowledge of them, just as this has happened to those who deny the knowledge established by mass-transmitted reports and other self-evident matters.

As for someone who concedes that generality is established and has evidentiary force, but says, “Its indication is weak,” or, “Most general expressions are subject to qualification, and no general expression remains unqualified apart from one or a few expressions,” we reply:

First: This objection has no sound basis. The point you have mentioned must either preclude arguing from generality or not preclude it. If it does preclude it,

---

## Page 2880

then that is the position of those who deny generality—those who suspend judgment and those who restrict its scope—an absurd position that has not been openly professed. If, however, it does not preclude arguing from generality, then these are empty words. At most, one could say that general expressions have weaker evidentiary force than other expressions with an apparent meaning. Yet even this is not conceded, for unless evidence establishing a qualification is forthcoming, one must act upon the general expression.

Second: Who has conceded to you that an unqualified general expression, for which no qualifying evidence has appeared, constitutes weak evidence? Who has conceded that most general expressions are qualified? Or who says that every general expression has been qualified except His words, “He has knowledge of all things”? Although some eminent scholars versed in jurisprudence may make this sweeping statement, and it may occur in the writings of some who discuss the principles of jurisprudence, it is among the falsest and most unsound of statements.

Presumably, whoever first said this meant only that the generality conveyed by the expression “all things” is qualified except in a few instances, as in His words:

“Destroying all things.”

“She has been given of all things.”

“We opened for them the gates of all things.”

Otherwise, what rational person would make this claim about every form expressing generality in the Quran and Sunnah, in all the other Books of Allah and the speech of His prophets, and in the speech of all nations, Arab and non-Arab alike?

If you read the Quran from beginning to end, you will find that most of its general expressions retain their full scope and are not qualified. This holds whether you mean the generality of a plural expression encompassing its individual members, of a whole encompassing its parts, or of a universal encompassing its particular instances.

Consider His words:

“All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.”

Can you find anyone among the worlds whose Lord is not Allah?

“Sovereign of the Day of Recompense.”

Is there anything on the Day of Recompense that is not under the dominion of

---

## Page 2881

Allah?

“Not of those who have incurred anger, nor of those who are astray.”

Is there anyone among those who have incurred anger or gone astray whose condition—the condition by which he incurred anger or went astray—need not be avoided?

“A guidance for those mindful of Allah.”

“Who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided for them”—to the end of the verse.

Is there anyone among these people mindful of Allah who has not been guided by this Book?

“And who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you.”

Is there anything Allah has revealed in which the believers have believed neither in general terms nor specifically?

“Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.”

Is any one of these people mindful of Allah excluded from guidance in this world and success in the Hereafter?

Then consider His words:

“Indeed, those who disbelieve.”

It has been said that this is a general expression whose scope has been qualified. It has also been said that it identifies a particular, known group, so no qualification is involved: qualification presupposes that the wording has an established general scope. Here many fall into error: they assume that an expression is general, then assume that some cases have been excluded from its scope. Had they examined it carefully, they would have realized from the outset that the wording never encompassed what they excluded. A distinction must therefore be drawn between the conditions for generality and what prevents it, on the one hand, and the conditions for a meaning to fall within the speaker’s intent and what prevents that, on the other.

Then consider His words:

“They will not believe.”

Does this not apply to everyone to whom the pronoun refers, with its general scope fully intact?

“Allah has set a seal upon their hearts, their hearing, and their sight.”

Does this not apply generally to their hearts, hearing, and sight, and to those to whom these are attributed, without any qualification of its scope? The same applies to “And for them.” Likewise, if you reflect upon the remaining verses, you will find the same holds true, down to His words:

“O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you.”

Who, then, is excluded from this second general expression, such that Allah did not create them for Himself? This is a vast subject.

## Page 2882

If you go through the verses of the Quran as children are taught them, you will find the same holds true. For He, glorified be He, says:

“Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind,
the King of mankind,
the God of mankind.”

Which people do not have Allah as their Lord, their King, or their God?

Then His words:

“From the evil of the retreating whisperer.”

If this designation refers to a single individual, it has no general scope. If it denotes a class, it is general. Which retreating whisperer should one not seek refuge in Allah from?

Likewise, His words:

“In the Lord of daybreak.”

Which part of “daybreak,” or which daybreak, does not have Allah as its Lord?

“From the evil of what He has created.”

What evil in creation should one not seek refuge from?

Which woman who blows on knots should one not seek refuge from?

Likewise, His words:

“And from the evil of an envier.”

The general scope of this expression does, however, involve a subtle question whose discussion does not belong here.

Then Surah al-Ikhlās contains four instances of generality:

“He neither begets”

covers every kind of begetting. The same applies to:

“Nor is He born.”

Likewise:

“And there is none comparable to Him.”

This encompasses every individual and everything that falls within the meaning of comparability. Has the scope of any of this been qualified?

Another example is the declaration of pure faith, more familiar to Muslims than any other utterance:

“There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah.”

Has its general scope ever been qualified?

Anyone who, after this, says, “There is no general expression whose scope has not been qualified, except such-and-such,” is either profoundly ignorant or extremely deficient in expressing himself. For I think he only meant “among expressions that encompass everything.” Yet this statement is unsound, even if it is interpreted

---

## Page 2883

in this way. Even so, he has expressed himself poorly, for a general expression does not mean one that encompasses everything. Rather, it encompasses everything it denotes—that is, everything the expression was coined to signify. As a rule, every expression is narrower than those above it in generality and broader than those below it, yet all may be general expressions. Moreover, most speech among the Arabs and other nations consists of general terms. Generality in language corresponds to generality in thought, which is a distinctive property of the “intellect,” the most basic distinction between human beings and beasts.

If it is objected:

We concede that the apparent meaning of the Quran and Sunnah includes women. However, this general scope is qualified, for the hadith concerning men seeing Allah on Friday states:

“The men return to their homes, where their wives greet them and say to each man, ‘You have returned more beautiful than when you left us.’ He replies, ‘Today we sat with our Lord, the Compeller, and it is only fitting that we should return as we have.’”

This indicates that women did not share in seeing Him. If this applies to seeing Him on Friday, it applies all the more to seeing Him morning and evening, since the latter is a higher privilege than the former. How could someone unfit to see Him once a week be fit to see Him twice every day?

If women do not see Him on these two occasions, and it has not been established that people see Him on any other occasion, then it has been established that women are excluded from the general scope of these texts on these two occasions. As for other occasions, this has not been established for either men or women. Thus, nothing remains to indicate that women see Him on another occasion. Either this is left unqualified, in accordance with the default presumption of nonoccurrence, or their seeing Him is denied on these two occasions and judgment is suspended concerning any others, without invoking those general expressions as evidence that they see Him on such occasions

---

## Page 2884

because their general scope has been qualified. This is the strongest possible formulation of this objection. Had it not been put to me, I would not have mentioned it, since it has no force.

We reply:

There are several answers. Their logical sequence would call for a particular order, but I shall arrange them differently to make them easier to understand.

First: Even if we supposed it established that women do not see Him on the two occasions mentioned, this would not exclude their seeing Him on other occasions. The specific evidence would thus neither affirm nor deny their seeing Him on other occasions, whereas the general evidence establishes this vision in general terms. No evidence negates their seeing Him on occasions other than these two. The general evidence therefore remains unopposed by the specific evidence and must be acted upon. This is perfectly clear.

If someone says, “I saw a man,” and another says, “You did not see a black man, nor did you see him in Damascus,” the two statements do not contradict one another. When specific evidence does not contradict the corresponding part of a general statement, it cannot be used to qualify that statement. Had there been evidence that women never see Him under any circumstances, this specific evidence would have conflicted with the corresponding part of the general evidence. But if it is said that it indicates seeing Him in a particular setting, how can this be negated by denying vision altogether? And how can negating the particular amount to negating the general?

If it is said, “The people of Paradise see Him only on these two occasions,” we reply, “What evidence establishes this?”

If it is said, “Because the default presumption is that nothing beyond this occurs,” we reply:

Nonoccurrence cannot be invoked as evidence when reporting matters of fact, as all rational people agree. Rather, anyone who asserts it speaks of what he has no knowledge of. If it were asked

---

## Page 2885

of a man, “Is such-and-such to be found in that town, and such-and-such in that mosque?” and he replied, “No, because the default presumption is that it is absent,” he would, by the agreement of all rational people, be denying something of which he has no knowledge.

Likewise, if someone else said, “Only the prophets see Allah twice each day, because the default presumption is that others do not see Him, and the prophets possess distinctions in which no others share,” this would be speaking without knowledge—if it escaped being falsehood.

Nor is there any implied restriction here upon which to rely, such as that conveyed by His saying:

“Flog them with eighty lashes.”

The Messenger did not say that the people of Paradise have two occasions for seeing Him, such that this would exclude all other occasions. Rather, his words indicate the contrary, as we shall explain. Even if we supposed that judgments in such matters could be based on the presumption of continuity, general textual evidence and analogy are two proofs that take precedence over that presumption: “general textual evidence” according to the consensus of the jurists, and “analogy” according to their overwhelming majority. It is known that “general textual evidence” and “analogy” both establish this vision, as explained above. It therefore cannot be denied on the basis of the presumption of continuity.

And if it were permissible to qualify that general scope on the grounds of women’s deficient reason, then one would have to say that the “simple-minded” and the “uncouth” among the Bedouins, and others like them who enter Paradise, do not see Allah. There is no doubt that some women possess greater reason than many men. Indeed, a woman’s testimony counts as half that of a man, whereas the testimony of a heedless man and others like him is rejected altogether, even if he is not insane.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Many men attained perfection, but only four women attained perfection.”

Those women are more perfect than men who have not attained perfection. By what reasoning, then, would vision be granted to the imperfect but not to the perfect?

---

## Page 2886

The second answer is this:

The very hadith cited as evidence indicates that the people of Paradise will see Allah on numerous occasions, for he said:

“Those highest in rank among the people of Paradise are those who see Allah twice each day, morning and evening.”

If this is for those of the highest rank, the implication is that those of lower rank have less than this. It is not permissible to restrict this lesser share to “the Friday vision,” since there is no evidence for doing so. Rather, some may see Him once every day, some once every two days, and some more often than that. Wisdom calls for this: all men share in the Friday vision—those of the highest ranks, those of intermediate ranks, and those below them—whereas seeing Him twice each day is for those of the highest ranks. Those above the lowest ranks but below the highest must therefore be distinguished from those beneath them, just as their share is less than that of those above them.

The third answer is that hadiths have been transmitted concerning seeing Allah on occasions other than these two. Among them is the report transmitted by Ibn Mājah in his Sunan and al-Dāraqutnī in al-Ruʾyah, from al-Fadl ibn ʿĪsā ibn al-Munkadir, from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“While the people of Paradise are enjoying their bliss, a light suddenly shines upon them. They raise their heads, and behold, the Lord, blessed and exalted, appears above them and says, ‘Peace be upon you, people of Paradise.’ This is what Allah says: ‘“Peace!”—a word from a Merciful Lord.’ They pay no attention to any of the bliss they are enjoying as long as Allah is in their midst, until He veils Himself from them, while His blessing and His light remain among them.”

---

## Page 2887

We have also transmitted it through another known chain reaching Salamah ibn Shabīb, who said: Bishr ibn Hajar narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd Allāh narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jābir, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“While the people of Paradise are enjoying their dominion and bliss, a light suddenly shines upon them. They raise their heads, and behold, the Lord, blessed and exalted, appears above them and says, ‘Peace be upon you, people of Paradise.’ This is His saying, blessed and exalted: ‘“Peace!”—a word from a Merciful Lord.’ They look at Him, and He looks at them. They pay no attention to any of their dominion or bliss until He veils Himself from them.” He said: “His light and blessing then remain upon them and in their dwellings.”

This chain establishes that al-Fadl al-Raqāshī was not alone in transmitting it. The general wording of this hadith implies that all of them will see Him. However, it was not cited as the initial proof because its chain of transmission is open to criticism. The point here is that this has been reported, that it is possible, and that there is no basis for ruling it out in itself. Authentic reports with general wording establish the same kind of occurrence affirmed by this hadith.

Moreover, the authentic hadith states:

“When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, a caller will announce, ‘O people of Paradise, Allah has made you a promise which He wishes to fulfill for you.’ They will say, ‘What is it? Has He not brightened our faces, made our scales heavy, admitted us to Paradise, and saved us from the Fire?’ Then the veil will be lifted, and they will look at Him. He has given them nothing dearer to them than looking at Him.”

This is not the Friday vision, because it occurs upon their entry, when they were neither expecting it nor gathered for it. For the Friday vision, however, they come from their dwellings and gather for it

---

## Page 2888

as the hadiths report. The hadiths indicate a difference between this manifestation and that one.

Nor is this manifestation one of the two occasions reserved for those of the highest ranks. Rather, it encompasses everyone who enters Paradise, as the hadith indicates, in agreement with His words:

“For those who do good is the best reward and more”—“Those are the people of Paradise.”

It has also been reported as a statement of Ibn ‘Abbās himself, and through Ka‘b al-Ahbār in a report traced back to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that “They see Him on every festival day.”

Furthermore, reports transmitted through numerous independent chains establish that He will be seen more than once on the gathering grounds of the Resurrection, before entry into Paradise. This falls outside the two occasions—unless some qualification is proposed, although he stated none, nor does anything in the question indicate it. This therefore decisively invalidates his restriction. Anyone wishing to avoid this objection should formulate the question differently from the wording given above; we have merely presented it as it was put to us.

Moreover, Allah Most High says:

“No soul knows what delights have been hidden for them.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah says: ‘I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever imagined.’”

How, then, can anyone say, “Those other than the highest-ranking will only ever see Allah once a week,” and allow that argument to pass judgment on what He has hidden from every soul and of which He has denied knowledge to every eye, ear and heart? There is a difference between not knowing and knowing that something does not exist, and between the absence of evidence and evidence of absence. If, regarding occasions other than the one in question, a person has nothing beyond a lack of knowledge and a lack of evidence, then, as a matter of necessity and consensus, this cannot preclude what the general evidence entails.

The crux of the first answer is that when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, says, “The people of

---

## Page 2889

Paradise see Allah Most High,” and explains by this His words,

“For those who do good is the best reward and more,”

through to His words,

“Those are the people of Paradise; they will abide therein forever,”

he thereby informs us that the people of Paradise will receive the “more,” which is gazing upon Him. We know that righteous women are among the people and inhabitants of Paradise, and that they outnumber men. Suppose he then tells us, for example, that men, but not women, will see Him on Friday, and also tells us that only the highest-ranking inhabitants of Paradise will see Him twice each day; and we suppose that women never see Him under any circumstances—not twice each day, nor on Friday, nor on any other occasion whatsoever.

Anyone who examines this discussion knows that there is no disagreement among scholars—or indeed among rational people—that this does not establish the denial of the vision altogether, nor does it restrict that general wording or qualify that unqualified statement. I have repeated the discussion only because the point has been disputed. It should not be thought that we have discussed it at length because it is obscure, but rather because it has been rejected despite its clarity.

You may express “this answer” in several ways.

You may say: “The hadiths affirming the vision” establish, without qualification, that both men and women will see Him. Denying a qualified instance does not negate the unqualified statement. The unqualified statement therefore remains unnegated, and what it entails may not be denied.

Or you may say: “The hadiths affirming the vision” encompass both men and women, whereas “the hadiths denying it” deny women what is known to be granted to men, or the vision on occasions when it is established to occur; or they deny women the vision on the two occasions on which people have been told it will occur. But this is a negation applying to a particular circumstance. It addresses neither occasion beyond those two, whether by denial or affirmation; and what is denied in that particular case does not contradict the general statement.

---

## Page 2890

Or, if you wish, you may say: An unqualified affirmative proposition is contradicted only by a universal negation. This, however, is not a universal negation, so it does not contradict that proposition. Nor may we disregard what either of the two pieces of evidence entails.

Or you may say: Mentioning these two occasions amounts only to not informing us of any others. Not informing us of a particular reward—whether gazing upon Him or something else—does not establish that it does not exist. How could it, when this reward is among the things Allah has kept hidden? Since the absence of a report does not establish the absence of that reward, and the generality of both the wording and the meaning either conclusively includes women or apparently does so, an absence of evidence cannot restrict the scope of existing evidence, whether apparent or conclusive. All this is not only known by self-evident reason but also agreed upon by the Muslim community, as established among scholars in both legal theory and substantive rulings.

The error arises when someone hears what the hadiths say about the vision in general, unqualified terms, then encounters other hadiths reporting a particular, qualified vision. He imagines that the general, unqualified vision occurs only in this qualified form, or, because of this possibility, denies that those general reports convey a general meaning.

This is like a man saying, “I used to welcome my companions into my house and honour them.” Then, on another occasion, he says, “On such-and-such a day, I welcomed so-and-so and so-and-so among my companions into my house.” Anyone who assumes that he did not welcome his other companions—because he did not mention them on this occasion—has erred. He would be asked, “How do you know that he did not welcome them at another time?”

If he says, “He may have welcomed them, or he may not have, so I suspend judgment,” he would be told, “But he said, ‘I used to welcome my companions into my house,’ and this encompasses all his companions.”

---

## Page 2891

And we do not dispute that “general wording” may, in principle, be intended in a restricted sense even without this contextual indication; with it, that possibility is stronger still. Our dispute, however, concerns the “apparent meaning.” We say that this less likely possibility does not prevent the wording from apparently conveying a general meaning, as explained above. Generality therefore remains its apparent meaning, even though another meaning is possible. The remaining “responses” establish that the “vision” occurs on occasions other than these two.

The fourth response: Even if we assumed that the “hadith concerning twice each day” contradicted the authentic texts cited earlier, which are general in both wording and meaning, we should not set aside what those hadiths indicate on the strength of a hadith like this. This is for the reasons already mentioned: first, its chain of transmission is open to criticism; moreover, such a restriction would exclude most of those encompassed by the general wording, which is either inadmissible or far-fetched. It would also entail making an exception to the operation of the effective cause without any impediment being present or any condition being absent—which the majority hold to be inadmissible—or without any apparent impediment, which is far-fetched and cannot be accepted without strong evidence.

The fifth response: Even if we assumed that no vision occurs except on these two occasions, on what basis could we conclude that women do not see Allah on either of them? Suppose we conceded that they do not see Him on Friday: on what basis could we conclude that they do not see Him twice each day?

As for the objection, “This is higher, and that is lower; how, then, can the one who grants the higher withhold the lower?”—there are several responses:

---

## Page 2892

The first response:

Those singled out for seeing Allah twice each day also share with the rest in seeing Him on Friday, and thus enjoy both kinds of vision. If their superiority lies in enjoying both, what prevents some of those below them from sharing with them in the “Friday vision” but not in the “morning and evening vision,” while others share with them in the “morning and evening vision” but not in the “Friday vision”? Those who enjoy the morning and evening vision without the Friday vision would not be superior in absolute terms. Rather, those who enjoy all of these are superior in absolute terms.

But it may be said: This would imply that women are superior to those men who enjoy the Friday vision but not the vision at the “two cool periods.” The reply is: This need not follow; the Friday vision alone may be better than the vision at the “two cool periods” alone.

It may also be said: Grant that this is so. At most, it entails preferring women over lower-ranking men. Although this is possible, it is far-fetched that every woman who enters Paradise should be superior to those who do not see Allah twice each day, for that would entail lower-ranking women being superior to lower-ranking men. This possibility should therefore be set aside, and we should confine ourselves to what was stated: those who enjoy the twice-daily vision together with the Friday vision are superior in absolute terms. This implication arose only because we are discussing the matter on the assumption that there is no vision apart from these two kinds. There is no doubt that this assumption is unquestionably false.

(The second response:

On what basis do you claim that “seeing Allah twice each day” is better than “seeing Him on Friday”? Certainly, it occurs more frequently, but the latter may be superior in quality. Thus, one kind may be greater in number, while the other is better in kind—as with a dinar and five dirhams

---

## Page 2893

and there is no doubt that this is an entirely plausible possibility. For Allah rewards His servant for reciting:

“Say: He is Allah, the One,”

despite its few letters, as much as He rewards him for reciting a third of the Quran. This being so, someone denied the kind that is superior in quality may be granted the inferior kind, even if the latter occurs more frequently—whether the qualitatively superior kind is superior overall or the two are equivalent when weighed against each other. The hadiths concerning the increase in bliss contain indications of this. For they return to their families having grown more handsome and beautiful, and say:

“Today we sat with our Lord, the Compeller, so it is only fitting that we should return as we have.”

Another hadith states:

“There is nothing they need more than Friday, so that they may gaze upon their Lord more and receive greater honour.”

Anyone who reflects on the context of “the aforementioned hadiths” will realize that Allah’s revealing Himself on Friday has a tremendous impact upon them, unlike anything they experience on other days. This implies that this kind of vision is superior to the vision occurring twice each day, even though the latter is more frequent. Thus, if women are denied this favour, it does not follow that they are denied what is below it. This is clear to anyone who reflects upon it.

(The third response:

Grant that seeing Allah twice each day is superior overall to seeing Him on Friday. Their being deprived of the lesser reward does not necessarily entail their being deprived of what is greater. A servant may perform a superior deed for which he deserves a tremendous reward, yet not perform a lesser deed and therefore not deserve its particular reward. Allah, glorified be He, has always singled out those of lesser rank in every category for special privileges not granted to those of higher rank. This is well established both with respect to individuals among the prophets and the steadfastly truthful, and with respect to deeds.

---

## Page 2894

And if a superior deed invariably secured all the rewards of inferior deeds, Allah would never have prescribed an inferior deed at any time. Thus, granting the higher reward does not necessarily entail granting the lower, nor does it necessarily follow that the higher must be withheld. Such a possibility is consistent with the revealed Law in the case of rewards generally. Do you not see that those occupying the highest ranks in Paradise are not granted the lower ranks, yet this constitutes no deficiency for them? Allah, glorified be He, makes every servant content with what He has given him. It is therefore possible that He has made women content with the higher form of “the vision” instead of both its higher and lower forms together.

What supports this is the possibility that the vision on Friday is a reward for deeds performed on Friday in this world, while the vision in the morning and evening is a reward for deeds performed in the morning and evening. This is rationally possible, even if no report has been transmitted to that effect. If it is possible, then withholding “the Friday vision” from women because its requisite cause is absent in their case does not entail withholding “the vision at the two cool times of day” when its requisite cause is present in their case.

It is also rationally possible that they do not attend the Friday vision simply because it is a gathering of men, and protective jealousy exists in Paradise. Do you not recall:

“When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saw Paradise and saw a palace with a young woman at its gate, he said, ‘I wanted to enter, but I remembered your protective jealousy.’ ‘Umar replied, ‘Would I be jealous of you?’”

Allah knows best the true nature of things. If that is so, this consideration does not apply to the vision in the morning and evening, because that vision may occur while the people of Paradise are in their dwellings.

Furthermore, regarding the possibility that “the vision is a reward for deeds,” reports have been transmitted indicating that the vision on Friday is a reward for attending the Friday prayer, as indicated by the fact that, during it, they will be in

---

## Page 2895

varying degrees of proximity to Him, according to how promptly they hastened to the Friday prayer. The variation in reward according to the variation in deeds indicates that the reward results from those deeds. Further evidence is the statement found in more than one hadith:

“It will take place at a time corresponding to their departure from the Friday prayer in this world.”

The correspondence between the reward and the deed, in both timing and measure, making it a fitting recompense, implies that the deed is its cause. Further evidence is that this is mentioned among the virtues of Friday in this world and the Hereafter. It is thus known that its reward in the Hereafter is linked to the deeds performed on that day in this world.

Further evidence is that, when people depart from the Friday gathering, the righteous return to their dwellings, while the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, and the martyrs return to their Lord. This corresponds to their condition in this world: when the Friday prayer is over, a righteous person occupies himself with the worldly pursuits permitted to him, whereas those others occupy themselves with drawing near to Him through voluntary acts of worship. Thus, they drew near to Him after the Friday prayer in this world, and so they will be near Him after the Friday gathering in the Hereafter.

This “evident correspondence,” borne out by consideration of comparable cases, implies that this divine manifestation is a reward for their deeds on Friday. If that is so, women’s not being granted this vision is due to their not attending the Friday prayer. Hence the report that they will see Him on Eid, just as attending the Eid prayer has been prescribed for them.

If it is said: “What you have mentioned of this additional wording is unfamiliar. The widely known, unanimously accepted hadiths do not contain this addition, so it cannot be relied upon. Everyone has heard the hadiths concerning the vision on Friday, but they have not heard this addition.”

---

## Page 2896

We reply:

We have already answered this by discussing the hadith’s chains of transmission and the standing of both its core wording and its addition. We explained that the addition’s evidentiary standing concerning the vision is not so much lower than that of the core hadith as to preclude accepting it alongside that hadith. Rather, it is either equal to it, close to it, or stronger. We have also answered what has been said here and what has not been said.

If it is said:

“Believing women used to attend the Friday prayer with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

By this reasoning, women who attended the Friday prayer should therefore attend the Day of Increase in Paradise.

We reply:

Only a small minority of women used to attend the Friday and congregational prayers, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Do not prevent Allah’s female servants from attending Allah’s mosques, though their homes are better for them.”

Agreed upon by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

He also said:

“For any one of you, praying in her private chamber is better than praying in her room; praying in her room is better than praying in her house; praying in her house is better than praying in her people’s mosque; and praying in her people’s mosque is better than praying with me—or he said: behind me.”

Reported by Abū Dāwūd.

Thus, he informed believing women that praying in their homes is better for them than attending the Friday and congregational prayers. Eid is the exception, for he commanded them to go out for it. Perhaps—and Allah knows best—this is for several reasons:

First: It occurs twice a year, so attendance was accepted, unlike attendance at the Friday and congregational prayers.

Second: It has no substitute, unlike the Friday and congregational prayers, for a woman’s Zuhr prayer at home takes the place of Friday prayer for her.

---

## Page 2897

Third: It involves going out into the open countryside to remember Allah, and thus resembles Hajj in certain respects. This is why the greater Eid, during the Hajj season, was an occasion of assembly for the pilgrims. Clearly, if the female Companions knew that praying in their homes was better for them, most of them would not have agreed to forgo what was better. Otherwise, this would mean that the best of generations engaged in the less meritorious deeds.

If it is said:

“This preference applied only to women after the female Companions, once women began behaving as they did, and because none of the prayer leaders after the Messenger is his equal. As for the female Companions, praying behind the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was better for them. This would therefore be a general address from which the first generation was excepted, since restricting the scope of a general statement is permissible.”

We reply:

This contradicts what is self-evidently known about the languages of Arabs and non-Arabs, what is self-evidently known from the religion of the Muslims, the natural disposition Allah has given rational people, and the consensus of the Muslims.

For concerning his words:

“Do not prevent Allah’s female servants from attending Allah’s mosques, though their homes are better for them,”

the Muslims unanimously agree that those present were certainly included. They differed concerning the second and third generations: were they included by the address itself, or by separate evidence? There are two views on this. But all agree that including those absent while excluding those present is impossible.

Language itself also rules this out, for his words:

“Do not prevent Allah’s female servants”

were undoubtedly addressed first and foremost to the Companions—may Allah be pleased with them. How, then, does language rule out their being excluded from it while those who came after them are included? Those versed in language have no doubt that this is impossible.

---

## Page 2898

Moreover, we know with certainty that the commands of the Quran and Sunnah applied to the Companions and then to those who came after them. It may be said or imagined that some of these commands applied to the Companions alone, rather than to later generations. But commands conveyed through direct address applying exclusively to later generations, to the exclusion of the Companions, have no existence.

As for its contradiction of “natural dispositions,” no person of sound mind could be presented with this claim without rejecting it most vehemently. Even supposing this were possible in the case of his words:

“Do not prevent Allah’s female servants from attending Allah’s mosques,”

what, then, of his words:

“The prayer of any one of you in her community’s mosque is better than her prayer with me—or behind me”?

Does this not explicitly refer to their praying in their homes and to their praying behind the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in his mosque? May Allah bless Muhammad.

## Page 2899

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

What is meant by “meeting Allah, glorified is He”? He describes the humbly submissive as being assured of it in His words:

“Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and that to Him they will return.”

He commands the God-fearing to know it in His words:

“Fear Allah and know that you will meet Him.”

He gives glad tidings to the patient who acknowledge it when calamity strikes, and indicates to those who hope for it that its appointed time will surely come, saying:

“Whoever hopes to meet Allah—indeed, the time appointed by Allah is surely coming.”

It is also frequently mentioned in the words of the foremost of the messengers, in numerous hadiths, such as his words in supplication:

“Meeting You is true,”

and his words:

“Whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him; and whoever hates to meet Allah, Allah hates to meet him”—to the end of the hadith.

Is the statement of some Quran commentators correct that this requires an omitted expression, understood as “the recompense of their Lord” or something similar, on the grounds that meeting cannot truly be ascribed to Allah Most High, so that its apparent meaning is impossible, something other than its apparent meaning must be intended, and a particular interpretation must therefore be adopted? Or does it have no need of this, since such a meeting is possible in itself?

How can we conceive of loving One whom we neither know nor behold? How can we yearn for Him, our hearts long for Him, and prefer Him over everything else that we know and that our hearts are accustomed to—things that bring us immediate benefit and pleasure we already experience?

---

## Page 2900

‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said, “Disliking death? We all dislike death.” He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, corrected her understanding with the explanation contained in the hadith: “The believer sees the bliss awaiting him with Allah, and so Allah loves to meet him”—to the end of the hadith.

This, however, raises a question: if his love of that meeting is due to the bliss he has seen, then his love is for the bliss that he himself will enjoy, not simply for meeting Allah Most High. How, then, is he rewarded with Allah Most High loving to meet him, when his love is not pure, and Allah accepts only deeds that are pure in intention? Please clarify these matters for us with a sound and sufficient answer that fully resolves the question, seeking the abundant reward, if Allah Most High wills.

He replied—may Allah be pleased with him and grant him His pleasure:

Praise be to Allah.

As for “meeting,” a group of the early and later scholars explained it as involving seeing and beholding after travelling and journeying. They said that meeting Allah includes seeing Him, glorified and exalted is He. They cited the verses concerning “meeting” against those Jahmiyyah, such as the Mu‘tazilah and others, who deny that Allah will be seen in the Hereafter.

It is reported that ‘Abdullāh ibn al-Mubārak said, concerning His words:

“So whoever hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and associate no one in the worship of his Lord,”

“He must not show off,” or he said, “He must not tell anyone about it.”

They understood meeting to encompass two meanings: first, journeying to the king; and second, beholding him. As He says:

“O mankind,

---

## Page 2901

you are indeed toiling laboriously towards your Lord, and you will meet Him.”

He thus mentions that man toils towards Allah and then meets Him. Toiling towards Him entails following a path and journeying towards Him, and the meeting follows these. Merely beholding something without journeying towards it—as when beholding the sun and moon—is not called a meeting. “Meeting” may also mean reaching something, and what it means to reach something depends on its nature.

Evidence for this is that Allah Most High says:

“When you meet an enemy force, stand firm.”

“When you meet those who disbelieve advancing for battle, do not turn your backs on them.”

He also says:

“When they meet those who believe, they say, ‘We believe’; but when they are alone with their devils, they say, ‘We are with you’”—to the end of the verse.

And He says:

“When they meet those who believe, they say, ‘We believe’; but when they are alone with one another, they say, ‘Do you tell them what Allah has disclosed to you?’”

And He says:

“And when you met, He made them appear few in your eyes and made you appear few in theirs.”

Allah Most High also says:

“There was a sign for you in the two forces that met: one fighting in the way of Allah and the other disbelieving. They saw them with their own eyes as twice their number.”

In the two Sahīh collections, it is reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Do not wish to meet the enemy, and ask Allah for well-being. But when you meet them, remain steadfast.”

The two Sahīh collections also relate that Abū Hurayrah met the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on one of the streets of Medina while he was in a state of major ritual impurity. He slipped away and went to bathe. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, noticed his absence. When he returned, he asked, “Where were you?”

He replied, “O Messenger of Allah, you met me while I was in a state of major ritual impurity, and I did not wish to sit with you until I had bathed.”

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “Glory be to Allah! A believer does not become impure.”

In another wording:

---

## Page 2902

“I met the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

Muslim also relates it from Hudhayfah: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, met him while he was in a state of major ritual impurity,” followed by an account to the same effect.

In Sahīh Muslim, Buraydah reports:

“When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, appointed a commander over an army or a detachment, he would personally enjoin him to fear Allah and treat the Muslims accompanying him well. He would then say: ‘Fight in the name of Allah, in the cause of Allah. Fight those who disbelieve in Allah. Fight, but do not misappropriate the spoils, mutilate, or kill a child. When you encounter your enemy from among the polytheists, offer them three options.’”

The hadith continues.

In the hadith of ʿUtbah ibn ʿUbayd, he reports that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Those slain are of three kinds. The first is a believer who strives with his wealth and his life in Allah’s cause, then encounters an enemy and fights them until he is killed. That is the martyr who exults in Allah’s tent beneath the shade of His Throne. None surpass him except the prophets, by virtue of their rank of prophethood.

“The second is a man who fears for himself because of his sins and transgressions. He strives with his life and wealth in Allah’s cause, then encounters the enemy and fights until he is killed. This is a cleansing beneath his sins and transgressions. Indeed, the sword effaces sins. He is admitted through whichever gate of Paradise he wishes, for it has eight gates, while Hell has seven gates, and some are superior to others.

“The third is a hypocrite who strives with his life and wealth, then encounters the enemy and fights in Allah’s cause until he is killed. That man is in the Fire. Indeed, the sword does not efface hypocrisy.”

Ahmad and Abū Hātim, in his Sahīh, related it. Examples of this are numerous in Arabic speech, such as the poet’s words:

“Whenever you meet, send back the one …
you hope for, and Abū al-Sanl.”

---

## Page 2903

And “meeting” is used of meeting an enemy, a friend, someone beloved, or someone disliked. It may also describe direct physical contact and touching, involving pleasure or pain, as in his saying:

“When the two circumcised parts meet, a full ritual bath becomes obligatory.”

And in the authentic hadith:

“When he sits between her four limbs and the two circumcised parts touch, a full ritual bath becomes obligatory.”

Similar examples include His sayings:

“Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you.”

“So Allah will protect them from the evil of that Day and grant them radiance and joy.”

“Those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber for their patience, and will be received there with greetings and peace.”

One also says that someone has encountered good or encountered evil. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“You will encounter favouritism after me, so be patient until you meet me at the Cistern.”

It may be said that “meeting” in such instances includes the meaning of witnessing, as Allah Most High says:

“You had certainly longed for death before you encountered it; now you have seen it.”

This is because a person witnesses these things himself. It has been said that death itself is witnessed and plainly seen; others have said that what is seen are its causes.

The Quran and Sunnah also contain expressions akin to “meeting Allah,” such as His sayings:

“You have certainly come to Us alone, just as We created you the first time.”

“If only you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord. He will say, ‘Is this not the truth?’ They will say, ‘Yes, by our Lord.’”

“They will be presented before your Lord in ranks: ‘You have certainly come to Us just as We created you the first time.’”

“Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful.”

“When he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, but finds Allah there, who settles his account in full.”

And His saying: “No! There is no
