## Page 2950

He was asked:

About people who claim that they see Allah with their own eyes in this world, and that they obtain without asking what Moses obtained by asking.

He replied:

The “early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars” unanimously agreed that the believers will see Allah with their own eyes in the Hereafter. They also unanimously agreed that they do not see Him with their own eyes in this world. Their only disagreement concerned the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace).

It is established in the authentic hadith collection that he said:

“Know that none of you will see his Lord until he dies.”

Anyone who says that the friends of Allah or others see Allah with their own eyes in this world is a misguided innovator, opposing the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community. This is especially so if they claim to be superior to Moses. Such people are to be called upon to repent; unless they repent, they are to be put to death. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 2951

The shaykh, imam and erudite scholar, Shaykh al-Islām Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah be pleased with him—was asked:

What do the esteemed scholars and leading authorities in religion—may Allah be pleased with them all—say concerning the hadith that al-Bukhārī cited as supporting evidence in his Sahīh, namely the statement of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Allah, Mighty and Majestic, calls out in a voice that those far away hear just as those nearby do: ‘I am the King; I am the Judge’”?

And concerning his statement (peace be upon him) in the well-known hadith:

“Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ‘O Adam, rise and send forth those destined for the Fire.’ Then comes a call in a voice: ‘Allah commands you to send forth those destined for the Fire.’”

Some people have said: “An attribute of Allah cannot be established on the basis of a single hadith.” What, then, is the answer to this question, drawing upon the Quran, the Sunnah, transmitted reports, reasoned argument, examples and analogous cases? Please explain this matter at length and give us a ruling. May you be rewarded.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. The fundamental principle in “this subject” is that a person must speak only with knowledge. Although this is commanded in all matters, it is even more obligatory in this subject. Allah Most High says:

“Say:

---

## Page 2952

‘My Lord has only forbidden shameful deeds, whether open or secret, sin, unjust aggression, associating with Allah anything for which He has sent down no authority, and saying about Allah what you do not know.’”

Allah Most High also says:

“He only commands you to commit evil and shameful deeds, and to say about Allah what you do not know.”

And He says:

“Do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge.”

And He says:

“O People of the Scripture, do not exceed the bounds in your religion, nor say anything about Allah except the truth.”

And He says:

“Was not the covenant of the Scripture taken from them, that they would say nothing about Allah except the truth?”

Just as a person may not affirm anything without knowledge, neither may he deny anything without knowledge. Thus, the burden of proof rests upon the one who denies, just as it rests upon the one who affirms.

Another principle that must be understood is that “proofs of the truth do not contradict one another.” When Allah reports something—whether affirming or denying—it is impossible for another of His reports to contradict that first report. Nor can anything understood through reason independently of revelation contradict what that report conveys.

Proofs that yield knowledge cannot contradict one another, whether both are based on revelation, both are rational, or one is based on revelation and the other is rational. Contradiction may, however, arise between things that some people suppose to be proofs but are not. Someone may hear a report and suppose it to be authentic when it is not, or understand it to mean something it does not indicate. Or a specious argument may occur to him which he supposes to be a rational proof, though it is false: truth has become confused with falsehood in his mind, and on that basis he rejects what Allah and His Messenger have reported.

This is one of the reasons why those who reject the messengers go astray: either by rejecting them altogether, as did those who rejected all the messengers, such as the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd and others like them; or by believing in some and disbelieving

---

## Page 2953

in others, such as those among the People of the Scripture who believed in some messengers but not others, and those among the philosophers who believed in some of what the messengers brought but not all of it. Some innovators within the religious communities—Muslims, Jews and Christians—have fallen into error in this way. Specious arguments arose in their minds which they thought disproved what the messengers had conveyed concerning Allah Most High’s names and attributes. They therefore supposed that they were obliged to give their own views precedence over the revealed texts. These specious arguments have been discussed at length elsewhere, where the errors of the philosophically inclined Jahmiyyah, the Muʿtazilah, and those misguided followers who agreed with them have been explained.

The guiding principle in affirming the divine attributes is to uphold the position of the early generations of this Ummah and its leading scholars: Allah is to be described as He described Himself and as His Messenger described Him, while safeguarding this description against distortion, likening Him to creation, specifying how His attributes are, or negating them. Nothing is like Allah in His essence, His attributes or His actions. Whoever denies His attributes negates them, and whoever likens His attributes to those of His creatures likens Him to creation. What is required is to affirm His attributes while denying that they resemble the attributes of created beings: affirmation without likening Him to creation, and declaring His transcendence without negating His attributes. As Allah Most High says:

“There is nothing like Him”

—this refutes those who liken Him to creation—

“and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing”

—this refutes those who negate His attributes. Thus, whoever likens Him to creation worships an idol, while whoever negates His attributes worships a nonentity.

“The way of the messengers”—may Allah’s blessings be upon them—is to affirm Allah’s attributes of perfection in detail and to declare, in general terms, that He bears no likeness to creation. Their way is therefore “detailed affirmation” and “general negation.” The heretics among the philosophers, the Qarāmitah, the Jahmiyyah and others like them follow the opposite course: detailed negation and general affirmation.

---

## Page 2954

Thus Allah Most High states in His Book that He “has knowledge of all things,” “has power over all things,” and is “Most Forgiving, Most Merciful,” “Almighty, All-Wise,” and “All-Hearing, All-Seeing”; that He “created the heavens and the earth and everything between them in six days, then rose over the Throne”; that He “loves those who fear Him,” is pleased with the believers and angry with the disbelievers; and that He “does whatever He wills.” He also states that He spoke directly to Moses, called to him from the right side of the Mount, and brought him near for a private conversation; and that He will call to His servants, saying: “Where are My partners whom you used to claim?” There are many other such statements.

Allah Most High also says:

“There is nothing like Him.”

“Do you know of any equal to Him?”

“And there is none comparable to Him.”

He thereby makes clear that Allah has no likeness, equal or peer. Thus none of His attributes can resemble any attribute of created beings, nor can any created being equal or rival Him in any of His attributes—glorified and exalted is He.

The heretics, however, have reversed this approach, likening Him to nonexistent things, impossibilities and contradictions. Their extremists say: He is neither living nor dead, neither knowing nor ignorant, neither hearing nor deaf, neither speaking nor mute. Indeed, they may even say: He is neither existent nor nonexistent, neither something nor not something.

Others say: He is neither inside the world nor outside it, neither separate from the world nor indwelling within it. They use similar expressions to negate mutually opposed alternatives that cannot both be absent. Thus the leading exponents among them say that He is absolute existence.

Some of them then say: He is absolute existence, either with absoluteness stipulated—as maintained by Ibn

---

## Page 2955

Sīnā and his followers—even though they have established in “logic” what all rational people know: that what is absolute with absoluteness stipulated exists only in the mind, not in concrete reality. Their claim thus amounts to saying that the Necessary Existent does not exist in external reality, although they acknowledge what rational people do not dispute: that existence necessarily includes a being whose existence is necessary in itself.

Others say that He is absolute without any stipulation—as al-Qūnawī and others maintain. They identify Him with the “existence” predicated of the necessary and the contingent, the one and the many, the mental and the external, the eternal and the originated. He would therefore be either an attribute of created things, a part of them, or those very things themselves.

The former group identify Him with abstract “existence,” unrestricted by any qualification. This entails that He is neither necessary nor contingent, neither knowing nor ignorant, neither powerful nor powerless. Yet they also say that He is intellective and intelligible, lover and beloved. Thus they contradict themselves in their misguidance, making one into two and two into one. Likewise, they seek to affirm an existence stripped of every attribute and unrestricted by any qualification, yet they distinguish it by what belongs to no other existent.

For this reason, some of them say that the knower and knowledge are one, and that He is knowledge itself. They thus identify the knower by himself with the knower through another, and the bearer of an attribute with the attribute itself. Their contradictions are even greater than those of the Christians in their “Trinity” and “union,” through which they corrupted faith in divine oneness and the prophetic message.

---

## Page 2956

The statements of Ibn Sab'īn, Ibn Rushd the Younger, Ibn al-Tūmart, Ibn 'Arabī al-Tā'ī, and others like them among the Jahmiyyah—those who deny the divine attributes—revolve around this principle, as has been explained at length elsewhere. Something approaching this union is also found in the statements of many speculative theologians and Sufis, into whose thought certain strands of the doctrine of union had entered without their realizing the corruption they contained.

The discussion of “the question of Allah Most High’s speech,” and people’s confusion concerning it, rest upon this principle, for it is one of “the questions concerning the divine attributes.” It has ramifications that distinguish it from all the other questions concerning the attributes. People have fallen into great confusion over it, as we have explained elsewhere. We have also explained that “the early generations of the Muslim community and its imams” adhered to the faith with which Allah sent His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They described Allah as He described Himself and as His Messenger described Him, without distorting or denying His attributes, specifying their modality, or likening them to those of creation.

They affirmed that the Quran is the speech of Allah Most High. They attributed to Allah the speaking, private discourse, and calling with which He described Himself, as well as what the Prophetic traditions and transmitted reports affirm in accordance with the Book of Allah Most High.

None of the Companions, those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment, or the other imams of the Muslims said that Allah’s speech is created—that He created it in something other than Himself, with no speech subsisting in Him—as the “Jahmiyyah” among the Mu'tazilah and others claimed. Rather, when they openly introduced this innovation, the early generations and the imams condemned it vehemently. They recognized that its true implication was that Allah neither speaks, commands, nor forbids, for speech, like every other attribute, is predicated only of the one in whom it subsists.

---

## Page 2957

Thus, if He were to create speech in the tree—“Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me”—that would be the tree’s speech, and the tree itself would be saying, “Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me.” This would be like the speech uttered by people’s skins when their owners ask them, “Why have you testified against us?” They will reply, “Allah, who causes all things to speak, has caused us to speak.” Likewise, the Most High said, “And We subjected the mountains to glorify Us along with David.”

If His speaking meant that He created speech in something other than Himself, then all speech in existence would be His speech, since He is its Creator. Indeed, the proponents of divine indwelling among the Jahmiyyah explicitly stated this, as in the verse attributed to Ibn ‘Arabī, the author of al-Fusūs and al-Futūhāt:

All speech in existence is His speech;
Prose or verse—to us it is the same.

It is known that when Allah creates knowledge, power, movement, or will in a particular entity, that entity is the one that knows, has power, moves, or wills. Thus, if His speech were nothing but what He creates in something other than Himself, that other thing would be the one speaking it. This is discussed at length in its proper place.

The well-known specious argument of those who deny divine speech is that they believed “speech” to be an attribute that can exist only through an act subsisting in the speaker. Thus, if the Lord spoke, attributes and actions would subsist in Him, and they alleged that this was impossible.

They said: “For we inferred that the world came into being only by establishing that bodies came into being; and we inferred that bodies came into being from the accidents subsisting in them—that is, their attributes and actions. If attributes and actions subsisted in the Lord, it would necessarily follow that He too had come into being, and the proof by which we established that the world came into being and that the Maker exists would be invalidated.”

---

## Page 2958

The adherents of the Sunnah who affirm the divine attributes replied to them:

“Your argument is an innovation in religion; none of the early generations of this community or its leading scholars used it. Indeed, al-Ash‘arī stated in his ‘Epistle to the People of the Frontier’ that this argument is forbidden in the religion of the Messengers and that the religion of the Muslims must not be founded upon it. Others stated that it is rationally invalid, just as it is religiously forbidden, and that when the early generations and leading scholars condemned the speculative theologians, the Jahmiyyah, and those who engaged in speculation about accidents and bodies, their foremost intention was to condemn arguments such as this. This has been discussed at length in its proper place.”

After “the doctrine of the Jahmiyyah” emerged, “Abū Muhammad ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb” appeared, agreeing with the early generations and leading scholars in affirming “Allah’s attributes and His exaltedness above His creation.” He explained that His “exaltedness above His creation” is known through reason, whereas His “rising over the Throne” is known through revelation. Likewise, al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī, Abū al-‘Abbās al-Qalānisī, and other speculative theologians who affiliated themselves with the Sunnah and hadith came after him.

Then “Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī” came and followed the approach of Ibn Kullāb and others like him. In his books, he outlined the doctrines of the adherents of the Sunnah and hadith, noting that Ibn Kullāb agreed with most of them. These men are called “the Sifātiyyah” (affirmers of the divine attributes), because they affirm Allah’s attributes, in opposition to the Mu‘tazilah. However, “Ibn Kullāb and his followers” did not affirm that acts connected to Allah’s will and power subsist in Him, nor did they affirm anything else connected to His will and power as subsisting in Him.

The “Mu‘tazilah” would say: “Neither accidents nor temporally originated occurrences inhere in Him.” By “accidents,” they do not mean only diseases and afflictions; rather, they mean attributes. Nor do they mean

---

## Page 2959

by “temporally originated occurrences” created things, or events that alter the subject in which they occur, or similar things that people mean by this expression. Rather, they mean to deny any acts or other matters connected to His will and power. They therefore deny that there can subsist in Him any act of creating, rising over the Throne, coming, arriving, speaking, calling out, speaking privately, or anything else that He is described as willing and having power to do.

Ibn Kullāb disagreed with their statement, “No accidents subsist in Him.” He said, “Attributes subsist in Him, but they are not called accidents.” Yet he agreed with what they intended by saying, “No temporally originated occurrences subsist in Him”: namely, that nothing connected to His will subsists in Him.

From the time he drew this distinction, those who affiliated themselves with the Sunnah and the community—who held that the Quran is uncreated, that Allah will be seen in the Hereafter, and that Allah is above His heavens, over His Throne, distinct from His creation—came to hold two positions, mentioned by al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī and others.

One group agreed with Ibn Kullāb, including al-Qalānisī, al-Ashʿarī, Abū al-Hasan ibn Mahdī al-Tabarī, and their followers. Many followers of the four imams and others agreed with these men, including adherents of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abū Hanīfah, and others.

Al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī used to agree with him, but it was later said that he withdrew his agreement. Ahmad ibn Hanbal had instructed people to shun al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī and other followers of Ibn Kullāb when they openly expressed this position, just as al-Sarī al-Saqatī instructed al-Junayd to beware of some of al-Hārith’s statements. They reported that al-Hārith—may Allah have mercy on him—repented of this. He possessed knowledge and virtue

---

## Page 2960

and asceticism, and was renowned for his discourses on spiritual realities. Abū Bakr al-Kalābādhī, author of Maqālāt al-Sūfiyyah (The Doctrines of the Sufis), reported that he used to say that Allah speaks with sound. This accords with the account that he abandoned Ibn Kullāb’s position.

Abū Bakr al-Kalābādhī said:

“A group of Sufis said: ‘Allah’s speech consists of letters and sound, and speech is known only in this form,’ while affirming that it is an attribute of Allah inherent in His Essence and that it is uncreated.” He said: “This is the position of al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī and, among later scholars, Ibn Sālim.”

This principle continued to be debated until it occasioned a dispute between Abū Bakr ibn Khuzaymah, known as the Imam of Imams, and some of his companions. He learned that they had agreed with Ibn Kullāb, so he forbade them from doing so, censured them, and criticized Ibn Kullāb’s doctrine on grounds well known among the imams of hadith and the Sunnah.

From that time onward, those who affiliated themselves with the Sunnah disputed whether Allah speaks with sound or not. Ibn Kullāb’s followers denied this, saying that speaking with sound entails an act subsisting in the speaker and connected to his will. In their view, nothing connected to Allah’s will and power can subsist in Him, whether an act or anything else. They therefore said:

“Allah does not speak with sound. Rather, His speech is a single meaning that is command, prohibition, and statement. If expressed in Arabic, it is the Quran; if expressed in Hebrew, it is the Torah; and if expressed in Syriac, it is the Gospel.”

The majority of rational people, both among the adherents of the Sunnah and others, said that this view is known to be

---

## Page 2961

false by the self-evident dictates of reason, just as it contradicts the Book and the Sunnah. We know that when the Torah is translated into Arabic, it does not become the Quran; indeed, its meanings are not those of the Quran. We know that when the Quran is translated into Hebrew, it does not become the Torah revealed to Moses. We also know that the meaning of the verse on debt is not the meaning of the Verse of the Footstool, nor is the meaning of “May the hands of Abū Lahab perish” the meaning of “Say, ‘He is Allah, One.’”

They said: Whoever regards commands and prohibitions as attributes of speech rather than types of speech holds a position whose falsity is self-evident. This is akin to the position of those who profess the unity of existence. Whoever holds that existence is one and the same entity, both necessary and contingent, makes a claim whose falsity is self-evident. The same applies to whoever regards the meanings of speech as a single meaning that is command, prohibition, and statement.

Rather, speech is divided into non-declarative utterances and statements. Non-declarative utterances are divided into requests to act and requests to refrain from acting; statements are divided into negative and affirmative statements. Likewise, that which exists is divided into the necessary and the contingent. The contingent is divided into a living entity subsisting in itself and an entity subsisting in another. What subsists in another is divided into that which requires life and that which does not require life.

Thus, the term “one” may signify oneness in kind or oneness as an individual entity. Saying “Speech is a single meaning” is like saying “Existence is one.” If the speaker means that it is one kind, one genus, one category, or the like, this is not the same as meaning that it is a single entity, a single essence, and a single individual. For this is a willful denial

---

## Page 2962

of sense perception, reason, and revelation. As for the former, what is meant is that these things share something in common, just as existing things share in what is designated by “existence,” and the various types of speech share in what is designated by “speech.” All of this has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Then another group recognized the falsity of Ibn Kullāb’s position on speech, yet agreed with his fundamental premise that nothing connected with Allah’s will and power subsists in Him. They also held that the Quran is Allah’s uncreated speech. Since they recognized only two possibilities—something eternal, unconnected with Allah’s will and power, or something created and separate from Him—they were compelled to say that Allah speaks with a sound, or sounds, that are eternal and beginningless, unconnected with His will and power; and that He has always been, and will always be, characterized by those eternal, beginningless sounds inseparable from His essence.

This position is attributed to Abū al-Hasan ibn Sālim, the teacher of Abū Tālib al-Makkī—if the attribution to him is authentic. It is, however, the position of many followers of Ibn Sālim and those who agreed with them among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others.

The Karrāmiyyah, together with a large group among the Murjiʾah, the Shia, and others, said that Allah speaks with sounds that subsist in Him and are connected with His will and power, and that temporal occurrences connected with His will and power subsist in Him. However, they held that this comes into being after not having existed; that in pre-eternity Allah was not a speaker except in the sense of having the power to speak; and that He comes to be characterized by what occurs through His power and will after not having been so characterized. These people considered themselves to agree with the community that Allah has acts subsisting in Him which are connected with His will and power, and that, besides these, there subsist in Him volitions and speech connected with His will

---

## Page 2963

and power. But they said: A succession of temporal occurrences cannot take place in Him, for whatever is subject to such a succession must itself have originated. They agreed with the Muʿtazilah in using this argument to establish that the world had a beginning.

Just as Ibn Kullāb distinguished between accidents and temporal occurrences, these people distinguished between temporal occurrences arising anew and their being inseparable from Him. They denied that such occurrences were inseparable from Him, without denying that they arise in Him—just as they said that created things separate from Him come into existence, after not having existed, through His will and power.

The eternalist philosophers demand that all these groups explain what causes temporal occurrences to arise after not having existed. They argue that this entails giving one alternative precedence without a determining factor, and temporal occurrences arising without a newly occurring cause. They say that this is impossible according to clear reason. This is their most formidable specious argument for “the eternity of the world”—a thorny predicament and an overwhelming difficulty. These groups found themselves unable to answer them, to the point that they resorted to concessions.

We have discussed this at length elsewhere and set out “the decisive answers” to the philosophers’ arguments according to the approach of the early generations and the imams. We have explained that whoever affirms what the texts of the Quran and Sunnah entail can engage the philosophers in rational debate and decisively refute them, and will recognize that sound reason accords with authentic revelation.

We have also explained how “each of the groups within the Muslim community” can answer them. Since these groups are closer to the truth than the philosophers, they can answer them by showing what necessarily follows from the philosophers’ own premises, in a way the philosophers cannot evade. They can say to the philosophers: “Your position is more evidently false, according to revelation and reason, than the position of any Muslim group.” Thus, each Muslim group can say to them:

---

## Page 2964

“If the only way we can give you a conclusive answer that dispels your specious argument—apart from an answer based on your own premises—is either to agree with you in something contrary to revelation and reason, or to agree with our fellow Muslims in something that does not contradict revelation—and may not contradict reason either—then the latter is preferable.”

The philosophers saw an opportunity to prevail over the various Muslim groups because of the innovations each group had introduced. They seized upon each group’s innovation and used it as an argument against them. Someone holding such an innovated position could therefore say:

“I would rather abandon this innovated position and agree with what the Quran, the Sunnah, and the statements of the early generations of the Muslim community indicate than agree with the philosophers on a position that I know constitutes disbelief according to revelation, and whose falsity reason also demonstrates.”

“As for the early generations and the imams,” none of them is reported to have held that the Quran is created; nor that it is a single meaning subsisting in His essence, which is at once command, prohibition, and statement, and which is what the Torah, the Gospel, the Quran, and other verbal expressions signify; nor that it consists of eternal, beginningless sounds unrelated to His will and power; nor that Allah did not speak until He brought speech into being for Himself, thereby becoming one who speaks.

As for the claim that people’s voices when reciting the Quran, or their utterances, are eternal and beginningless, this too is among the “newly introduced innovations” whose falsity is more evident than that of others. The early generations and the imams are among those furthest removed from this position. Sound reason recognizes that the claim that people’s voices are eternal and beginningless is self-evidently false.

---

## Page 2965

However, this originated in their dispute over the “question of utterance.” The explicitly recorded position of Imam Ahmad and other scholars of his standing is that whoever says that uttering and reciting the Quran are created is a Jahmī, while whoever says that they are uncreated is an innovator. This is because “utterance and recitation” may mean the words uttered and recited, which are Allah’s speech. Whoever regards Allah’s speech, which He sent down to His Prophet, as created is a Jahmī. These expressions may also refer to the act itself and to human attributes. Whoever regards human actions and voices as uncreated is therefore a misguided innovator.

This is also how al-Ashʿarī reported the position of the people of the Sunnah and hadith in his book al-Maqālāt (Accounts of Doctrines). He said:

“They say that the Quran is uncreated speech, and that discussing the positions concerning suspension of judgment and utterance is an innovation. Whoever adopts either the position concerning utterance or that of suspending judgment is an innovator. According to them, one should neither say that uttering the Quran is created nor say that it is uncreated.”

None of the imams or the early generations said that Allah does not speak with a voice. Rather, it is firmly established from more than one of them that Allah speaks with a voice. This is conveyed in well-known reports from the early generations and the imams. They would relate the reports mentioning Allah’s speaking with a voice, and none of them rejected those reports. Indeed, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ahmad said:

“I said to my father, ‘Some people say that Allah does not speak with a voice.’ He replied, ‘My son, these people are Jahmīs; all their arguments revolve around denying the divine attributes.’”

He then mentioned some of the reports transmitted on this subject. Al-Bukhārī’s statements in The Creation of Actions explicitly affirm that Allah speaks with a voice and distinguish between Allah’s voice and human voices. He cited several hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on this subject. Likewise, in his Sahīh, he included a chapter on the words of the Most High:

---

## Page 2966

“Until, when fear is removed from their hearts, they say, ‘What has your Lord said?’ They say, ‘The truth.’ And He is the Most High, the Most Great.”

He cited evidence that Allah speaks with a voice. That is the extent of the point. Just as this is the recognized position among the “people of the Sunnah and hadith,” it is also the position of the great majority of the Muslim community’s groups. Most of these “groups” affirm that Allah speaks with a voice, despite their disagreement over whether His speech is created or subsists in Him; whether it is eternal or originated in time; or whether He has always spoken whenever He wills.

This is the position of the Muʿtazilah, the Karrāmiyyah, the Shīʿah, most of the Murjiʾah, the Sālimiyyah, and others among the Hanafīs, Mālikīs, Shāfiʿīs, Hanbalīs, and Sufis.

Among the Muslim groups, none denied that Allah speaks with a voice except Ibn Kullāb and his followers. Likewise, none maintained that speech is a single meaning subsisting in the speaker except him and his followers. Nor did any Muslim group maintain that people’s voices when reciting the Quran are eternal and beginningless, that an eternal voice is heard from people, or that we ourselves hear “the Quran” from Allah, except a small group claiming affiliation with the people of hadith among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, Dāwūd, and others.

No Muslim maintains that the written letter formed by the ink in copies of the Quran is eternal and beginningless. Thus, affirming “letters and voice” in the sense that the ink and people’s voices are eternal is a false innovation that none of the imams espoused. Likewise, denying that Allah speaks with a voice and treating His speech as a single meaning subsisting within Him is a false innovation that none of the early generations or the imams espoused. What the “early generations and the imams” agreed upon is that the Quran is Allah’s speech, sent down and uncreated

---

## Page 2967

—from Him it originated, and to Him it will return. The early generations said, “From Him it originated,” because the Jahmiyyah—among the Muʿtazilah and others—used to say that He created speech in a locus. The early generations therefore said, “From Him it originated,” meaning that He Himself spoke it: it originated from Him, not from any created being. As Allah Most High says:

“The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

And He Most High says:

“But the word from Me will come into effect.”

And He Most High says:

“Those who have been given knowledge see that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth.”

And He Most High says:

“Say, ‘The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth.’”

Their statement, “To Him it will return,” means that it will be taken away from people’s hearts and from copies of the Quran, so that not a single verse or letter of it will remain in their hearts, as related in several reports.
